title: Maîtriser le français, pas à pas
description: A practical French curriculum in eight modules: precise rules with their exceptions, realistic examples, and targeted correction practice.

modules.title: Les bases de la grammaire
modules.description: Build accurate sentences with articles, gender, agreement, comparison, and reference.

lessons.title: Les articles et le genre grammatical
lessons.summary: Every French noun carries a gender, so store it with its determiner. Use `le/la/l’/les` for an identified item or a whole category, `un/une/des` for a countable item introduced for the first time, and `du/de la/de l’` for an unspecified amount. After `parler`, the article is normally dropped (`parler français`), although `parler le français` is also correct; after `aimer`, `étudier`, `apprendre`, and `détester`, the definite article stays.
objectives: Record every new noun as a complete group: determiner plus noun plus gender marker.
Decide between a definite, indefinite, and partitive article from the meaning you intend.
Recognise which verbs impose their own article pattern.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: A determiner is the small word placed before a noun: `le`, `une`, `des`, `du`. French common nouns normally need a determiner, though some constructions omit it, as in `sans rendez-vous`. Memorise each noun with an article to retain its gender. A definite article (`le`, `la`, `l’`, `les`) points to something already identified or to a category as a whole. An indefinite article (`un`, `une`, `des`) introduces a countable item not yet identified. A partitive article (`du`, `de la`, `de l’`) presents an unmeasured portion of something uncountable.

Ask two questions in order. First: is the noun countable here? If yes, choose between `un/une/des` and `le/la/les`; if no, choose between `du/de la/de l’` and `le/la/l’`. Second: is the item already identified, or is the whole class meant? If either is true, use the definite article. Suffixes give useful hints about gender but never a guarantee: `-age`, `-isme`, `-ment`, and `-eau` are usually masculine, while `-té`, `-tion`, `-ance`, and `-ette` are usually feminine. The suffix `-eur` is masculine when it names a person or machine (`un vendeur`) and feminine when it names a quality (`la chaleur`, `la peur`).
points: Write the article into the vocabulary card itself, never the bare noun.
Use the definite article for a whole category: `Le logement coûte cher dans cette ville`.
Use the partitive for an unspecified amount of a mass noun: `du matériel`, `de la documentation`.
Keep the definite article after `aimer`, `étudier`, `apprendre`, and `détester`, even when speaking generally.
Treat `-age` as a masculine hint with known feminine exceptions: `une image`, `une page`, `une plage`.
Do not read a final `-e` as feminine: `un poème`, `un problème`, `un musée`, `un ordinateur` are masculine.

Use a bare noun in general expressions such as `sans rendez-vous`, `sans voiture`, and `avec plaisir`; retain a determiner for a specific or qualified referent: `sans le document demandé`, `sans une aide suffisante`.

examples.french: Le logement abordable favorise l’intégration des nouveaux arrivants.
examples.english: Affordable housing supports the integration of newcomers.
examples.note: The definite article presents housing as a whole category.

examples.french: Le centre distribue du matériel et de la documentation aux nouvelles familles.
examples.english: The centre hands out materials and documentation to new families.
examples.note: Partitive articles present an unspecified amount.

examples.french: Elle parle français au travail et elle étudie le français le soir.
examples.english: She speaks French at work and studies French in the evening.
examples.note: No article after « parler »; the definite article stays after « étudier ».

examples.french: Une conseillère nous a remis un formulaire et des brochures utiles.
examples.english: An adviser gave us a form and some useful brochures.
examples.note: Indefinite articles introduce countable items for the first time.

examples.french: L’image du quartier a changé depuis l’ouverture de la bibliothèque.
examples.english: The image of the neighbourhood has changed since the library opened.
examples.note: « Image » ends in -age but is feminine.

examples.french: Le poème affiché dans le hall a été écrit par une élève du quartier.
examples.english: The poem displayed in the lobby was written by a student from the neighbourhood.
examples.note: « Poème » ends in -e but is masculine; the ending is not a gender clue.

examples.french: La clinique reçoit sans rendez-vous, et je viens sans voiture.
examples.english: The clinic takes walk-ins, and I am coming without a car.
examples.note: These general expressions with « sans » omit the article.

examples.french: Je suis venu sans le document demandé et je ne peux pas continuer sans une aide suffisante.
examples.english: I came without the requested document, and I cannot continue without sufficient help.
examples.note: « Sans » can retain a determiner when the noun is identified or qualified.

mistakes.avoid: Je cherche information sur le programme.
mistakes.prefer: Je cherche des informations sur le programme.
mistakes.why: A French common noun needs a determiner; here the plural indefinite `des` introduces items not yet identified.

mistakes.avoid: J’aime français et je parle le français couramment.
mistakes.prefer: J’aime le français et je parle le français couramment.
mistakes.why: `Aimer` needs the article here. Both `parler français` and `parler le français` are correct.

mistakes.avoid: Je suis venu sans la document demandé ce matin.
mistakes.prefer: Je suis venu sans le document demandé ce matin.
mistakes.why: `Document` is masculine, so the identified document takes `le`. The preposition `sans` does not prohibit an article.

vocabulary.example: Le logement social reste difficile à obtenir dans cette ville.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; learn it with its determiner.

vocabulary.example: Une image bien choisie aide à retenir un mot nouveau.
vocabulary.note: Feminine despite the masculine-looking ending -age; compare `une page` and `une plage`.

vocabulary.example: L’argent économisé servira à financer une formation professionnelle.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; often used with a partitive article: `gagner de l’argent`.

vocabulary.example: La documentation remise à l’accueil explique chaque étape de la demande.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; the ending -tion is a reliable feminine hint.

vocabulary.example: Un paysage urbain bien entretenu attire de nouveaux résidents.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; the ending -age is a masculine hint.

vocabulary.example: Un poème court se mémorise facilement et enrichit le vocabulaire.
vocabulary.note: Masculine despite its final -e, like `un problème` and `un système`.

vocabulary.example: Une clinique sans rendez-vous accueille les patients jusqu’à vingt heures.
vocabulary.note: This fixed expression uses a bare noun; other complements of `sans` can keep a determiner.

practice.prompt: Complete with the right article: « Elle apprend ___ français et elle a besoin ___ documentation. »
practice.hint: `Apprendre` keeps the definite article; `avoir besoin de` is followed by a partitive form.
practice.answer: Elle apprend le français et elle a besoin de documentation.

takeaways: A French noun is never learned alone: article plus noun plus gender.
Definite for the identified item or the whole class; indefinite for a new countable item; partitive for an unmeasured amount.
`Parler français` but `aimer le français`: some verbs impose the pattern.

lessons.title: Les articles après la négation
lessons.summary: After `ne… pas`, `ne… jamais`, and `ne… plus`, an indefinite or partitive article becomes `de` or `d’`: `J’ai une voiture` becomes `Je n’ai pas de voiture`. Two cases keep the original article: after `être` (`Ce n’est pas une solution`), and when a definite article names the category being rejected (`Je n’aime pas les formulaires`).
objectives: Convert an affirmative sentence to the negative without leaving the article unchanged.
Identify the two situations where the article survives negation.
Apply the rule with the negatives `pas`, `jamais`, and `plus`.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: The rule concerns quantity. `Un`, `une`, `des`, `du`, `de la`, and `de l’` all express an amount, and negating the verb reduces that amount to zero, which French marks with a single `de`. A definite article expresses identity rather than quantity, so it has nothing to reduce and stays as it is.

Two checks settle every case. Is the verb `être`? Then keep the article, because `être` identifies rather than quantifies: `Ce n’est pas une erreur`. Otherwise, is the article definite? Then keep it: `Elle n’aime pas les réunions longues`. In all remaining cases, replace the article with `de`, elided to `d’` before a vowel or mute h.
points: Replace `un`, `une`, `des`, `du`, `de la`, and `de l’` with `de` after a negated verb.
Elide to `d’` before a vowel sound: `Je n’ai pas d’expérience`.
Keep the full article after `être`, whatever the negative word.
Keep a definite article when the negation rejects a named category.
Apply the same conversion after `ne… jamais` and `ne… plus`, not only after `ne… pas`.

examples.french: Nous n’avons pas de preuve suffisante pour appuyer cette conclusion.
examples.english: We do not have enough evidence to support this conclusion.
examples.note: `Une preuve` becomes `de preuve` after the negated verb.

examples.french: Ce n’est pas une solution durable pour le quartier.
examples.english: This is not a sustainable solution for the neighbourhood.
examples.note: After « être » the article is kept.

examples.french: Je n’aime pas les formulaires trop longs.
examples.english: I do not like forms that are too long.
examples.note: The definite article stays when the category itself is rejected.

examples.french: Elle n’a plus d’argent sur sa carte de transport.
examples.english: She has no money left on her transit card.
examples.note: `De` elides to `d’` before a vowel.

examples.french: Ce service ne demande jamais de frais supplémentaires.
examples.english: This service never charges any extra fees.
examples.note: The rule also applies after « ne… jamais ».

mistakes.avoid: Je n’ai pas du temps cette semaine.
mistakes.prefer: Je n’ai pas de temps cette semaine.
mistakes.why: The partitive `du` becomes `de` after a negated verb that is not `être`.

mistakes.avoid: Ce n’est pas de problème.
mistakes.prefer: Ce n’est pas un problème.
mistakes.why: After `être` the indefinite article is kept.

vocabulary.example: Une preuve de résidence est exigée pour ouvrir le dossier.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; learn it with its determiner.

vocabulary.example: Des frais de dossier s’appliquent après la date limite.
vocabulary.note: Masculine plural noun with no singular in this sense.

vocabulary.example: Le temps consacré à la relecture réduit beaucoup les erreurs.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; also means weather in `Quel temps fait-il ?`.

vocabulary.example: Une solution durable demande l’accord de tous les partenaires.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; the ending -tion is a feminine hint.

practice.prompt: Put in the negative: « J’ai des documents originaux. » and « C’est un dossier complet. »
practice.hint: Only the first sentence changes its article, because the second uses `être`.
practice.answer: Je n’ai pas de documents originaux. Ce n’est pas un dossier complet.

takeaways: Negation cancels quantity, so `un/une/des/du/de la` collapse to `de`.
`Être` protects its article: `Ce n’est pas une erreur`.
A definite article survives because it identifies rather than counts.

lessons.title: Les articles contractés
lessons.summary: `À` and `de` merge with `le` and `les` into single obligatory forms: `au`, `aux`, `du`, `des`. They never merge with `la` or with an elided `l’`, which stay as `à la`, `à l’`, `de la`, `de l’`. The contraction is required, not optional.
objectives: Produce the four contracted forms automatically after `à` and `de`.
Leave `à la`, `à l’`, `de la`, and `de l’` uncontracted.
Recognise the contraction inside fixed expressions and compound nouns.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: A contracted article is one word that carries both a preposition and a definite article. French has exactly four: `à + le = au`, `à + les = aux`, `de + le = du`, `de + les = des`. Writing `à le` or `de le` is never correct.

The contraction is blocked in two situations: before the feminine `la`, and before `l’` used for a noun beginning with a vowel or mute h. So you write `au bureau` but `à la mairie`, `du centre` but `de l’école`. Note that `des` is ambiguous in isolation: it is a contracted article in `Je reviens des bureaux`, and a plural indefinite article in `J’ai des questions`. The preposition in the sentence tells you which one you are looking at.
points: Merge `à` with `le` and `les`, and `de` with `le` and `les`; never write the two words separately.
Keep `à la`, `à l’`, `de la`, and `de l’` in two words.
Check gender before contracting: `au centre` but `à la clinique`.
Read `des` in context: contracted after a verb built with `de`, indefinite elsewhere.

examples.french: Je vais au bureau des services municipaux.
examples.english: I am going to the municipal services office.
examples.note: `À + le` gives `au`; `de + les` gives `des`.

examples.french: Ils reviennent du centre de formation.
examples.english: They are coming back from the training centre.
examples.note: `De + le` gives `du`.

examples.french: Je vais à la mairie, puis je reviens de l’école.
examples.english: I am going to the town hall, then coming back from the school.
examples.note: No contraction before « la » or before an elided « l’ ».

examples.french: La réponse aux demandes de logement arrive dans un délai de six semaines.
examples.english: The answer to housing applications arrives within six weeks.
examples.note: `À + les` gives `aux`.

mistakes.avoid: Je téléphone à le service d’immigration.
mistakes.prefer: Je téléphone au service d’immigration.
mistakes.why: `À + le` must be written `au`; the two-word form does not exist.

mistakes.avoid: Je parle à la directeur du programme.
mistakes.prefer: Je parle au directeur du programme.
mistakes.why: `Directeur` is masculine, so `à + le` contracts to `au`; `à la` is used only before a feminine noun.

vocabulary.example: Le bureau des admissions ouvre à neuf heures.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; plural `les bureaux`.

vocabulary.example: La mairie délivre les attestations de résidence.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; used with `à la`, never with `au`.

vocabulary.example: Un centre de formation professionnel a ouvert près de la gare.
vocabulary.note: Masculine compound noun; learn the whole group together.

vocabulary.example: Une salle d’attente calme rend le rendez-vous moins stressant.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; the gender comes from `salle`.

practice.prompt: Contract where required: « Je parle (à + le) conseiller (de + la) mairie et (à + les) agents (de + l’) accueil. »
practice.hint: Only `le` and `les` contract.
practice.answer: Je parle au conseiller de la mairie et aux agents de l’accueil.

takeaways: Four forms to automate: `au`, `aux`, `du`, `des`.
`La` and `l’` never contract.
`Des` can be a contraction or a plural indefinite article; the preposition decides.

lessons.title: Le pluriel des noms et les noms propres
lessons.summary: The default written plural adds `-s`. Most nouns in `-al` become `-aux` (`un journal` / `des journaux`); common exceptions keeping `-als` include `un bal`, `un carnaval`, `un festival`, `un récital`, `un régal`, and `un chacal`. Most nouns in `-eau`, `-au`, and `-eu` add `-x` (`un bateau` / `des bateaux`, `un joyau` / `des joyaux`); exceptions taking `-s` include `un landau`, `un sarrau`, `un pneu`, and `un bleu`. A noun already ending in `-s`, `-x`, or `-z` does not change, and an ordinary French family surname takes no plural ending.
objectives: Apply the default plural and the two main irregular families.
Recall common exceptions in `-als` and exceptions to the `-au` and `-eu` patterns.
Leave invariable nouns and family surnames unchanged.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: Look at the last letters of the singular before choosing an ending. Nouns in `-al` normally give `-aux`; most nouns in `-eau`, `-au`, and `-eu` add `-x`. Seven common nouns in `-ou` also add `-x`: `un bijou`, `un caillou`, `un chou`, `un genou`, `un hibou`, `un joujou`, `un pou`. The default for other regular plurals is `-s`. Nouns whose singular already ends in `-s`, `-x`, or `-z` are identical in the plural: `un cours` / `des cours`, `une voix` / `des voix`.

Learn exceptions alongside the patterns without treating these examples as exhaustive lists. Common plurals keeping `-als` include `des bals`, `des carnavals`, `des festivals`, `des récitals`, `des régals`, `des chacals`, and `des avals`. Examples taking `-s` instead of `-x` include `des landaus`, `des sarraus`, `des pneus`, and `des bleus`. Thus `un joyau` gives `des joyaux`, but `un landau` gives `des landaus`. An ordinary family surname stays unchanged in writing and only the article is plural, as in `les Tremblay`.
points: Add `-s` unless the ending signals another family.
Most `-al` nouns give `-aux`; common exceptions include `bal`, `carnaval`, `festival`, `récital`, `régal`, `chacal`, and `aval`.
Most nouns in `-eau`, `-au`, and `-eu` add `-x`: `des bateaux`, `des joyaux`, `des jeux`.
Learn exceptions such as `des landaus`, `des sarraus`, `des pneus`, and `des bleus` with `-s`.
Leave a noun ending in `-s`, `-x`, or `-z` unchanged.
Write a family surname without `-s`: `les Tremblay`, `les Diallo`.

examples.french: Les nouveaux arrivants lisent les journaux locaux pour mieux connaître Montréal.
examples.english: Newcomers read local newspapers to learn more about Montreal.
examples.note: Both the noun and the adjective follow the -al / -aux pattern.

examples.french: La ville organise deux festivals, trois bals et plusieurs récitals chaque été.
examples.english: The city runs two festivals, three dances, and several recitals every summer.
examples.note: Three common exceptions that keep -als.

examples.french: Les bureaux du quartier ont changé leurs pneus avant l’hiver.
examples.english: The neighbourhood offices changed their tires before winter.
examples.note: « Bureaux » takes -x, but « pneus » takes -s.

examples.french: Les joyaux du musée sont exposés dans deux salles seulement.
examples.english: The museum’s jewels are displayed in only two rooms.
examples.note: « Joyau » follows the usual -au plural pattern, adding -x.

examples.french: Les parents rangent les landaus à l’entrée, et les enfants mettent leurs sarraus pour peindre.
examples.english: The parents leave the prams at the entrance, and the children put on their smocks to paint.
examples.note: « Un landau » and « un sarrau » are masculine nouns whose plurals add -s.

examples.french: Les Tremblay habitent ce quartier depuis vingt ans.
examples.english: The Tremblays have lived in this neighbourhood for twenty years.
examples.note: A family surname takes no plural ending.

examples.french: Les cours de français du soir affichent complet.
examples.english: The evening French courses are fully booked.
examples.note: A noun ending in -s is identical in the plural.

mistakes.avoid: Les festivaux d’été attirent beaucoup de visiteurs.
mistakes.prefer: Les festivals d’été attirent beaucoup de visiteurs.
mistakes.why: `Festival` is one of the exceptions that keeps `-als`, like `bal`, `carnaval`, `récital`, `régal`, and `chacal`.

mistakes.avoid: Les Tremblays sont arrivés en 2019.
mistakes.prefer: Les Tremblay sont arrivés en 2019.
mistakes.why: A French family surname is invariable; only the article marks the plural.

vocabulary.example: Un journal local a publié un article sur le nouveau centre communautaire.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; plural `des journaux`.

vocabulary.example: Un festival de quartier réunit les familles chaque mois de juin.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; irregular plural `des festivals`, not `festivaux`.

vocabulary.example: Un joyau ancien a été prêté au musée pour l’exposition.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; plural `des joyaux`, like `-eau` nouns.

vocabulary.example: Un régal pareil mérite une deuxième visite au marché.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; exceptional plural `des régals`.

vocabulary.example: Un cours de conversation a lieu tous les mardis soir.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; identical in the plural because it already ends in -s.

vocabulary.example: Un pneu d’hiver est obligatoire au Québec à partir de décembre.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; exceptional plural `des pneus`.

vocabulary.example: Le projet attend encore l’aval du conseil municipal.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; joins the `-als` list, so the plural is `des avals`.

practice.prompt: Put in the plural: « le journal régional », « le carnaval », « le joyau », « le pneu », « la voix ».
practice.hint: Two take `-aux` or `-x`, one keeps `-als`, one takes `-s`, one does not change.
practice.answer: les journaux régionaux, les carnavals, les joyaux, les pneus, les voix

takeaways: Most `-al` nouns give `-aux`; memorise common exceptions such as `des festivals`.
Most `-eau`, `-au`, `-eu` nouns add `-x`; exceptions include `des landaus`, `des sarraus`, `des pneus`, and `des bleus`.
Nouns in `-s`, `-x`, `-z` and family surnames do not change.

lessons.title: Les adjectifs et les pronoms possessifs
lessons.summary: A possessive adjective agrees with the thing possessed, not with the owner: `son dossier` can mean his file or her file. Before a feminine noun beginning with a vowel, use `mon`, `ton`, `son` for sound (`mon expérience`). A possessive pronoun replaces the whole noun phrase and keeps its article: `le mien`, `la sienne`, `les nôtres`. With a body part affected by the subject’s own action, French uses a definite article: `Elle se lave les mains`.
objectives: Select a possessive adjective from the gender and number of the possessed noun.
Replace a full noun phrase with the matching possessive pronoun.
Choose between a definite article and a possessive with parts of the body.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: A possessive adjective sits in the determiner slot before a noun and therefore agrees with that noun: `mon dossier`, `ma demande`, `mes documents`. English speakers must resist agreeing with the owner: `son` before a masculine noun covers both his and her. A possessive pronoun does a different job: it replaces the entire noun phrase and carries its own definite article, as in `Ce dossier est le mien`.

For a feminine noun starting with a vowel or mute h, French uses the masculine-looking forms `mon`, `ton`, `son` to avoid two vowels in a row: `mon expérience`, `son adresse`. With body parts, use the definite article when the subject is clearly the owner, usually with a reflexive verb: `Elle se lave les mains`. Switch to a possessive only when the owner is genuinely in doubt or is being contrasted: `Sa main droite est blessée, pas la mienne`.
points: Identify the possessed noun first, then pick the form that matches its gender and number.
Use `mon`, `ton`, `son` before a feminine noun beginning with a vowel sound.
Give the possessive pronoun its article: `le mien`, `la mienne`, `les nôtres`, `les leurs`.
Use `être à + stressed pronoun` to state ownership in conversation: `Ce dossier est à moi`.
Prefer the definite article for a body part when the subject already identifies the owner.

examples.french: Leurs enfants sont déjà inscrits, mais les nôtres attendent encore une place.
examples.english: Their children are already enrolled, but ours are still waiting for a place.
examples.note: `Les nôtres` replaces the whole noun phrase « nos enfants ».

examples.french: Mon expérience professionnelle figure à la deuxième page de mon dossier.
examples.english: My professional experience is on the second page of my file.
examples.note: `Expérience` is feminine, but takes « mon » because it begins with a vowel.

examples.french: Ce dossier est à moi ; le sien est resté à l’accueil.
examples.english: This file is mine; hers is still at the reception desk.
examples.note: « Être à » for spoken ownership, then the possessive pronoun.

examples.french: L’infirmière se lave les mains avant chaque examen.
examples.english: The nurse washes her hands before every examination.
examples.note: Definite article with a body part when the owner is already clear.

examples.french: Sa demande a été acceptée, mais la mienne est encore à l’étude.
examples.english: His application was accepted, but mine is still under review.
examples.note: `Sa` agrees with « demande », not with the owner.

mistakes.avoid: Il se brosse ses dents avant de partir.
mistakes.prefer: Il se brosse les dents avant de partir.
mistakes.why: The reflexive pronoun already identifies the owner, so French uses the definite article.

mistakes.avoid: Ma adresse a changé le mois dernier.
mistakes.prefer: Mon adresse a changé le mois dernier.
mistakes.why: Before a feminine noun beginning with a vowel, French uses `mon` for pronunciation.

vocabulary.example: Une attestation de résidence accompagne toujours ce type de demande.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; `attester` is the related verb.

vocabulary.example: Une demande de logement se dépose en ligne ou à la mairie.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; `faire une demande` means to submit an application.

vocabulary.example: Une adresse à jour évite la perte du courrier officiel.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun, but takes `mon`, `ton`, `son` because it begins with a vowel.

vocabulary.example: Une main levée suffit pour demander la parole.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; used with the definite article after a reflexive verb.

practice.prompt: Replace the underlined group with a possessive pronoun: « Voici mon dossier et voici ___ (le dossier de Marie). »
practice.hint: The pronoun agrees with `dossier`, which is masculine singular.
practice.answer: Voici mon dossier et voici le sien.

takeaways: The possessive agrees with what is owned, never with the owner.
`Mon expérience`, `mon adresse`: sound wins before a vowel.
Body part plus reflexive verb equals definite article.

lessons.title: Le choix entre « ce », « ça », « c’est », « il » et « elle »
lessons.summary: `Ce`, `cet`, `cette`, and `ces` are determiners placed before a noun. `Il` and `elle` replace a specific noun already mentioned and take its gender. `Ça` refers to an idea, a situation, or an unspecified thing and never agrees. Use `c’est` before a noun phrase, a name, or a general comment, and `il/elle est` before an adjective describing a specific item already identified.
objectives: Choose the demonstrative determiner that matches the noun.
Decide whether a reference points to a noun, an idea, or a general judgement.
Apply the split between `c’est` and `il/elle est`.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: A demonstrative determiner introduces a noun and agrees with it: `ce dossier`, `cette mesure`, `ces documents`, and `cet` before a masculine noun beginning with a vowel or mute h (`cet immeuble`). A subject pronoun does the opposite job: `il` and `elle` stand in place of a noun already named and inherit its gender, including for objects.

The practical test for `c’est` versus `il/elle est` is what follows. A noun phrase, a name, or a stressed pronoun follows `c’est`: `C’est une priorité`, `C’est Marie`. A bare adjective describing an item already identified follows `il/elle est`: `Le formulaire ? Il est incomplet`. `Ça` is the informal way to point at a whole idea or situation and stays invariable; in careful writing, `cela` is its neutral equivalent.
points: Put `ce`, `cet`, `cette`, or `ces` directly before the noun you are naming.
Use `cet` before a masculine noun beginning with a vowel or mute h.
Use `il` or `elle` when the noun is already identified, whether it is a person or an object.
Use `ça` or `cela` for an idea, an activity, or a situation as a whole.
Follow `c’est` with a noun phrase and `il/elle est` with an adjective.
Resume a whole adjective or predicate with the invariable neuter `le`: `Ce dossier est complet ; le mien ne l’est pas.`

examples.french: Ce formulaire et cette attestation doivent être joints à la demande.
examples.english: This form and this certificate must be attached to the application.
examples.note: Demonstrative determiners agree with the nouns they introduce.

examples.french: Cet immeuble accueille une clinique et une garderie.
examples.english: This building houses a clinic and a daycare.
examples.note: `Cet` before a masculine noun beginning with a vowel.

examples.french: Où est le formulaire ? Il est sur le comptoir.
examples.english: Where is the form? It is on the counter.
examples.note: `Il` resumes a specific masculine noun.

examples.french: Réduire la pollution, ça demande des mesures concrètes.
examples.english: Reducing pollution takes concrete measures.
examples.note: `Ça` refers to a whole idea and never agrees.

examples.french: C’est une priorité pour la municipalité, et elle est urgente.
examples.english: It is a priority for the city, and it is urgent.
examples.note: `C’est` before a noun phrase, « elle est » before an adjective.

examples.french: Ce dossier est complet ; le mien ne l’est pas encore.
examples.english: This file is complete; mine is not yet.
examples.note: The neuter « le » resumes the adjective « complet » and never agrees.

mistakes.avoid: Où est le livre ? Ça est sur la table.
mistakes.prefer: Où est le livre ? Il est sur la table.
mistakes.why: A specific masculine noun is resumed by `il`, not by `ça`.

mistakes.avoid: Il est une bonne idée de relire le dossier.
mistakes.prefer: C’est une bonne idée de relire le dossier.
mistakes.why: A noun phrase follows `c’est`, not `il est`.

mistakes.avoid: Ce logement est libre, mais l’autre n’est pas.
mistakes.prefer: Ce logement est libre, mais l’autre ne l’est pas.
mistakes.why: French cannot leave the attribute unexpressed: the invariable `le` resumes `libre`, where English simply stops after `is not`.

vocabulary.example: Un formulaire signé doit accompagner chaque demande.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; very frequent in administrative contexts.

vocabulary.example: Une mesure temporaire a été adoptée pour réduire la circulation.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; also means measurement.

vocabulary.example: Un immeuble récent offre de meilleures performances énergétiques.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun beginning with a vowel; takes `cet`.

vocabulary.example: Une priorité claire aide l’équipe à organiser son travail.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; the ending -té is a feminine hint.

vocabulary.example: Elle est bilingue ; son collègue ne l’est pas.
vocabulary.note: The neuter `le` stands for a whole adjective or predicate and never agrees.

practice.prompt: Fill in: « ___ dossier est prêt. ___ une bonne nouvelle, et ___ est déjà en ligne. »
practice.hint: Determiner, then `c’est` before a noun phrase, then a pronoun before a verb.
practice.answer: Ce dossier est prêt. C’est une bonne nouvelle, et il est déjà en ligne.

takeaways: `Ce/cet/cette/ces` introduce a noun; `il/elle` replace one.
`Ça` and `cela` point at ideas and situations, never agreeing.
Noun phrase after `c’est`, adjective after `il/elle est`.
keywords: choosing ce, ça, c’est, il, and elle

lessons.title: L’accord des adjectifs
lessons.summary: An adjective agrees in gender and number with the noun it describes. The default written pattern adds `-e` for the feminine and `-s` for the plural. Several frequent families double the final consonant: `gras/grasse`, `gros/grosse`, `épais/épaisse`, `bas/basse`, `las/lasse`. Others change shape completely: `mou/molle`, `doux/douce`, `frais/fraîche`, `actif/active`, `bref/brève`, `beau/belle`, `vieux/vieille`, `nouveau/nouvelle`. Before a masculine singular noun starting with a vowel or mute h, use `bel`, `vieil`, `nouvel`.
objectives: Locate the noun that governs the adjective before writing an ending.
Reproduce the doubling family and the irregular pairs.
Apply the special forms used before a vowel sound.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: Agreement means copying the grammatical gender and number of the noun onto the adjective. An adjective that already ends in `-e` in the masculine does not add a second one: `un dossier utile`, `une mesure utile`. Regular families are worth grouping: `-eux` becomes `-euse` (`heureux` / `heureuse`), `-if` becomes `-ive` (`actif` / `active`), and a set of adjectives in `-s` doubles the consonant before `-e`: `gras` / `grasse`, `gros` / `grosse`, `épais` / `épaisse`, `bas` / `basse`, `las` / `lasse`.

A short list changes shape more deeply and has to be learned as pairs: `mou` / `molle`, `doux` / `douce`, `frais` / `fraîche`, `bref` / `brève`, `beau` / `belle`, `vieux` / `vieille`, `nouveau` / `nouvelle`. Two further situations complete the picture. When one adjective describes several nouns of mixed gender, the masculine plural is used: `un dossier et une lettre complets`. And before a masculine singular noun beginning with a vowel or mute h, `beau`, `vieux`, and `nouveau` change to `bel`, `vieil`, `nouvel` purely for pronunciation: `un nouvel immeuble`, `un bel hôtel`.
points: Find the noun first; the nearest word is not always the one that governs the adjective.
Add `-e` for the feminine unless the masculine already ends in `-e`.
Double the consonant in `gras`, `gros`, `épais`, `bas`, `las` before `-e`.
Learn the reshaping pairs as single items: `mou/molle`, `doux/douce`, `frais/fraîche`, `bref/brève`.
Use `bel`, `vieil`, `nouvel` before a masculine singular vowel sound.
Use the masculine plural when the adjective covers nouns of both genders.

examples.french: Le programme offre de nouvelles possibilités professionnelles.
examples.english: The program offers new professional opportunities.
examples.note: Both adjectives agree in the feminine plural.

examples.french: Il y a un nouvel immeuble près de la station de métro.
examples.english: There is a new building near the subway station.
examples.note: « Nouvel » before a masculine noun beginning with a vowel.

examples.french: La couche de neige est épaisse et la température reste basse.
examples.english: The layer of snow is thick and the temperature stays low.
examples.note: « Épais » and « bas » double their consonant in the feminine.

examples.french: Cette laine douce et cette pâte molle conviennent aux enfants.
examples.english: This soft wool and this soft dough are suitable for children.
examples.note: « Doux » gives douce and « mou » gives molle.

examples.french: La conseillère est très active et ses réponses sont brèves.
examples.english: The adviser is very proactive and her answers are brief.
examples.note: Irregular pairs actif/active and bref/brève.

examples.french: Le dossier et la lettre de motivation sont complets.
examples.english: The file and the cover letter are complete.
examples.note: Masculine plural agreement covers nouns of both genders.

mistakes.avoid: Une réponse bref suffit pour cette demande.
mistakes.prefer: Une réponse brève suffit pour cette demande.
mistakes.why: `Bref` has the irregular feminine `brève`.

mistakes.avoid: La couche de neige est épaise ce matin.
mistakes.prefer: La couche de neige est épaisse ce matin.
mistakes.why: `Épais` doubles its final consonant before the feminine `-e`, like `gras`, `gros`, `bas`, `las`.

mistakes.avoid: Il a acheté un nouveau appartement au centre-ville.
mistakes.prefer: Il a acheté un nouvel appartement au centre-ville.
mistakes.why: Before a masculine singular noun beginning with a vowel, `nouveau` becomes `nouvel`.

vocabulary.example: Une possibilité concrète s’ouvre après cette formation.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; the ending -té is a feminine hint.

vocabulary.example: Une épaisse couche de verglas couvre les trottoirs.
vocabulary.note: Doubles its consonant in the feminine, like `gras`, `gros`, `bas`, `las`.

vocabulary.example: Une douce hausse des températures est annoncée pour la fin de semaine.
vocabulary.note: Irregular feminine in -ce.

vocabulary.example: Une pâte molle se travaille plus facilement.
vocabulary.note: Irregular feminine; the masculine before a vowel is `mol`, as in `un mol oreiller`.

vocabulary.example: Une brève présentation suffit pour introduire le projet.
vocabulary.note: Irregular feminine with an accent: brève.

vocabulary.example: Une salade fraîche accompagne le plat du jour.
vocabulary.note: Irregular feminine with a circumflex.

vocabulary.example: Un bel hôtel accueille les délégations près de la gare.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun with a mute h; triggers `bel`, `vieil`, `nouvel`.

practice.prompt: Agree the adjectives: « une couche (épais) », « une voix (doux) », « une réponse (bref) », « un (vieux) immeuble ».
practice.hint: One doubles its consonant, two reshape, one comes before a vowel.
practice.answer: une couche épaisse, une voix douce, une réponse brève, un vieil immeuble

takeaways: Agreement follows the noun, not word order.
`Gras`, `gros`, `épais`, `bas`, `las` double the consonant; `mou`, `doux`, `frais`, `bref` reshape.
`Bel`, `vieil`, `nouvel` exist only before a masculine singular vowel sound.

lessons.title: La place et le sens des adjectifs
lessons.summary: Most French adjectives follow the noun. A small group of short, frequent adjectives normally precedes it, remembered through the English mnemonic BANGS — Beauty, Age, Number, Goodness, Size — or its variant BRAGS, where Rank replaces Number. A few adjectives change meaning with position: `un ancien musée` is a former museum, `un musée ancien` is an old one; `un grand homme` is a great man, `un homme grand` is a tall one.
objectives: Place a descriptive adjective correctly by default.
Recall which frequent adjectives sit before the noun.
Interpret and produce the meaning-sensitive pairs accurately.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: A mnemonic is a memory aid, not a grammatical law. BANGS stands for Beauty, Age, Number, Goodness, and Size; BRAGS stands for Beauty, Rank, Age, Goodness, and Size. They help you remember common words placed before a noun: `beau`, `joli`, `jeune`, `vieux`, `nouveau`, `premier`, `dernier`, `bon`, `mauvais`, `grand`, `petit`, and `gros`. Numbers such as `deux` also precede nouns, though modern grammar classifies them as determiners rather than descriptive adjectives. Colour, shape, nationality, and category adjectives normally follow the noun. Other adjectives can precede it too, especially for an evaluation: `une excellente nouvelle`, `une merveilleuse occasion`. Length alone does not determine position.

Some adjectives change meaning with position; learn each pair rather than applying one figurative-versus-literal rule to all adjectives. Compare `un ancien musée` (a former museum) with `un musée ancien` (an old museum), and `un grand homme` (a great man) with `un homme grand` (a tall man). `Nouveau` can mean new to someone, recent, or next in a series; `neuf` emphasises that something has not been used. `Ancien` before a noun often means former, while `vieux` describes age.
points: Use the post-noun position as a default, then learn frequent pre-noun adjectives and meaning-sensitive pairs.
BANGS: Beauty, Age, Number, Goodness, Size. BRAGS: Beauty, Rank, Age, Goodness, Size. Neither is an exhaustive rule.
In careful writing, normally use `de` instead of indefinite `des` before a preposed plural adjective: `de nouvelles mesures`; fixed groups such as `des petits pois` keep `des`.
Read a preposed `ancien` or `grand` figuratively and a postposed one literally.
Choose `neuf` for an item never used and `nouveau` for an item new to its owner.
Reduce only the indefinite `des` to `de` before a preposed plural adjective; the definite `les` never changes.
Use no `de` after `plusieurs`, `quelques`, or a number: `plusieurs jolies affiches`.

examples.french: Mon ancien employeur m’a fourni une lettre de recommandation.
examples.english: My former employer gave me a letter of recommendation.
examples.note: Preposed « ancien » means former.

examples.french: La ville a rénové un bâtiment ancien pour y installer la bibliothèque.
examples.english: The city renovated an old building to house the library.
examples.note: Postposed « ancien » refers to age.

examples.french: J’ai trouvé un appartement neuf près de mon travail.
examples.english: I found a brand-new apartment near my workplace.
examples.note: « Neuf » means never lived in, unlike « nouveau ».

examples.french: Une belle occasion permet à un jeune candidat de présenter un bon projet.
examples.english: A great opportunity lets a young candidate present a strong project.
examples.note: Three preposed adjectives: Beauty, Age, Goodness.

examples.french: Les deux premières mesures concernent les petits logements.
examples.english: The first two measures concern small housing units.
examples.note: Number and Rank also sit before the noun.

examples.french: Un grand homme n’a pas nécessairement la même taille qu’un homme grand.
examples.english: A great man is not necessarily the same height as a tall man.
examples.note: Position alone changes the meaning.

examples.french: Il y a de jolies affiches dans le hall, et plusieurs jolies affiches sont déjà réservées.
examples.english: There are some attractive posters in the lobby, and several attractive posters are already reserved.
examples.note: Indefinite « des » normally becomes « de » before a preposed adjective in careful writing. « Plusieurs » directly determines « jolies affiches » here; the separate construction « plusieurs de ces affiches » selects some of an identified group.

examples.french: C’est une excellente nouvelle pour les familles du quartier.
examples.english: That is excellent news for the neighbourhood’s families.
examples.note: An evaluative adjective can come before the noun without belonging to the mnemonic’s short list.

mistakes.avoid: Cette voiture est neuf : elle sort de l’usine.
mistakes.prefer: Cette voiture est neuve : elle sort de l’usine.
mistakes.why: `Voiture` is feminine, so `neuf` becomes `neuve`. `Neuf` emphasises unused condition; `nouveau` has a broader meaning and is not inherently wrong for a recently made item.

mistakes.avoid: Elle a présenté des nouvelles mesures au conseil municipal.
mistakes.prefer: Elle a présenté de nouvelles mesures au conseil municipal.
mistakes.why: Careful written French normally uses `de` before a preposed plural adjective here. Keeping `des` is common in informal speech.

mistakes.avoid: Il y a plusieurs de jolies affiches dans le hall.
mistakes.prefer: Il y a plusieurs jolies affiches dans le hall.
mistakes.why: `Plusieurs` is a determiner in its own right and is never followed by `de` before the adjective.

vocabulary.example: Un employeur sérieux fournit une attestation de travail sur demande.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; feminine form `une employeuse` is rare, `une employeure` is used in Canada.

vocabulary.example: Un bâtiment ancien demande souvent des travaux d’isolation.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; the ending -ment is a masculine hint.

vocabulary.example: Une voiture neuve perd de la valeur dès la première année.
vocabulary.note: Always follows the noun, unlike `nouveau`.

vocabulary.example: Une occasion de stage a été annoncée par le centre d’emploi.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; `d’occasion` separately means second-hand.

vocabulary.english: de before a preposed plural adjective
vocabulary.example: Le centre propose de nouvelles activités et de bons ateliers gratuits.
vocabulary.note: Only the indefinite `des` reduces to `de`; the definite `les bonnes idées` never changes.

practice.prompt: Translate keeping the intended meaning: « She rented a former office that is now an old but pleasant building. »
practice.hint: Preposed `ancien` for former, postposed for age.
practice.answer: Elle a loué un ancien bureau, un bâtiment ancien mais agréable.

takeaways: The default position is after the noun; BANGS and BRAGS recall common pre-noun patterns, not every exception.
`Ancien`, `grand`, `pauvre` change meaning with position.
`Neuf` equals never used; `nouveau` equals new to you.

lessons.title: Les couleurs et les nationalités
lessons.summary: An ordinary colour adjective agrees with its noun: `une veste bleue`, `des chaussures noires`. A colour named after a thing stays invariable: `des yeux marron`, `des chemises orange`. Five colour words of that origin agree anyway and must be learned: `rose`, `mauve`, `pourpre`, `écarlate`, `fauve`. A two-word colour never agrees: `des vestes vert foncé`. A nationality adjective is lowercase; a noun naming a person is capitalised: `une candidate canadienne` but `une Canadienne`.
objectives: Classify a colour word before deciding whether it agrees.
Apply the invariability rule for noun-based and compound colours.
Use the correct capitalisation for nationalities.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: Deciding on agreement means first classifying the colour word. Ordinary colour adjectives (`bleu`, `vert`, `noir`, `blanc`, `gris`) agree normally. Colours borrowed from a noun (`marron` chestnut, `orange` orange, `cerise` cherry, `crème` cream, `turquoise`) keep the invariable form of that noun. Five borrowed colours have been fully absorbed into the adjective class and do agree: `rose`, `mauve`, `pourpre`, `écarlate`, `fauve`. Finally, a colour written with two words — a colour plus `clair`, `foncé`, or a second colour — is frozen and never agrees.

Nationality words follow a different logic, based on function rather than form. Used as an adjective after a noun or after `être`, the word is lowercase: `une candidate canadienne`, `Elle est canadienne`. Used as a noun that names a person, it takes a capital letter: `une Canadienne`, `les Québécois`. Languages are always lowercase: `Elle parle français`.
points: Ask whether the colour word is originally a noun; if it is, keep it invariable.
Memorise the five agreeing exceptions: `rose`, `mauve`, `pourpre`, `écarlate`, `fauve`.
Freeze any two-word colour: `bleu clair`, `vert foncé`, `bleu-vert`.
Write a nationality adjective in lowercase and a person noun with a capital.
Keep language names lowercase in every position.

examples.french: Elle porte une veste bleue et des chaussures noires pour l’entrevue.
examples.english: She is wearing a blue jacket and black shoes for the interview.
examples.note: Ordinary colour adjectives agree in gender and number.

examples.french: La brochure verte et les affiches marron annoncent la consultation publique.
examples.english: The green brochure and the brown posters announce the public consultation.
examples.note: « Marron » comes from a noun and stays invariable.

examples.french: Les bénévoles portent des vestes vert foncé.
examples.english: The volunteers wear dark green jackets.
examples.note: A two-word colour never agrees.

examples.french: La boutique du musée vend des affiches roses et mauves.
examples.english: The museum shop sells pink and mauve posters.
examples.note: « Rose » and « mauve » agree even though they come from nouns.

examples.french: Une candidate canadienne a parlé avec une Canadienne installée à Montréal.
examples.english: A Canadian candidate spoke with a Canadian woman living in Montreal.
examples.note: Lowercase adjective, capitalised noun naming a person.

mistakes.avoid: Elle a acheté des chemises oranges et des gants marrons.
mistakes.prefer: Elle a acheté des chemises orange et des gants marron.
mistakes.why: Colours borrowed from nouns stay invariable, unlike `rose` or `mauve`.

mistakes.avoid: Il est Français et il parle Français.
mistakes.prefer: Il est français et il parle français.
mistakes.why: After `être` the word is an adjective, and a language name is always lowercase.

vocabulary.example: Une brochure verte présente les services offerts aux nouveaux arrivants.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; useful for describing information material.

vocabulary.example: Une affiche marron annonce la prochaine consultation publique.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; `afficher` is the related verb.

vocabulary.example: La nationalité du candidat figure sur le formulaire officiel.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; distinguish it from `la citoyenneté`.

vocabulary.example: Une entreprise québécoise recrute des techniciens bilingues.
vocabulary.note: Lowercase as an adjective, capitalised as a noun: `une Québécoise`.

practice.prompt: Agree where required: « des dossiers (bleu) », « des chaises (orange) », « des affiches (rose) », « des murs (bleu clair) ».
practice.hint: Two of the four never change.
practice.answer: des dossiers bleus, des chaises orange, des affiches roses, des murs bleu clair

takeaways: Classify first: ordinary adjective, borrowed noun, listed exception, or compound.
`Rose`, `mauve`, `pourpre`, `écarlate`, `fauve` agree; `marron` and `orange` do not.
Lowercase for the adjective and the language, capital for the person.

lessons.title: La formation et la place des adverbes
lessons.summary: Form a regular adverb from the feminine adjective plus `-ment`: `lente` gives `lentement`. When the masculine already ends in a vowel, add `-ment` to it directly: `vrai` gives `vraiment`, `absolu` gives `absolument`. Adjectives in `-ant` give `-amment` (`constant` / `constamment`) and adjectives in `-ent` give `-emment` (`prudent` / `prudemment`), both pronounced the same way. Learn the lexical forms `bon` / `bien`, `mauvais` / `mal`, `gentil` / `gentiment`, `bref` / `brièvement`.
objectives: Derive an adverb from the right base form of the adjective.
Recognise the two nasal families and their shared pronunciation.
Place a short adverb correctly in a simple and in a compound tense.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: An adverb modifies a verb, an adjective, another adverb, or a whole clause. The regular French adverb is built on the feminine adjective: `heureuse` gives `heureusement`, `franche` gives `franchement`. The feminine step matters only when it changes the written form; if the masculine adjective already ends in a vowel, the adverb is built on it directly, which is why `vraiment` and `poliment` have no `e`.

The nasal families are the frequent trap. Adjectives ending in `-ant` produce `-amment` and adjectives ending in `-ent` produce `-emment`, and the two endings are pronounced identically. These forms are built on the masculine adjective, not on the feminine, so `patient` gives `patiemment`. On placement, a short adverb of manner follows the conjugated verb in a simple tense (`Elle répond clairement`) but slips between auxiliary and past participle in a compound tense (`Elle a bien répondu`). Long adverbs and sentence adverbs may open the sentence instead. One small ordering point follows from this: `assez` modifies the adverb it precedes, so *quite closely* is `assez près`, and after a verb of observation the usual form is `d’assez près`, as in `Nous suivons ce dossier d’assez près`. The reverse order, `assez de près`, is not French.
points: Start from the feminine adjective when the feminine adds a written letter.
Add `-ment` straight to a masculine adjective already ending in a vowel.
Convert `-ant` to `-amment` and `-ent` to `-emment`, both built on the masculine form.
Place a short manner adverb after the finite verb in a simple tense.
Place it between the auxiliary and the participle in a compound tense.
Put the short adverbs `déjà`, `bien`, `mal`, `encore`, `toujours`, `jamais`, and `souvent` between the auxiliary and the past participle.
Use `de près` or `attentivement` for closely; `prochainement` means soon and never closely.
Modify an adverb of degree with `assez` placed before it: `assez près`, and `d’assez près` after a verb of observation.

examples.french: La conseillère explique clairement les démarches d’immigration.
examples.english: The adviser clearly explains the immigration procedures.
examples.note: Built on the feminine « claire ».

examples.french: Les candidats attendent patiemment leur tour.
examples.english: The applicants wait patiently for their turn.
examples.note: « Patient » ends in -ent, so the adverb is patiemment.

examples.french: Le service a vraiment simplifié la procédure en ligne.
examples.english: The service has genuinely simplified the online procedure.
examples.note: « Vrai » ends in a vowel, so no feminine step.

examples.french: Elle a bien répondu à toutes les questions du jury.
examples.english: She answered all the panel’s questions well.
examples.note: In a compound tense the short adverb sits between auxiliary and participle.

examples.french: La porte-parole répond franchement aux journalistes.
examples.english: The spokesperson answers the journalists frankly.
examples.note: Built on the feminine « franche ».

examples.french: Après deux ans au Québec, elle parle couramment français.
examples.english: After two years in Quebec, she speaks French fluently.
examples.note: « Couramment » comes from « courant » and follows the -ant / -amment pattern.

examples.french: J’ai déjà déposé ma demande et je n’ai jamais reçu d’accusé de réception.
examples.english: I have already submitted my application and I have never received an acknowledgement.
examples.note: Short adverbs sit between the auxiliary and the participle, not after it.

examples.french: Nous suivons ce dossier de près et nous lisons attentivement chaque réponse.
examples.english: We are following this file closely and we read every reply carefully.
examples.note: « De près » and « attentivement » both render closely; « prochainement » means soon.

mistakes.avoid: Il a répondu bien à la question du jury.
mistakes.prefer: Il a bien répondu à la question du jury.
mistakes.why: In a compound tense, a short adverb of manner goes between the auxiliary and the participle.

mistakes.avoid: Elle explique vraiement la règle aux nouveaux arrivants.
mistakes.prefer: Elle explique vraiment la règle aux nouveaux arrivants.
mistakes.why: `Vrai` already ends in a vowel, so the adverb is built on the masculine and has no `e`: `vraiment`.

mistakes.avoid: J’ai déposé déjà ma demande la semaine dernière.
mistakes.prefer: J’ai déjà déposé ma demande la semaine dernière.
mistakes.why: In a compound tense a short adverb such as `déjà` goes between the auxiliary and the participle.

mistakes.avoid: Nous suivons le dossier assez de près depuis janvier.
mistakes.prefer: Nous suivons le dossier d’assez près depuis janvier.
mistakes.why: `Assez` is placed immediately before the adverb it modifies, and the resulting phrase after a verb of observation is `d’assez près`.

mistakes.avoid: Nous suivons les informations prochainement.
mistakes.prefer: Nous suivons les informations de près.
mistakes.why: `Prochainement` means soon; following something closely is `de près` or `attentivement`.

vocabulary.example: Une explication claire évite beaucoup de questions inutiles.
vocabulary.note: Feminine `claire` gives the adverb `clairement`.

vocabulary.example: Un agent patient reformule la consigne sans s’impatienter.
vocabulary.note: Adjectives in -ent give -emment: patient gives patiemment, not from the feminine.

vocabulary.example: Une démarche en ligne prend généralement moins de temps qu’un rendez-vous.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; very frequent in public-service contexts.

vocabulary.example: Une porte-parole a présenté les résultats de la consultation.
vocabulary.note: Feminine form for a woman; the compound is invariable in the singular.

vocabulary.example: Il lit couramment le français administratif depuis sa formation.
vocabulary.note: Built on `courant`, so it belongs to the `-amment` family; do not confuse it with `couramment` in the sense of commonly.

vocabulary.example: La municipalité suit de près l’évolution des demandes de logement.
vocabulary.note: Adverbial phrase; `attentivement` is its neutral single-word equivalent.

vocabulary.example: Le nouveau portail sera mis en service prochainement.
vocabulary.note: Refers to time, never to manner; do not use it for closely.

practice.prompt: Form the adverbs: `constant`, `prudent`, `absolu`, `heureux`.
practice.hint: Two nasal families, one vowel-final adjective, one regular feminine.
practice.answer: constamment, prudemment, absolument, heureusement

takeaways: Feminine plus `-ment`, unless the masculine already ends in a vowel.
`-ant` gives `-amment`, `-ent` gives `-emment`, built on the masculine.
Simple tense: after the verb. Compound tense: inside the verb group.

lessons.title: Les comparaisons et le superlatif
lessons.summary: Compare a quality with `plus/moins/aussi + adjective + que`, an action with `plus/moins/autant + que`, and a quantity with `plus/moins/autant de + noun + que`. The superlative adds the definite article: `le plus rapide`, `la moins chère`, and uses `de` for the group: `le quartier le plus vert de la ville`. Two irregular forms matter: the adjective `bon` becomes `meilleur` and the adverb `bien` becomes `mieux`.
objectives: Choose between `aussi`, `autant`, and `autant de` from what is being compared.
Build a superlative with the correct article and preposition.
Distinguish the irregular pair `meilleur` and `mieux`.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: The comparative word depends on the part of speech being compared. An adjective or an adverb takes `aussi`: `aussi fiable que`, `aussi rapidement que`. A verb takes `autant`: `Il travaille autant que moi`. A noun takes `autant de`: `autant de services que`. `Plus` and `moins` follow exactly the same distribution, and `de` is added before a noun.

A superlative marks the top or bottom of a group. Put the definite article before `plus` or `moins`, agreeing with the noun: `la solution la plus efficace`, `les quartiers les moins denses`. The group is introduced by `de`, where English uses in: `le quartier le plus vert de la ville`. Two irregular forms must be kept apart. `Meilleur` is the comparative of the adjective `bon` and agrees with the noun: `une meilleure solution`, `la meilleure candidate`. `Mieux` is the comparative of the adverb `bien` and never agrees: `Ce service fonctionne mieux`.

Comparison of identity works differently from comparison of degree. `Le même` states that two things are identical, it agrees with the noun it introduces — `le même`, `la même`, `les mêmes` — and the second term is always introduced by `que`, never by `comme`: `J’ai les mêmes documents que toi`, `Elle suit le même cours que moi`, `Les consignes sont les mêmes que l’an dernier`. The agreement follows the noun and not the person compared, so the form is `le même formulaire` even when speaking to a woman.
points: Use `aussi` before an adjective or an adverb, `autant` after a verb, `autant de` before a noun.
Add the definite article to form a superlative and agree it with the noun.
Introduce the reference group with `de`, not with `dans`.
Replace `plus bon` with `meilleur` and `plus bien` with `mieux`.
Check whether the word you are grading is an adjective or an adverb before choosing between `meilleur` and `mieux`.
Introduce the second term of `le même` with `que`, never with `comme`.
Agree `même` with the noun it introduces: `le même cours`, `les mêmes consignes`.

examples.french: Le transport en commun est aussi fiable que la voiture dans ce quartier.
examples.english: Public transit is as reliable as the car in this neighbourhood.
examples.note: « Aussi » before an adjective.

examples.french: Cette formation coûte autant que l’autre, mais elle propose plus de stages.
examples.english: This training course costs as much as the other one, but it offers more placements.
examples.note: « Autant » after a verb, « plus de » before a noun.

examples.french: Elle travaille moins rapidement que son collègue, mais elle relit davantage.
examples.english: She works less quickly than her colleague, but she proofreads more.
examples.note: « Moins » before an adverb.

examples.french: C’est la solution la plus efficace de toutes celles qui ont été proposées.
examples.english: It is the most effective solution of all those that were proposed.
examples.note: Superlative: definite article plus « de » for the group.

examples.french: Cette méthode est meilleure que l’autre, et elle fonctionne mieux en petit groupe.
examples.english: This method is better than the other one, and it works better in a small group.
examples.note: « Meilleure » grades a noun; « mieux » grades a verb.

examples.french: J’ai les mêmes documents que toi, et ce logement a le même loyer que l’autre.
examples.english: I have the same documents as you, and this unit has the same rent as the other one.
examples.note: Identity comparison agreeing with the noun and completed by « que ».

examples.french: Les consignes sont les mêmes que l’an dernier pour toutes les candidates.
examples.english: The instructions are the same as last year for all the applicants.
examples.note: « Les mêmes que » with a plural noun.

mistakes.avoid: Il travaille aussi que moi.
mistakes.prefer: Il travaille autant que moi.
mistakes.why: A verb is compared with `autant`; `aussi` is reserved for adjectives and adverbs.

mistakes.avoid: Ce logement est plus bon et il est chauffé plus bien.
mistakes.prefer: Ce logement est meilleur et il est mieux chauffé.
mistakes.why: `Bon` has the irregular comparative `meilleur`, and `bien` has `mieux`.

mistakes.avoid: J’ai le même formulaire comme toi.
mistakes.prefer: J’ai le même formulaire que toi.
mistakes.why: The second term of an identity comparison is introduced by `que`; `comme` expresses resemblance, not identity.

mistakes.avoid: Elle a rempli la même formulaire que moi.
mistakes.prefer: Elle a rempli le même formulaire que moi.
mistakes.why: `Même` agrees with the noun it introduces, and `formulaire` is masculine.

vocabulary.example: Le transport en commun coûte moins cher que la voiture au quotidien.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; often used in the plural `les transports en commun`.

vocabulary.example: Une formation courte permet de compléter rapidement un profil professionnel.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; `suivre une formation` means to take a course.

vocabulary.example: Une meilleure organisation réduit le nombre de rendez-vous manqués.
vocabulary.note: Comparative of `bon`; it agrees with the noun, unlike the adverb `mieux`.

vocabulary.french: le plus / la plus / les plus
vocabulary.example: C’est le quartier le plus vert de la ville.
vocabulary.note: Superlative marker; the group is introduced by `de`.

vocabulary.french: le même / la même / les mêmes
vocabulary.example: Les mêmes pièces justificatives sont exigées dans les deux bureaux.
vocabulary.note: Agrees with the noun; the second term is introduced by `que`.

practice.prompt: Complete: « Ce quartier a ___ services ___ le centre-ville, mais c’est le centre-ville qui reste ___ animé ___ la ville. »
practice.hint: Quantity first, then a superlative with its group.
practice.answer: Ce quartier a autant de services que le centre-ville, mais c’est le centre-ville qui reste le plus animé de la ville.

takeaways: Adjective or adverb: `aussi`. Verb: `autant`. Noun: `autant de`.
Superlative equals definite article plus `plus/moins`, with the group after `de`.
`Meilleur` grades nouns; `mieux` grades actions.
`Le même … que` for identity, agreeing with the noun, never with `comme`.

lessons.title: Les pronoms relatifs « qui », « que », « dont » et « où »
lessons.summary: A relative pronoun links a noun, its antecedent, to a clause that describes it. Choose by the role of the missing element in that clause: `qui` is its subject, `que` its direct object, `dont` replaces a complement built with `de`, and `où` replaces a complement of place or time. `Que` elides to `qu’` before a vowel; `qui` never elides.
objectives: Identify the antecedent and the missing role inside the relative clause.
Select among `qui`, `que`, `dont`, and `où` on that basis.
Avoid eliding `qui` and avoid repeating `de` after `dont`.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: An antecedent is the noun the relative clause describes. Rebuild the clause as an independent sentence and see what is missing. If the missing element performs the verb, use `qui`: `La conseillère vous reçoit` gives `la conseillère qui vous reçoit`. If it receives the verb directly, use `que`: `Vous devez remplir le formulaire` gives `le formulaire que vous devez remplir`.

Two further pronouns cover the most frequent prepositional cases. `Dont` replaces any complement introduced by `de`, whether it depends on a verb (`parler de`), a noun (`le titre de`), or an adjective (`fier de`); because `dont` already contains `de`, the preposition is never repeated. `Où` replaces a complement of place or of time, so it translates both where and when: `la ville où j’habite`, `l’année où je suis arrivé`. Note that `que` elides before a vowel (`qu’il`), while `qui` keeps its form (`qui a`).
points: Rebuild the clause as a full sentence to see which element is missing.
Use `qui` for the missing subject and `que` for the missing direct object.
Use `dont` whenever the original complement started with `de`, and drop that `de`.
Use `où` for a place and also for a moment in time.
Elide `que` to `qu’` before a vowel, but never write `qu’` for `qui`.

examples.french: La conseillère qui vous reçoit connaît bien le programme.
examples.english: The adviser who is meeting with you knows the program well.
examples.note: The missing element is the subject of « reçoit ».

examples.french: Le formulaire que vous devez remplir se trouve en ligne.
examples.english: The form that you must complete is online.
examples.note: The missing element is the direct object of « remplir ».

examples.french: Le programme dont je vous ai parlé accepte encore des candidatures.
examples.english: The program I told you about is still accepting applications.
examples.note: « Parler de » becomes « dont »; the preposition is not repeated.

examples.french: C’est un quartier dont les services de proximité sont excellents.
examples.english: It is a neighbourhood whose local services are excellent.
examples.note: « Dont » also renders whose with a noun complement.

examples.french: La ville où je me suis installé offre des cours de français gratuits.
examples.english: The city where I settled offers free French classes.
examples.note: « Où » replaces a complement of place.

examples.french: L’année où j’ai obtenu mon permis, tout est devenu plus simple.
examples.english: The year when I got my permit, everything became easier.
examples.note: « Où » also covers time, where English uses when.

mistakes.avoid: Le dossier dont j’ai besoin de est incomplet.
mistakes.prefer: Le dossier dont j’ai besoin est incomplet.
mistakes.why: `Dont` already contains `de`, so the preposition must not be repeated.

mistakes.avoid: La candidate qu’a déposé son dossier attend une réponse.
mistakes.prefer: La candidate qui a déposé son dossier attend une réponse.
mistakes.why: The missing element is the subject, and `qui` never elides.

vocabulary.example: Une conseillère en emploi aide à préparer les entrevues.
vocabulary.note: Feminine form; the masculine is `un conseiller`.

vocabulary.example: Un programme d’intégration accompagne les familles pendant un an.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; false friend with English `programme` in the sense of schedule.

vocabulary.example: Le service dont je parle a déménagé au rez-de-chaussée.
vocabulary.note: Relative pronoun replacing any complement built with `de`.

vocabulary.example: Le jour où j’ai reçu la réponse, j’ai appelé toute ma famille.
vocabulary.note: Relative pronoun of place and of time.

practice.prompt: Join with the right pronoun: « C’est un quartier. Je rêve de ce quartier. » and « Voici le bureau. J’ai déposé le dossier à ce bureau. »
practice.hint: One complement begins with `de`, the other is a place.
practice.answer: C’est un quartier dont je rêve. Voici le bureau où j’ai déposé le dossier.

takeaways: Missing subject: `qui`. Missing direct object: `que`.
Complement with `de`: `dont`, and never repeat `de`.
Place or moment: `où`.
keywords: relative pronouns qui, que, dont, and où

lessons.title: La possession avec « de »
lessons.summary: French has no apostrophe-s. Possession between two nouns is expressed with `de`, and the possessed item comes first: `le dossier de la candidate`. `De` contracts with `le` and `les` into `du` and `des`, but not with `la` or `l’`. A proper name takes no article: `le bureau de Marie`. To state belonging with a verb, use `appartenir à`, which takes an indirect complement.
objectives: Order the two nouns correctly in a possessive group.
Contract `de` with the article when the owner requires it.
Use `appartenir à` and `être à` for explicit ownership.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: Where English writes the applicant’s file, French reverses the order and inserts `de`: `le dossier de la candidate`. The rule is mechanical: possessed item, then `de`, then owner. The owner keeps its own determiner, which is why the contraction rules apply: `le bureau du directeur`, `la porte des bureaux`, but `le dossier de la candidate` and `l’adresse de l’école`.

Two verbs express the same idea explicitly. `Appartenir à` is the formal one and always takes an indirect complement: `Ce logement appartient à une coopérative`, `Ce dossier lui appartient`. `Être à` is the conversational equivalent and is followed by a stressed pronoun or a name: `Ce dossier est à moi`, `Ce vélo est à Sofia`. Note that `de` also introduces many non-possessive relationships, such as content or category (`un cours de français`), so the possessive reading depends on the meaning of the two nouns.
points: Write the possessed item first, then `de`, then the owner.
Contract to `du` or `des` when the owner takes `le` or `les`.
Leave a proper name without an article after `de`.
Use `appartenir à` plus an indirect complement for a formal statement of ownership.
Use `être à` plus a stressed pronoun in conversation.

examples.french: Voici le dossier de la candidate retenue pour le poste.
examples.english: Here is the file of the candidate selected for the position.
examples.note: Possessed item first, then « de » and the owner.

examples.french: Le bureau du directeur se trouve au deuxième étage.
examples.english: The director’s office is on the second floor.
examples.note: « De + le » contracts to « du ».

examples.french: L’adresse de l’école figure sur l’attestation d’inscription.
examples.english: The school’s address appears on the enrolment certificate.
examples.note: No contraction before an elided « l’ ».

examples.french: Ce logement appartient à une coopérative d’habitation.
examples.english: This housing unit belongs to a housing cooperative.
examples.note: « Appartenir à » takes an indirect complement.

examples.french: Ce dossier est à moi ; celui de Marie est resté à l’accueil.
examples.english: This file is mine; Marie’s is still at the reception desk.
examples.note: « Être à » in conversation, and a proper name with no article.

mistakes.avoid: C’est la candidate dossier.
mistakes.prefer: C’est le dossier de la candidate.
mistakes.why: French has no apostrophe-s construction; the possessed item comes first and is linked by `de`.

mistakes.avoid: Ce logement appartient une coopérative.
mistakes.prefer: Ce logement appartient à une coopérative.
mistakes.why: `Appartenir` requires the preposition `à` before its complement.

vocabulary.example: Le dossier de la candidate contient toutes les pièces justificatives.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; `monter un dossier` means to put an application together.

vocabulary.example: Une coopérative d’habitation gère cet immeuble depuis dix ans.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; common in Canadian housing vocabulary.

vocabulary.example: Ce terrain appartient à la municipalité depuis 1998.
vocabulary.note: Always followed by `à`; conjugated like `tenir`.

vocabulary.example: Le manuel de la professeure est resté sur son bureau.
vocabulary.note: Feminine form used in Canada; `une professeur` also occurs.

practice.prompt: Translate: « the director’s decision », « the students’ results », « the school’s address ».
practice.hint: Two of the three require a contraction.
practice.answer: la décision du directeur, les résultats des étudiants, l’adresse de l’école

takeaways: Possessed item, `de`, owner — always in that order.
`Du` and `des` are obligatory; `de la` and `de l’` are not contracted.
`Appartenir à` for formal ownership, `être à` for conversation.

lessons.title: Les nombres cardinaux et les nombres ordinaux
lessons.summary: Cardinal numbers count and are invariable, with two exceptions: `vingt` and `cent` take `-s` when multiplied and not followed by another number (`quatre-vingts`, `deux cents`, but `quatre-vingt-deux`, `deux cent trois`). `Million` and `milliard` are nouns and take `-s` plus `de` before a noun. Ordinal numbers rank and behave like adjectives, so `premier` has the forms `première`, `premiers`, `premières`.
objectives: Keep cardinal numbers invariable except in the two documented cases.
Treat `million` and `milliard` as nouns.
Agree an ordinal adjective with its noun.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: A cardinal number counts (`deux`, `vingt`, `cent`) and an ordinal number ranks (`deuxième`, `vingtième`). Cardinals do not agree, so `quatre étapes` and `quatre dossiers` are both correct. The only written variation concerns `vingt` and `cent`: they add `-s` when they are multiplied and end the number, so `quatre-vingts` and `trois cents`, but `quatre-vingt-cinq` and `trois cent dix` lose it again.

`Million` and `milliard` are ordinary nouns rather than numbers, so they take a plural `-s` and are linked to what they count by `de`: `deux millions de dollars`. Ordinals are formed by adding `-ième` to the cardinal (`trois` gives `troisième`), dropping a final `e` first (`quatre` gives `quatrième`). Only `premier` and `dernier` have a full set of agreeing forms; `deuxième` and the rest end in `-ième` and vary only in number.
points: Leave a cardinal number unchanged in front of any noun.
Add `-s` to `vingt` and `cent` only when multiplied and final in the number.
Write `million` and `milliard` with `-s` and follow them with `de`.
Form ordinals with `-ième`, dropping a final `e` from the cardinal.
Agree `premier` and `dernier` in gender and number with the noun.

examples.french: Les deux premières étapes de la demande se font en ligne.
examples.english: The first two steps of the application are completed online.
examples.note: Cardinal invariable, ordinal agreeing in the feminine plural.

examples.french: Le programme a accueilli quatre-vingts participants et deux cents visiteurs.
examples.english: The program welcomed eighty participants and two hundred visitors.
examples.note: « Vingt » and « cent » take -s when multiplied and final.

examples.french: La ville a investi quatre-vingt-cinq millions de dollars dans le transport.
examples.english: The city invested eighty-five million dollars in transportation.
examples.note: No -s on « vingt » before another number; « millions » is a noun followed by « de ».

examples.french: La troisième entrevue aura lieu vendredi matin.
examples.english: The third interview will take place on Friday morning.
examples.note: Ordinals in -ième vary only in number.

examples.french: C’est la dernière semaine pour déposer un dossier complet.
examples.english: It is the last week to submit a complete application.
examples.note: « Dernier » agrees like an ordinary adjective.

mistakes.avoid: Le projet coûte deux cents mille dollars.
mistakes.prefer: Le projet coûte deux cent mille dollars.
mistakes.why: `Cent` loses its `-s` when another number follows it.

mistakes.avoid: Les trois premiers étapes sont terminées.
mistakes.prefer: Les trois premières étapes sont terminées.
mistakes.why: `Premier` is an adjective and agrees with the feminine noun `étape`.

vocabulary.example: Une étape essentielle consiste à relire la consigne avant de répondre.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; `par étapes` means step by step.

vocabulary.example: Un participant sur trois a demandé une attestation de présence.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; feminine `une participante`.

vocabulary.example: La troisième inscrite a présenté un projet très structuré.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun from the participle of `inscrire`; masculine `un inscrit`.

vocabulary.example: Un million de dollars a été réservé au programme de rénovation.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun, not a determiner; it is followed by `de`.

practice.prompt: Write out: 80 participants, 82 participants, 300 dollars, 2 000 000 dollars.
practice.hint: Two of them lose the plural `-s`.
practice.answer: quatre-vingts participants, quatre-vingt-deux participants, trois cents dollars, deux millions de dollars

takeaways: Cardinals are invariable; `vingt` and `cent` are the two written exceptions.
`Million` and `milliard` are nouns and take `de`.
`Premier` and `dernier` agree fully; other ordinals only vary in number.

lessons.title: La ponctuation et les espaces typographiques
lessons.summary: Typography varies by region and publication. Quebec commonly omits spaces before `;`, `?`, and `!`, but also accepts narrow spaces; France commonly uses non-breaking spaces, often narrow, before these marks. This lesson illustrates the no-space Quebec convention. Both conventions use a non-breaking space before a colon and spaces inside French guillemets. Apostrophes stay attached to the words they join. Hyphens link inversion and affirmative imperative pronouns; traditional and rectified number spellings are both accepted.
objectives: Apply the Quebec spacing convention illustrated here and recognise accepted regional alternatives.
Use French guillemets, typographic apostrophes, dialogue dashes, and hyphens correctly.
Format percentages, currency amounts, times, abbreviations, and lists consistently.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: Distinguish grammar from typographic convention. The Office québécois de la langue française favours no space before `;`, `?`, and `!`, while also accepting a narrow space when available. France commonly uses a non-breaking space, often narrow, before these marks. Neither regional convention makes a sentence ungrammatical. The examples here use the no-space Quebec convention. Keep periods and commas attached to the preceding word, and put a non-breaking space before a colon so it cannot begin a new line.

In polished French typography, prefer guillemets with non-breaking spaces inside: `« texte »`, and curly apostrophes in `l’école`, `d’accord`, and `qu’il`. Straight quotation marks and apostrophes are common in plain text and are not grammar errors. Whichever apostrophe you use, do not insert spaces around an elision. Do not elide before an aspirated `h` or certain number words: `le héros`, `le onze`. Dialogue commonly starts each speaker’s turn on a new line with an em dash; some publications use an en dash instead.

A hyphen joins the verb and subject pronoun in inversion (`vient-il?`), including the euphonic `-t-` inserted between two vowel sounds (`va-t-il?`). It also joins an affirmative imperative to its pronouns (`donnez-le-moi`, `vas-y`, `prends-en`). Under the 1990 spelling recommendations, every element of a compound number is hyphenated (`vingt-et-un`, `cent-vingt-trois`); traditional spellings such as `vingt et un` and `cent vingt-trois` remain accepted.
