Symbols and abbreviations follow their own patterns: write a non-breaking space before `%`, `$`, and `€`; write time as `14 h 30`; write `M.` because the abbreviation cuts off the end of `monsieur`, but `Dr` and `Dre` without a period because their final letters remain. The abbreviation `etc.` already includes its period.
points: Keep periods and commas attached to the preceding word; before `;`, `?`, and `!`, follow the chosen regional convention.
Insert a non-breaking space before `:` and inside `«  »`.
Keep apostrophes attached to both sides; choose a consistent dialogue-dash convention.
Use hyphens in inversion, affirmative imperative pronoun groups, and rectified compound numbers.
Keep a non-breaking space between a number and `%`, `$`, or `€`, and around the `h` in a written time.

examples.french: Le dossier est complet : nous pouvons l’envoyer aujourd’hui.
examples.english: The file is complete: we can send it today.
examples.note: A non-breaking space precedes the colon.

examples.french: Avez-vous reçu mon courriel? Merci de me répondre rapidement!
examples.english: Did you receive my email? Please reply quickly!
examples.note: Canadian French normally places no space before the question or exclamation mark.

examples.french: La conseillère a répondu : « Votre demande est complète. »
examples.english: The adviser replied, “Your application is complete.”
examples.note: French guillemets contain non-breaking spaces.

examples.french:
— Avez-vous une pièce d’identité?
— Oui, je l’ai apportée.
examples.english: “Do you have a piece of identification?” “Yes, I brought it.”
examples.note: Each change of speaker is marked by an em dash; every reply starts a new line.

examples.french: Répondez-lui aujourd’hui et joignez-y les documents demandés.
examples.english: Reply to them today and attach the requested documents.
examples.note: Affirmative imperative pronouns are joined with hyphens.

examples.french: Le taux est de 15 %, les frais sont de 20 $ et le rendez-vous est fixé à 14 h 30.
examples.english: The rate is 15%, the fee is $20, and the appointment is set for 2:30 p.m.
examples.note: A non-breaking space separates a number from a symbol; written time uses `h`.

mistakes.avoid: « Votre dossier est prêt, dit-elle.
mistakes.prefer: « Votre dossier est prêt », dit-elle.
mistakes.why: Close the quotation before the narrator’s reporting clause. Opening and closing quotation marks must be paired.

mistakes.avoid: Je vais à l’ école demain.
mistakes.prefer: Je vais à l’école demain.
mistakes.why: An apostrophe is attached to the elided word and to the following word; no space is inserted.

mistakes.avoid: Va il venir à la réunion?
mistakes.prefer: Va-t-il venir à la réunion?
mistakes.why: Inversion takes hyphens, and a euphonic `t` separates the two vowel sounds.

vocabulary.example: La ponctuation claire rend une lettre officielle plus facile à lire.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; the ending `-tion` is a strong feminine clue.

vocabulary.example: Une espace insécable empêche le deux-points de commencer une nouvelle ligne.
vocabulary.note: In typography, `espace` is feminine.

vocabulary.example: Un guillemet français a la forme d’un petit chevron.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; normally used in the plural when naming the pair.

vocabulary.example: Une apostrophe remplace la voyelle supprimée dans « l’école ».
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; use the typographic apostrophe `’` in polished writing.

vocabulary.example: Un trait d’union relie le verbe et le pronom dans « vient-il ».
vocabulary.note: Masculine compound noun.

practice.prompt: Apply this lesson’s Quebec typography convention and correct the missing inversion hyphen: « Votre dossier est prêt : pouvez vous venir à 14h30 ? »
practice.hint: Use non-breaking spaces inside guillemets and before the colon, a hyphen in `pouvez-vous`, spaces around `h`, and this lesson’s no-space convention before `?`.
practice.answer: « Votre dossier est prêt : pouvez-vous venir à 14 h 30? »

takeaways: Quebec often omits spaces before `;`, `?`, and `!`, but accepts narrow spaces; France commonly uses non-breaking spaces.
Prefer guillemets and curly apostrophes in polished typography without treating plain-text alternatives as grammar errors.
Inversion and affirmative imperative pronouns require hyphens.

lessons.title: Les majuscules en français
lessons.summary: French uses capitals more sparingly than English. Days, months, seasons, languages, religions, professions, and nationality adjectives are lowercase. Proper place names and official names take capitals, as do nouns naming inhabitants. Generic words such as `rue`, `fleuve`, `ministère`, or `université` take a capital only when the official name requires it.
objectives: Distinguish common labels from proper names before choosing a capital.
Apply the nationality, language, title, profession, institution, and geographic-name rules.
Write dates, historical names, religious terms, and titles of works consistently.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: A capital letter signals a proper name, not importance. Write weekdays, months, and seasons in lowercase: `lundi`, `janvier`, `le printemps`. Languages and religions are also common nouns: `le français`, `l’anglais`, `le christianisme`, `l’islam`. A nationality adjective stays lowercase (`une candidate canadienne`), while the noun naming an inhabitant takes a capital (`une Canadienne`).

Titles and professions normally remain lowercase when an article introduces them: `le premier ministre`, `la docteure Tremblay`, `le professeur Dubois`. In direct address and formal correspondence, titles of civility may take a capital: `Madame, Monsieur`. For geographic names, capitalise the identifying element and keep the generic category lowercase: `le fleuve Saint-Laurent`, `la rue Sainte-Catherine`, `le mont Royal`. Follow the official spelling of an institution: `l’Université de Montréal`, but `une université montréalaise`.

Historical names and titles of works follow established forms rather than one mechanical rule. Write `le Moyen Âge`, `la Renaissance`, `la Révolution française`, and `la Première Guerre mondiale`; centuries stay lowercase. Sacred texts take capitals (`la Bible`, `le Coran`), but religions and followers remain lowercase. For books and films, reproduce the published title; frequent forms include `Le Petit Prince`, `Les Misérables`, `La Belle et la Bête`, and `L’Étranger`.
points: Lowercase weekdays, months, seasons, languages, religions, professions, and nationality adjectives.
Capitalise the noun naming an inhabitant: `une Canadienne`, but `une candidate canadienne`.
Keep a geographic generic word lowercase and capitalise the identifying proper name.
Use the institution’s official spelling; a generic description remains lowercase.
Preserve the established capitalisation of historical names and published titles.

examples.french: La réunion aura lieu lundi 15 janvier, au début de l’hiver.
examples.english: The meeting will take place on Monday, January 15, at the start of winter.
examples.note: Weekday, month, and season are lowercase.

examples.french: Une candidate canadienne a parlé français avec une Canadienne de Montréal.
examples.english: A Canadian candidate spoke French with a Canadian woman from Montreal.
examples.note: The adjective and language are lowercase; the inhabitant noun is capitalised.

examples.french: La docteure Tremblay rencontrera le ministre de la Santé.
examples.english: Dr. Tremblay will meet the minister of health.
examples.note: Professional and political titles remain lowercase after an article.

examples.french: Elle étudie à l’Université de Montréal, près du mont Royal.
examples.english: She studies at the Université de Montréal, near Mount Royal.
examples.note: The official institution name is capitalised; the geographic generic remains lowercase.

examples.french: La Première Guerre mondiale a profondément marqué le vingtième siècle.
examples.english: The First World War profoundly shaped the twentieth century.
examples.note: The event name is capitalised; the century is lowercase.

examples.french: Les musulmans lisent le Coran, et les chrétiens lisent la Bible.
examples.english: Muslims read the Quran, and Christians read the Bible.
examples.note: Followers and religions are lowercase; sacred texts are proper titles.

mistakes.avoid: Je pars Lundi 15 Janvier.
mistakes.prefer: Je pars lundi 15 janvier.
mistakes.why: French writes weekdays and months in lowercase.

mistakes.avoid: Elle est Canadienne et elle parle le Français.
mistakes.prefer: Elle est canadienne et elle parle le français.
mistakes.why: A nationality adjective and a language name are common words and therefore lowercase.

mistakes.avoid: Le Christianisme s’est développé pendant le moyen âge.
mistakes.prefer: Le christianisme s’est développé pendant le Moyen Âge.
mistakes.why: Religion names are lowercase, while the established historical name `Moyen Âge` takes capitals.

vocabulary.example: Une majuscule distingue le nom propre du nom commun.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun.

vocabulary.example: Une minuscule convient au nom d’une langue ou d’une profession.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun.

vocabulary.example: Un nom propre désigne une personne, un lieu ou une institution précise.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun phrase.

vocabulary.example: Un nom d’habitant comme « Canadienne » prend une majuscule.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun phrase; the adjective of nationality stays lowercase.

vocabulary.example: Un titre d’œuvre conserve la graphie choisie par l’éditeur.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun phrase.

practice.prompt: Correct the capitals: « Une Canadienne étudie le Français à l’université de Montréal depuis Septembre. »
practice.hint: Inhabitant noun, language, official institution, and month each follow a different rule.
practice.answer: Une Canadienne étudie le français à l’Université de Montréal depuis septembre.

takeaways: Capitalise proper names, not categories or titles merely because they seem important.
Person noun uppercase; nationality adjective and language lowercase.
For institutions, historical names, and works, follow the established official form.
keywords: proper names, nationalities, institutions, and titles

lessons.title: Les accents et les signes diacritiques
lessons.summary: A diacritic is a mark added to a letter that guides pronunciation or distinguishes words. The five main French marks are the acute accent, only on `e` (`créé`); the grave accent (`une règle`, `à`, `où`); the circumflex, often marking a lost letter (`une forêt`); the diaeresis, which changes how a vowel sequence is read (`le maïs`, `aiguë/aigüe`); and the cedilla, which keeps `c` soft before `a`, `o`, `u` (`une leçon`, `un reçu`). Some words have accepted traditional and rectified spellings, including `maître/maitre`.
objectives: Name the five French diacritics and the job each one does.
Decide when a mark changes pronunciation and when it only separates two words.
Write the cedilla and the diaeresis where the spelling requires them.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: The acute accent appears only on `e` and gives the closed sound found in `créé`, `déjà`, `une épaule`, and `léger`. The grave accent on `e` marks an open sound (`une règle`); `un décès` contains an acute accent first and a grave accent second. On `a` and `u`, the mark distinguishes words such as `a` (has) / `à` (to), `ou` (or) / `où` (where), and `la` (the) / `là` (there). These spelling distinctions do not necessarily imply different sounds. The circumflex often recalls a lost letter, especially `s`, as in `une forêt` and `une fête`; it can also distinguish words or pronunciations. The 1990 recommendations allow its omission in many words with `i` or `u`, so traditional `maître` and rectified `maitre` are both accepted.

The diaeresis, called `le tréma`, prevents a vowel sequence from being read in its usual way. In `le maïs`, `naïf`, `naïve`, `haïr`, `laïque`, `une faïence`, and `un canoë`, neighbouring vowels are pronounced separately. It does not always make the marked letter audible: in traditional `aiguë` and rectified `aigüe`, it signals that `u` is pronounced, while the final `e` remains silent. Both spellings are accepted. The cedilla under `c` keeps the soft sound before `a`, `o`, and `u`: `une leçon`, `un reçu`, `un caleçon`, `une façade`, `nous commençons`. It is not needed before `e` or `i`, where `c` is already soft.
points: Use the acute accent only on `e`, never on another vowel.
Use the grave accent to distinguish `a/à`, `ou/où`, and `la/là`; spelling and pronunciation distinctions do not always coincide.
Recognise the historical role of the circumflex and accepted variants such as `maître/maitre`.
Read the diaeresis by the word: separate vowels in `maïs`, but pronounced `u` and silent final `e` in `aiguë/aigüe`.
Add a cedilla to keep `c` soft before `a`, `o`, `u`, and never before `e` or `i`.

examples.french: Le dossier a déjà été créé, mais il reste léger.
examples.english: The file has already been created, but it is still thin.
examples.note: Acute accent on « déjà », « créé » and « léger ».

examples.french: Où est la salle ? Elle est là, à côté du bureau.
examples.english: Where is the room? It is there, next to the office.
examples.note: The grave accent distinguishes « où » from « ou », « là » from « la », and « à » from « a ».

examples.french: Nous avons marché dans la forêt jusqu’à la fête du village.
examples.english: We walked in the forest as far as the village festival.
examples.note: The circumflex marks an « s » that has disappeared from the spelling.

examples.french: Le maïs et une faïence naïve étaient exposés au musée.
examples.english: Corn and a naive piece of earthenware were on display at the museum.
examples.note: The diaeresis forces the two vowels to be pronounced separately.

examples.french: Nous commençons la leçon dès que le reçu est signé.
examples.english: We start the lesson as soon as the receipt is signed.
examples.note: The cedilla keeps « c » soft before « o »; « leçon » and « reçu » follow the same rule.

examples.french: Une douleur aiguë à l’épaule l’a empêché de travailler.
examples.english: A sharp pain in the shoulder prevented him from working.
examples.note: Traditional « aiguë » and rectified « aigüe » are both correct: the u is pronounced and the final e is silent.

mistakes.avoid: Nous commencons la leçon à neuf heures.
mistakes.prefer: Nous commençons la leçon à neuf heures.
mistakes.why: Before `o`, the letter `c` needs a cedilla to keep its soft sound.

mistakes.avoid: Je ne sais pas ou se trouve le bureau des permis.
mistakes.prefer: Je ne sais pas où se trouve le bureau des permis.
mistakes.why: `Ou` means or; the grave accent distinguishes `où`, which means where.

mistakes.avoid: Une douleur aigue l’a empêché de travailler.
mistakes.prefer: Une douleur aiguë l’a empêché de travailler.
mistakes.why: This feminine form needs a diaeresis: traditional `aiguë` and rectified `aigüe` are both accepted.

vocabulary.example: Un accent aigu ne se place jamais sur une autre voyelle que le « e ».
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun phrase; the mark appears in `créé` and `déjà`.

vocabulary.example: Un accent circonflexe rappelle souvent un « s » disparu, comme dans « forêt ».
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun phrase; found in `fête`, `pâte`, `mât`, and traditional `maître` (also accepted as `maitre`).

vocabulary.example: Un tréma sépare les deux voyelles de « maïs » et de « naïf ».
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun despite its final -a.

vocabulary.example: Une cédille garde le son doux du « c » dans « leçon » et « façade ».
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; used only before `a`, `o`, `u`.

vocabulary.example: Une forêt protégée borde le nord de la municipalité.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; the circumflex replaces an older `s`.

vocabulary.example: Un décès doit être déclaré à l’état civil dans les jours qui suivent.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; identical in the plural, with an acute accent on the first `e` and a grave accent on the second.

practice.prompt: Add the missing marks: « Nous commencons la lecon des que le recu est signe. »
practice.hint: Three cedillas, one acute accent on a past participle, and one grave accent.
practice.answer: Nous commençons la leçon dès que le reçu est signé.

takeaways: Acute accent: only on `e`.
Grave accent: opens `e`, or separates `a`/`à`, `ou`/`où`, `la`/`là`.
The circumflex can mark history or a distinction; traditional `maître` and rectified `maitre` are both accepted.
The diaeresis guides vowel reading; the cedilla softens `c` before `a`, `o`, `u`.

modules.title: Les verbes, les temps et les modes
modules.description: Master the present, past, future, conditional, subjunctive, and non-finite verb forms.

lessons.title: Les modèles du présent
lessons.summary: The present describes an action happening now, a habit, a general truth, a scheduled near-future event, or a historical event narrated vividly. Regular verbs follow three ending sets: `-er` takes `-e, -es, -e, -ons, -ez, -ent`; the `finir` type takes `-is, -is, -it, -issons, -issez, -issent`; `-re` takes `-s, -s, -, -ons, -ez, -ent`. Learn high-frequency irregular verbs in families.
objectives: Produce the three regular sets of present-tense endings without hesitation.
Group frequent irregular verbs into families instead of memorising them singly.
Predict which written forms are pronounced alike.
Recognise the present used for current, habitual, future, general, and historical meaning.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: A verb form has two parts: a stem carrying the meaning and an ending marking person and tense. For regular verbs the stem is the infinitive minus its last two letters, and the ending comes from the list matching that infinitive type. `Parler` gives `je parle, tu parles, il parle, nous parlons, vous parlez, ils parlent`; `finir` gives `je finis … nous finissons`; `attendre` gives `j’attends, tu attends, il attend, nous attendons`.

Irregular verbs are best learned in families, because one pattern then covers several verbs. `Tenir` and `venir` share `je tiens / nous tenons` and `je viens / nous venons`, and so do their derivatives `obtenir`, `maintenir`, `devenir`, `revenir`. `Ouvrir`, `offrir`, and `souffrir` end in `-ir` but take `-er` endings: `j’ouvre`, `il offre`. Pronunciation is a second organising principle: in `je parle`, `tu parles`, `il parle`, and `ils parlent` all four endings are silent, so only the subject distinguishes them in speech.

Context decides the time meaning. `Je travaille maintenant` is current; `Je travaille chaque samedi` is habitual; `L’eau bout à 100 °C` is a general truth; `Le train part demain` uses the present for a scheduled near future. In historical narration, the present can make a past event vivid, but ordinary personal narration normally uses past tenses.
points: Identify the infinitive type before choosing an ending set.
Use `-issons`, `-issez`, `-issent` for `-ir` verbs of the `finir` type only.
Learn `tenir` and `venir` together with their derivatives.
Remember that `ouvrir`, `offrir`, and `souffrir` take `-er` endings.
Expect `je parle`, `tu parles`, `il parle`, and `ils parlent` to sound the same.
Use a time marker such as `maintenant`, `chaque semaine`, or `demain` to make the intended present meaning clear.
Use the historical present as a narrative effect, not as the default past tense.
Study the spelling families — `-ayer`, `-oyer`, `-uyer`, `-indre`, `-aître`, `cueillir`, `vivre`, `suivre`, `servir`, `courir` — in the dedicated lesson that follows.

examples.french: Nous parlons français au travail, vous finissez le formulaire et ils attendent la réponse.
examples.english: We speak French at work, you finish the form, and they wait for the answer.
examples.note: One sentence showing the -er, -ir, and -re endings.

examples.french: Nous suivons un cours de français offert par le centre communautaire.
examples.english: We are taking a French course offered by the community centre.
examples.note: « Suivre » keeps its stem in the plural: nous suivons.

examples.french: Les familles reçoivent une réponse dans un délai de dix jours ouvrables.
examples.english: Families receive an answer within ten business days.
examples.note: « Recevoir » changes its stem in the third-person plural.

examples.french: J’obtiens mon attestation aujourd’hui et nous obtenons les nôtres demain.
examples.english: I am getting my certificate today and we are getting ours tomorrow.
examples.note: The `tenir` family alternates between « obtiens » and « obtenons ».

examples.french: Elle ouvre le dossier et elle offre son aide aux nouveaux arrivants.
examples.english: She opens the file and offers her help to newcomers.
examples.note: « Ouvrir » and « offrir » take -er endings despite their infinitive.

examples.french: Je travaille actuellement au service des permis.
examples.english: I currently work in the permits department.
examples.note: Current situation.

examples.french: Chaque samedi, nous faisons du bénévolat au centre communautaire.
examples.english: Every Saturday, we volunteer at the community centre.
examples.note: Habitual present.

examples.french: Le train part demain à huit heures.
examples.english: The train leaves tomorrow at eight o’clock.
examples.note: Present used for a scheduled near-future event.

examples.french: L’eau bout à 100 °C au niveau de la mer.
examples.english: Water boils at 100°C at sea level.
examples.note: Present used for a general scientific truth.

examples.french: En 1969, les premiers humains marchent sur la Lune.
examples.english: In 1969, the first humans walk on the Moon.
examples.note: Historical present used to make a past event vivid.

mistakes.avoid: Nous finons le formulaire avant midi.
mistakes.prefer: Nous finissons le formulaire avant midi.
mistakes.why: `Finir` belongs to the group that inserts `-iss-` in the plural forms.

mistakes.avoid: J’ouvris la porte du bureau chaque matin.
mistakes.prefer: J’ouvre la porte du bureau chaque matin.
mistakes.why: In the present, `ouvrir` takes the `-er` ending `-e`, not an `-ir` ending.

vocabulary.example: Je suis un cours de conversation deux soirs par semaine.
vocabulary.note: Irregular: `je suis`, `nous suivons`; identical to `être` in the first person singular.

vocabulary.example: Les candidats reçoivent une confirmation par courriel.
vocabulary.note: Stem change in the plural: `nous recevons`, `ils reçoivent`.

vocabulary.example: J’obtiens enfin une réponse du service d’immigration.
vocabulary.note: Belongs to the `tenir` family: `j’obtiens`, `nous obtenons`.

vocabulary.example: Un centre communautaire offre des cours de français gratuits.
vocabulary.note: Masculine compound noun; learn it as one unit.

vocabulary.example: Un délai de traitement de six semaines est indiqué sur le site.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; false friend, it does not mean delay in the sense of lateness.

practice.prompt: Conjugate for `nous` and `ils`: `parler`, `finir`, `attendre`, `venir`.
practice.hint: Only one of the four inserts `-iss-`.
practice.answer: nous parlons / ils parlent, nous finissons / ils finissent, nous attendons / ils attendent, nous venons / ils viennent

takeaways: Three ending sets cover every regular verb.
`Ouvrir`, `offrir`, `souffrir` look like `-ir` verbs but behave like `-er` verbs.
Four written forms, one sound: only the subject pronoun distinguishes them.
The present can locate an action now, regularly, tomorrow, generally, or in vivid historical narration.

lessons.title: Les familles orthographiques du présent
lessons.summary: Several verb groups change their written stem in the present. `-oyer` and `-uyer` change `y` to `i` before a silent ending (`je nettoie`), while `-ayer` accepts both spellings (`je paie` or `je paye`). `-indre` verbs use `-gn-` in the plural (`je crains`, `nous craignons`); `-aître` verbs have `-ss-` there (`nous connaissons`). `Cueillir` and its derivatives take `-er` endings. `Vivre`, `suivre`, and `servir` alternate stems, whereas `rire` and `courir` keep `ri-` and `cour-` in the present. Future forms must also be checked: `je verrai`, but `je prévoirai`.
objectives: Apply the `y` to `i` change to `-oyer` and `-uyer` verbs and recognise the double spelling allowed for `-ayer`.
Conjugate the `-indre`, `-aître`, `-ivre`, and `servir` families in the singular and the plural.
Distinguish `je verrai` from the futures `je prévoirai`, `je pourvoirai`, and `je fuirai`.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: A silent ending is one that is not pronounced: the `-e`, `-es`, and `-ent` of `je nettoie`, `tu nettoies`, `ils nettoient` are all silent, while the `-ons` and `-ez` of `nous nettoyons` and `vous nettoyez` are heard. Several families change their stem exactly at that boundary. Verbs in `-oyer` and `-uyer` write `i` instead of `y` before a silent ending: `je nettoie`, `nous nettoyons`; `j’essuie`, `vous essuyez`; `j’envoie`, `nous envoyons`. Verbs in `-ayer` accept both spellings, so `je paie` and `je paye` are equally correct, as are `j’essaie` and `j’essaye`. One irregularity is worth memorising separately: `envoyer` builds its future on `enverr-`, giving `j’enverrai`, not `j’envoierai`.

Three more families change the stem between singular and plural. Verbs in `-indre` — `craindre`, `joindre`, `peindre`, `atteindre`, `éteindre` — drop the `d` and write `-gn-` in the plural: `je crains`, `nous craignons`; `je joins`, `nous joignons`. Verbs in `-aître` — `connaître`, `paraître`, `disparaître`, `apparaître`, `naître` — double the `s` in the plural: `je connais`, `nous connaissons`; `vous paraissez`. `Cueillir`, `accueillir`, and `recueillir` end in `-ir` but take the `-er` endings, so `j’accueille`, `nous cueillons`, never `nous cueillissons`.

The last group is short but very frequent. `Vivre` and `suivre` give `je vis / nous vivons` and `je suis / nous suivons`; note that `je suis` is also the present of `être`, and context tells the two apart: `Je suis un cours de français` means *I am taking a French course*. `Servir` and its derivatives alternate stems too: `je sers / nous servons`. `Desservir` can mean to serve a place, as a transit line does, or to clear a table. In contrast, `rire`, `sourire`, and `courir` keep their written stems in the present: `je ris / nous rions`, `je souris / nous sourions`, `je cours / nous courons`; only the endings change. Do not extend the future of `voir` to every similar verb: `je verrai`, `je reverrai`, and `j’entreverrai`, but `je prévoirai`, `je pourvoirai`, and `je fuirai`.
points: Write `i` instead of `y` before a silent ending in `-oyer` and `-uyer` verbs.
Accept both `je paie` and `je paye`, and both `j’essaie` and `j’essaye`, for `-ayer` verbs.
Build the future of `envoyer` on `enverr-`: `j’enverrai`.
Replace `-nd-` with `-gn-` in the plural of `-indre` verbs: `nous craignons`, `nous joignons`.
Double the `s` in the plural of `-aître` verbs: `nous connaissons`, `vous paraissez`.
Give `cueillir`, `accueillir`, and `recueillir` the `-er` endings: `j’accueille`, `nous cueillons`.
Learn `je vis / nous vivons`, `je suis / nous suivons`, `je ris / nous rions`, `je sers / nous servons`, `je cours / nous courons` as fixed pairs.
Distinguish stem changes from ending changes: `rire` and `courir` keep `ri-` and `cour-` in the present.
Learn the futures `je verrai`, `je prévoirai`, `je pourvoirai`, and `je fuirai` separately.

examples.french: Je paie mon loyer par virement le premier du mois, et nous nettoyons les bureaux avant l’inspection.
examples.english: I pay my rent by transfer on the first of the month, and we clean the offices before the inspection.
examples.note: « Paie » with a silent ending, « nettoyons » with a pronounced one.

examples.french: J’envoie les documents numérisés ce soir et je vous enverrai l’original par la poste.
examples.english: I am sending the scanned documents tonight and I will send you the original by mail.
examples.note: Present « envoie », irregular future « enverrai ».

examples.french: Je crains un retard, mais nous joignons déjà toutes les pièces au dossier.
examples.english: I am afraid of a delay, but we are already attaching all the supporting documents to the file.
examples.note: « Crains » in the singular, « joignons » with -gn- in the plural.

examples.french: Elle connaît bien les services offerts aux nouveaux arrivants, et vous paraissez inquiets avant l’entretien.
examples.english: She knows the services offered to newcomers well, and you look worried before the interview.
examples.note: « Connaît » with a circumflex, « paraissez » with a doubled s.

examples.french: J’accueille les participants à la réception pendant que mes collègues cueillent les fruits du jardin communautaire.
examples.english: I welcome the participants at reception while my colleagues pick the fruit from the community garden.
examples.note: The « cueillir » family takes -er endings in the present.

examples.french: Je suis un cours de français le mardi soir et je vis dans ce quartier depuis deux ans.
examples.english: I take a French course on Tuesday evenings and I have lived in this neighbourhood for two years.
examples.note: « Je suis » is here the present of « suivre », not of « être ».

examples.french: Cette ligne d’autobus dessert le centre-ville toutes les dix minutes.
examples.english: This bus line serves the downtown area every ten minutes.
examples.note: « Desservir » in its transit meaning: to serve or link a place.

examples.french: Nous verrons la conseillère à quatorze heures, et les enfants courent déjà dans le parc.
examples.english: We will see the adviser at two o’clock, and the children are already running in the park.
examples.note: Future stem « verr- » for « voir »; « courent » for « courir ».

examples.french: Je prévoirai une journée de congé pour le déménagement.
examples.english: I will plan a day off for the move.
examples.note: « Prévoir » keeps prévoir- in the future; it does not follow « je verrai ».

mistakes.avoid: Je nettoye la cuisine avant l’inspection du logement.
mistakes.prefer: Je nettoie la cuisine avant l’inspection du logement.
mistakes.why: `-oyer` and `-uyer` verbs must write `i` before a silent ending; only `-ayer` verbs allow both spellings.

mistakes.avoid: Je vous envoierai les documents demain matin.
mistakes.prefer: Je vous enverrai les documents demain matin.
mistakes.why: `Envoyer` builds its future on the irregular stem `enverr-`.

mistakes.avoid: Je préverrai une journée de congé pour le déménagement.
mistakes.prefer: Je prévoirai une journée de congé pour le déménagement.
mistakes.why: `Prévoir` uses the future stem `prévoir-`, unlike `voir`, which uses `verr-`.

mistakes.avoid: Nous craindons un retard dans le traitement du dossier.
mistakes.prefer: Nous craignons un retard dans le traitement du dossier.
mistakes.why: `-indre` verbs replace `-nd-` with `-gn-` in the plural of the present.

mistakes.avoid: Nous connaisons bien cette procédure et nous cueillissons les documents à l’accueil.
mistakes.prefer: Nous connaissons bien cette procédure et nous recueillons les documents à l’accueil.
mistakes.why: `-aître` verbs double the `s` in the plural, and the `cueillir` family takes `-er` endings, never `-iss-`.

vocabulary.example: Nous nettoyons la salle communautaire après chaque activité.
vocabulary.note: `Y` becomes `i` before a silent ending: `je nettoie`.

vocabulary.example: Le centre accueille les nouveaux arrivants du lundi au vendredi.
vocabulary.note: Ends in `-ir` but takes the `-er` endings: `j’accueille`.

vocabulary.example: Deux lignes de métro desservent ce secteur depuis l’an dernier.
vocabulary.note: Transit meaning first; it also means to clear a table.

vocabulary.example: Une ligne d’autobus supplémentaire reliera le quartier à la gare.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun phrase; the gender comes from `ligne`.

vocabulary.example: Un virement automatique évite les retards de paiement du loyer.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; `faire un virement` is the usual verb phrase.

vocabulary.example: Nous craignons que le délai soit trop court pour rassembler les pièces.
vocabulary.note: Plural stem in `-gn-`; the participle is `craint`.

practice.prompt: Conjugate for `je` and `nous`: `nettoyer`, `craindre`, `connaître`, `suivre`. Then give the future of `envoyer`, `voir`, and `prévoir` for `je`.
practice.hint: All four present-tense pairs change their written stem; the future of `prévoir` does not follow `voir`.
practice.answer: je nettoie / nous nettoyons ; je crains / nous craignons ; je connais / nous connaissons ; je suis / nous suivons. J’enverrai ; je verrai ; je prévoirai.

takeaways: Silent ending equals `i` in `-oyer` and `-uyer`; `-ayer` allows both spellings.
`-indre` gives `-gn-` in the plural and `-aître` doubles the `s`.
`Rire` and `courir` keep their stems in the present; their endings change.
`Envoyer` has the future `enverr-`, `voir` has `verr-`, but `prévoir` keeps `prévoir-`.

lessons.title: La formation du passé composé
lessons.summary: The compound past combines a present-tense auxiliary with a past participle. Most verbs take `avoir`. `Être` is used by every reflexive verb and by a closed list of intransitive verbs of movement or change of state: `aller`, `venir`, `arriver`, `partir`, `entrer`, `sortir`, `monter`, `descendre`, `passer`, `rester`, `tomber`, `naître`, `mourir`, `devenir`, `retourner`. Six of these switch to `avoir` when they take a direct object: `monter`, `descendre`, `sortir`, `rentrer`, `passer`, `retourner`.
objectives: Select the auxiliary from the verb type and from the presence of a direct object.
Build the past participle of regular and frequent irregular verbs.
Agree the participle with the subject when the auxiliary is `être`.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: A past participle is the fixed form used after an auxiliary: `parlé` for `-er` verbs, `fini` for `-ir` verbs, `attendu` for `-re` verbs. The compound past then places a present-tense `avoir` or `être` in front of it. The default auxiliary is `avoir`; `être` covers all reflexive verbs and the closed movement list given above.

With `être`, the participle agrees with the subject exactly like an adjective: `elle est arrivée`, `ils sont partis`, `elles sont restées`. With `avoir` there is no subject agreement. Six movement verbs change auxiliary according to the sentence: used alone they take `être` (`Elle est montée au troisième étage`), but used with a direct object they take `avoir` (`Elle a monté les dossiers`). The test is simply whether something is being moved.
points: Ask first whether the verb is reflexive: if it is, the auxiliary is always `être`.
Check the closed movement list before choosing `être` for a non-reflexive verb.
Add a direct object test for `monter`, `descendre`, `sortir`, `rentrer`, `passer`, `retourner`.
Agree the participle with the subject whenever the auxiliary is `être`.
Leave the participle unchanged after `avoir` unless a direct object precedes it.

examples.french: Elle est arrivée au Canada avec sa famille l’an dernier.
examples.english: She arrived in Canada with her family last year.
examples.note: « Arriver » takes être, and the participle agrees with the subject.

examples.french: Nous nous sommes inscrits à un programme de formation professionnelle.
examples.english: We enrolled in a professional training program.
examples.note: Every reflexive verb takes être.

examples.french: La technicienne est montée au troisième étage pour réparer le réseau.
examples.english: The technician went up to the third floor to repair the network.
examples.note: « Monter » with no object: auxiliary être.

examples.french: Elle a monté les cartons au troisième étage avant la réunion.
examples.english: She carried the boxes up to the third floor before the meeting.
examples.note: The same verb with a direct object: auxiliary avoir, no agreement.

examples.french: Nous avons attendu la réponse pendant six semaines.
examples.english: We waited for the answer for six weeks.
examples.note: Default auxiliary avoir with a regular -re participle.

mistakes.avoid: Elle a allé à la clinique ce matin.
mistakes.prefer: Elle est allée à la clinique ce matin.
mistakes.why: `Aller` belongs to the `être` list, and its participle then agrees with the subject.

mistakes.avoid: Elle est montée les dossiers au deuxième étage.
mistakes.prefer: Elle a monté les dossiers au deuxième étage.
mistakes.why: With a direct object, `monter` switches to the auxiliary `avoir`.

vocabulary.english: to enrol in, to register for
vocabulary.example: Nous nous sommes inscrits à un cours de français avancé.
vocabulary.note: Reflexive, so the auxiliary is always `être`; participle `inscrit`.

vocabulary.english: to go up; to carry up
vocabulary.example: Elle est montée à l’étage, puis elle a monté les dossiers.
vocabulary.note: Auxiliary `être` alone, `avoir` with a direct object.

vocabulary.example: Une inscription tardive a tout de même été acceptée par le centre.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; the ending -tion is a feminine hint.

vocabulary.example: Un étage supplémentaire a été construit au-dessus du magasin.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; the ground floor is `le rez-de-chaussée`.

practice.prompt: Put into the compound past: « Elle (sortir) à midi. » and « Elle (sortir) les documents du classeur. »
practice.hint: The second sentence has a direct object.
practice.answer: Elle est sortie à midi. Elle a sorti les documents du classeur.

takeaways: Reflexive verbs and the movement list take `être`; everything else takes `avoir`.
Six movement verbs switch to `avoir` as soon as a direct object appears.
Subject agreement belongs to `être`, not to `avoir`.

lessons.title: Les familles de participes passés irréguliers
lessons.summary: Many irregular past participles follow useful ending patterns: `-u` in `voulu`, `reçu`, `tenu`; `-is` in `pris`, `mis`, `compris`; `-it` in `dit`, `écrit`, `conduit`; `-ert` in `ouvert`, `offert`, `couvert`; and `-int` in `peint`, `joint`, `atteint`. These are not the only endings: `ri`, `fui`, `lui`, and `nui` end in `-i`. A known base often helps predict a derivative, but auxiliary choice and agreement must be checked separately.
objectives: Sort a new irregular verb into the right participle family.
Derive compound verbs from the base verb you already know.
Reuse each participle immediately in a compound tense.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: A past participle is the verb form used with an auxiliary, as `reçu` in `nous avons reçu`. Its basic form may acquire agreement endings in other constructions. Many irregular participles cluster into useful families: `prendre` gives `pris`, and the related `apprendre`, `comprendre`, and `reprendre` give `appris`, `compris`, and `repris`. The five main patterns illustrated here are a learning aid, not an exhaustive list.

The same logic applies elsewhere: `tenir` gives `tenu`, so `obtenir` gives `obtenu` and `maintenir` gives `maintenu`; `écrire` gives `écrit`, so `décrire` gives `décrit` and `inscrire` gives `inscrit`; `ouvrir` gives `ouvert`, so `couvrir` gives `couvert` and `découvrir` gives `découvert`. Choosing the family does not settle the auxiliary or the agreement, which are decided separately.

Many verbs in `-uire` have participles in `-uit`: `conduit`, `traduit`, `construit`, `détruit`, `produit`, `introduit`, `réduit`. This is not universal: `luire` gives `lui`, and `nuire` gives `nui`. Check the construction separately from the ending. In ordinary active uses, these verbs take `avoir`: `Elle a conduit jusqu’à Laval`, even though driving involves movement. Pronominal forms take `être`: `Elle s’est conduite correctement` means she behaved correctly. The passive also uses `être`: `Elle est conduite à la clinique` means she is being driven to the clinic. Neither construction is an error.
points: Identify the base verb hidden inside a prefixed verb.
Look for common patterns in `-u`, `-is`, `-it`, `-ert`, and `-int`, while recognising other endings such as `-i`.
Use the base verb to help learn derivatives, and check their actual forms.
Check the auxiliary separately; the family says nothing about it.
Write each new participle inside a full compound-past sentence.
Use `avoir` in `elle a conduit`; distinguish the pronominal `elle s’est conduite` and the passive `elle est conduite`.
Many `-uire` participles end in `-uit`, but learn exceptions such as `lui` and `nui`.

examples.french: Nous avons reçu la confirmation de notre rendez-vous ce matin.
examples.english: We received confirmation of our appointment this morning.
examples.note: « Recevoir » belongs to the -u family.

examples.french: Avez-vous ouvert le courriel envoyé par le ministère ?
examples.english: Did you open the email sent by the ministry?
examples.note: « Ouvrir » belongs to the -ert family.

examples.french: J’ai pris rendez-vous et j’ai compris toute la procédure.
examples.english: I made an appointment and understood the whole procedure.
examples.note: « Prendre » gives pris, so « comprendre » gives compris.

examples.french: Elle a obtenu son permis et elle a écrit une lettre de remerciement.
examples.english: She obtained her permit and wrote a thank-you letter.
examples.note: The `tenir` and `écrire` families give `obtenu` and `écrit`.

examples.french: Le service a atteint son objectif et a produit un rapport détaillé.
examples.english: The department reached its target and produced a detailed report.
examples.note: « Atteindre » is in the -int family, « produire » in the -it family.

examples.french: Elle a conduit jusqu’à Laval pour l’entretien, et j’ai traduit les documents en anglais.
examples.english: She drove to Laval for the interview, and I translated the documents into English.
examples.note: « Conduire » takes « avoir » despite expressing movement.

examples.french: Nous avons construit un dossier complet et nous avons réduit le délai de traitement.
examples.english: We built a complete file and we shortened the processing time.
examples.note: Same family, same auxiliary and same participle ending.

examples.french: Ce retard a nui au projet, mais la responsable s’est conduite avec professionnalisme.
examples.english: This delay harmed the project, but the manager behaved professionally.
examples.note: « Nuire » gives « nui »; pronominal « se conduire » takes être.

mistakes.avoid: J’ai comprendu la consigne du premier coup.
mistakes.prefer: J’ai compris la consigne du premier coup.
mistakes.why: `Comprendre` follows `prendre`, whose participle is `pris`.

mistakes.avoid: Elle a ouvri le dossier hier après-midi.
mistakes.prefer: Elle a ouvert le dossier hier après-midi.
mistakes.why: `Ouvrir` belongs to the `-ert` family.

mistakes.avoid: Elle a conduis jusqu’à Laval pour son entretien.
mistakes.prefer: Elle a conduit jusqu’à Laval pour son entretien.
mistakes.why: The past participle is `conduit`; `conduis` is a present-tense form.

mistakes.avoid: J’ai traduis les documents demandés par le ministère.
mistakes.prefer: J’ai traduit les documents demandés par le ministère.
mistakes.why: `Traduis` is a present-tense form; the past participle of `traduire` is `traduit`.

vocabulary.example: J’ai compris la consigne après une deuxième lecture.
vocabulary.note: Participle `compris`, from the `prendre` family.

vocabulary.example: Le programme a atteint son objectif de participation.
vocabulary.note: Participle `atteint`, from the `-indre` family.

vocabulary.example: Une confirmation écrite a été reçue le lendemain matin.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; frequent in administrative correspondence.

vocabulary.example: Un courriel officiel a confirmé la date du rendez-vous.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; standard term in Canada, where `un mail` is avoided in writing.

vocabulary.example: Elle a conduit deux heures pour se rendre à la clinique.
vocabulary.note: Active `conduire` takes `avoir` here; distinguish pronominal `se conduire` and the passive, which use `être`.

practice.prompt: Give the past participle: `apprendre`, `découvrir`, `maintenir`, `décrire`.
practice.hint: Each one belongs to a family you already know.
practice.answer: appris, découvert, maintenu, décrit

takeaways: Five useful ending patterns cover many irregular participles, not all of them.
A prefix does not change the family: `comprendre` follows `prendre`.
The family gives the form, never the auxiliary.
Many `-uire` verbs give `-uit`, but `luire` gives `lui` and `nuire` gives `nui`; auxiliary choice depends on the construction.

lessons.title: L’accord du participe passé avec un complément placé avant
lessons.summary: With `avoir`, the past participle normally agrees with a preceding direct object: `les lettres que j’ai écrites`. With a non-pronominal verb using `être`, it agrees with the subject: `elles sont arrivées`. For ordinary reflexive or reciprocal uses, identify the direct object and its position: `elles se sont lavées`, but `elles se sont lavé les mains` and `elles se sont parlé`. Other pronominal meanings have their own pattern: `elles se sont plaintes`, but `elles se sont rendu compte`.
objectives: Locate the direct object and check whether it precedes the participle.
Apply subject agreement only where the auxiliary licenses it.
Analyse a reflexive pronoun before agreeing with it.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: A direct object answers whom or what without a preposition. With `avoir`, French agrees the participle only when that object has already appeared, which happens in three situations: after the object pronouns `le`, `la`, `les`, `me`, `te`, `nous`, `vous`; after the relative pronoun `que`; and in a question introduced by `quel` or `combien de`. In `Nous les avons envoyées`, `les` stands for `les demandes`, so the participle takes `-es`.

With `être` and a non-pronominal verb, agreement is with the subject. Ordinary reflexive and reciprocal uses need another step: find the direct object and check its position. In `elles se sont lavées`, `se` is the preceding direct object, so the participle agrees. In `elles se sont lavé les mains`, the direct object `les mains` follows and `se` is indirect, so there is no agreement. Moving that object before the verb restores agreement: `les mains qu’elles se sont lavées`. In `elles se sont parlé`, `parler à` makes `se` indirect, so there is no agreement.

Some verbs are essentially pronominal, such as `s’enfuir` and `se méprendre`; others acquire a distinct meaning with the pronoun, such as `se plaindre` (to complain) and `s’apercevoir` (to realise). These examples agree with the subject: `Elles se sont enfuies`, `Elles se sont méprises sur la date`, `Elle s’est plainte du bruit`. Do not say that `plaindre` exists only with `se`: `Je plains cette famille` means I feel sorry for this family. Check fixed expressions separately rather than extending subject agreement to every pronominal verb. In `se rendre compte`, the direct object is `compte`, placed after the participle, so `rendu` stays unchanged: `Elle s’est rendu compte de l’erreur`.
points: Identify the auxiliary before looking for anything else.
With `avoir`, search to the left of the participle for a direct object.
Agree with a preceding `le`, `la`, `les`, or with the relative `que`.
With non-reflexive `être`, agree with the subject.
For ordinary reflexive or reciprocal uses, agree with a preceding direct object, not with an indirect `se`.
Learn subject agreement in forms such as `elle s’est enfuie` and `elle s’est plainte`; `plaindre quelqu’un` has a different meaning.
Leave `se rendre compte` invariable, because `compte` is the direct object and follows the participle.
Remember that `monter`, `descendre`, `sortir`, `rentrer`, `passer`, and `retourner` switch to `avoir` with a direct object, and then follow the `avoir` rule.

examples.french: Les demandes ? Nous les avons envoyées hier après-midi.
examples.english: The applications? We sent them yesterday afternoon.
examples.note: The preceding direct object « les » is feminine plural.

examples.french: La lettre que j’ai écrite est restée sans réponse.
examples.english: The letter that I wrote went unanswered.
examples.note: The relative « que » is the preceding direct object.

examples.french: Les formulaires que nous avons remplis sont maintenant complets.
examples.english: The forms that we filled in are now complete.
examples.note: Masculine plural agreement after « que ».

examples.french: Elle s’est lavé les mains avant le rendez-vous.
examples.english: She washed her hands before the appointment.
examples.note: The direct object « les mains » follows, so no agreement.

examples.french: Les deux conseillères se sont parlé avant la réunion.
examples.english: The two advisers spoke to each other before the meeting.
examples.note: « Parler à » makes « se » indirect, so the participle does not agree.

examples.french: Elle s’est plainte du bruit, et elles se sont méprises sur la date de l’audience.
examples.english: She complained about the noise, and they were mistaken about the hearing date.
examples.note: These pronominal meanings take subject agreement; « plaindre quelqu’un » without se means to feel sorry for someone.

examples.french: Elle s’est rendu compte de l’erreur avant l’envoi du dossier.
examples.english: She realised the mistake before sending the file.
examples.note: « Compte » is the direct object and follows, so the participle stays invariable.

examples.french: Nous avons retourné le formulaire signé, puis nous sommes retournés au bureau des permis.
examples.english: We returned the signed form, then we went back to the permits office.
examples.note: « Retourner » takes « avoir » with a direct object and « être » without one.

mistakes.avoid: Les documents ? Elle les a envoyé hier.
mistakes.prefer: Les documents ? Elle les a envoyés hier.
mistakes.why: `Les` stands for the masculine plural `les documents` and precedes the participle.

mistakes.avoid: Elles se sont lavées les mains avant de partir.
mistakes.prefer: Elles se sont lavé les mains avant de partir.
mistakes.why: The direct object is `les mains`, which follows the verb; `se` is indirect.

mistakes.avoid: Elle s’est plaint du bruit auprès du propriétaire.
mistakes.prefer: Elle s’est plainte du bruit auprès du propriétaire.
mistakes.why: In the pronominal meaning to complain, `se plaindre` takes subject agreement: feminine singular `plainte`.

mistakes.avoid: Elle s’est rendue compte de l’erreur trop tard.
mistakes.prefer: Elle s’est rendu compte de l’erreur trop tard.
mistakes.why: In `se rendre compte`, the direct object `compte` comes after the participle, so there is no agreement.

vocabulary.example: Les formulaires que nous avons remplis étaient en double exemplaire.
vocabulary.note: Regular `-ir` verb of the `finir` type; participle `rempli`.

vocabulary.example: La lettre que j’ai écrite est partie ce matin.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; triggers a feminine singular participle when placed before.

vocabulary.example: Les pièces justificatives que j’ai jointes figurent en annexe.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun, usually plural in administrative language.

vocabulary.example: Une annexe détaillée accompagne le rapport final.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; `en annexe` means attached.

vocabulary.example: Plusieurs locataires se sont plaints du chauffage insuffisant.
vocabulary.note: This pronominal meaning takes subject agreement; non-pronominal `plaindre quelqu’un` means to feel sorry for someone.

practice.prompt: Agree if required: « Les attestations que j’ai (recevoir) », « Elle s’est (couper) le doigt », « Elles sont (partir) ».
practice.hint: One preceding direct object, one following direct object, one subject agreement.
practice.answer: Les attestations que j’ai reçues, Elle s’est coupé le doigt, Elles sont parties

takeaways: `Avoir` agrees only with a direct object placed before the participle.
Non-reflexive `être` agrees with the subject, automatically.
For ordinary reflexive and reciprocal uses, locate the direct object before deciding agreement.
Learn the pattern of each pronominal meaning: `elles se sont plaintes`, but `elles se sont rendu compte`.
keywords: past-participle agreement with a preceding object

lessons.title: L’imparfait
lessons.summary: The imperfect describes a past situation from the inside: background, description, a state, an action in progress, or a repeated habit. Build it from the present `nous` form minus `-ons`, then add `-ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient`. `Être` is the only verb with an irregular stem, `ét-`. Verbs in `-cer` write `ç` and verbs in `-ger` keep `e` before endings starting with `a`: `je commençais`, `il neigeait`.
objectives: Derive the imperfect stem from the present `nous` form.
Choose the imperfect for habit, description, and ongoing background.
Apply the spelling adjustments of `-cer` and `-ger` verbs.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: The imperfect presents a past situation without marking its beginning or end. It therefore covers four everyday uses: a repeated habit (`je faisais du bénévolat chaque semaine`), a description or state (`il faisait froid`), an action in progress interrupted by another (`je travaillais quand la connexion est tombée`), and a past viewpoint in reported speech (`il a dit qu’il voulait déménager`).

The formation is unusually regular. Take the present `nous` form, remove `-ons`, and add the endings: `nous finissons` gives `je finissais`, `nous prenons` gives `je prenais`, `nous faisons` gives `je faisais`. Only `être` escapes this, using `ét-`. Two spelling families protect pronunciation: `-cer` verbs write `ç` before `a` (`je commençais` but `nous commencions`), and `-ger` verbs keep the `e` (`il neigeait`, `je mangeais`, but `nous mangions`).
points: Start from the present `nous` form, not from the infinitive.
Use the imperfect for a habit, a description, or an action in progress.
Remember the single irregular stem: `ét-` for `être`.
Write `ç` in `-cer` verbs before `-ais`, `-ait`, `-aient`.
Keep the `e` in `-ger` verbs before those same endings.

examples.french: Je travaillais à distance lorsque la connexion est tombée en panne.
examples.english: I was working remotely when the connection went down.
examples.note: Imperfect for the ongoing action, compound past for the interruption.

examples.french: Quand j’étais étudiant, je faisais du bénévolat chaque semaine.
examples.english: When I was a student, I volunteered every week.
examples.note: Irregular stem ét- and a repeated habit.

examples.french: Il faisait froid et les routes étaient glissantes ce matin-là.
examples.english: It was cold and the roads were slippery that morning.
examples.note: Description and background.

examples.french: Je commençais mon bénévolat et il neigeait déjà sur la ville.
examples.english: I was beginning my volunteer work and it was already snowing over the city.
examples.note: `-cer` takes ç and `-ger` keeps e before -ait.

examples.french: Nous commencions toujours la réunion par un tour de table.
examples.english: We always started the meeting with a round of introductions.
examples.note: No ç before -ions, because the ending does not start with a.

mistakes.avoid: Quand j’étais petit, j’ai nagé chaque matin.
mistakes.prefer: Quand j’étais petit, je nageais chaque matin.
mistakes.why: A repeated childhood habit takes the imperfect, not the compound past.

mistakes.avoid: Je commencais mon stage en septembre.
mistakes.prefer: Je commençais mon stage en septembre.
mistakes.why: A `-cer` verb needs the cedilla before an ending starting with `a`.

vocabulary.example: Je faisais du bénévolat dans une banque alimentaire chaque samedi.
vocabulary.note: Fixed expression; `un bénévole` is the person.

vocabulary.example: Je commençais toujours par relire la consigne.
vocabulary.note: `-cer` verb: cedilla before `a` and `o`.

vocabulary.example: Une habitude quotidienne rend les progrès plus réguliers.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; `avoir l’habitude de` means to be used to.

vocabulary.example: Une connexion instable a interrompu l’entrevue en ligne.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; the ending -ion is a feminine hint.

practice.prompt: Put into the imperfect for `je` and `nous`: `manger`, `placer`, `être`.
practice.hint: The `nous` forms lose the spelling adjustment.
practice.answer: je mangeais / nous mangions, je plaçais / nous placions, j’étais / nous étions

takeaways: Stem from the present `nous` form; only `être` is irregular.
Habit, description, ongoing action, past viewpoint.
`ç` and `e` appear only before endings starting with `a`.

lessons.title: Le choix d’un temps du passé
lessons.summary: Use the compound past for a bounded, completed event and the imperfect for the surrounding description or habit. Add the pluperfect for an event completed before another past event: it is formed with the imperfect of `avoir` or `être` plus a past participle (`j’avais déposé`, `elle était partie`). The simple past (`il entra`) belongs to literary and historical writing; recognise it when reading, but use the compound past yourself.
objectives: Separate narrative events from background information.
Form and place the pluperfect for an earlier past event.
Recognise simple-past forms without producing them.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: A narrative has two planes. Events that advance the story are bounded and take the compound past. Description, states, weather, feelings, and repeated habits form the background and take the imperfect. A single sentence often contains both: `Je préparais mon entrevue` sets the scene, `quand la responsable m’a appelé` moves the story forward.

A third tense is needed as soon as one past event happens before another. The pluperfect, `le plus-que-parfait`, is built with the imperfect of the auxiliary plus the past participle, and it follows the same auxiliary and agreement rules as the compound past: `j’avais déposé ma demande`, `elle était déjà partie`, `nous nous étions inscrits`. It is also the tense used after `si` for an unreal past condition. The simple past, `le passé simple`, replaces the compound past in literary narration; forms such as `il entra`, `elle fut`, `ils prirent` are for recognition only.
points: Ask whether the verb advances the story or paints the scene.
Use the compound past for the event and the imperfect for the setting.
Use the pluperfect for whatever happened before the main past event.
Build the pluperfect with the imperfect of `avoir` or `être` plus a participle.
Recognise `il entra` or `elle fut` as literary narration, not as everyday speech.
Read `je devais` as a plan that may not have happened, and `j’ai dû` as an obligation that was carried out or a supposition.

examples.french: Je préparais mon entrevue quand la responsable m’a appelé.
examples.english: I was preparing for my interview when the manager called me.
examples.note: Background in the imperfect, event in the compound past.

examples.french: J’ai déménagé au Québec il y a quelques semaines.
examples.english: I moved to Quebec a few weeks ago.
examples.note: A single bounded event.

examples.french: Quand je suis arrivé au guichet, j’avais déjà rempli le formulaire en ligne.
examples.english: When I arrived at the counter, I had already completed the form online.
examples.note: Pluperfect for the action completed before the main past event.

examples.french: Elle était partie avant que la décision soit annoncée.
examples.english: She had left before the decision was announced.
examples.note: Pluperfect with the auxiliary être and subject agreement.

examples.french: Il entra dans la salle, salua l’assemblée et s’assit.
examples.english: He entered the room, greeted the assembly, and sat down.
examples.note: Simple past: recognise it in written narration.

examples.french: Je devais envoyer le dossier hier, mais j’ai dû reporter au lundi suivant.
examples.english: I was supposed to send the file yesterday, but I had to postpone it to the following Monday.
examples.note: « Je devais » is the unfulfilled plan; « j’ai dû » is what actually happened.

mistakes.avoid: Quand je suis arrivé, j’ai déjà envoyé le dossier la veille.
mistakes.prefer: Quand je suis arrivé, j’avais déjà envoyé le dossier la veille.
mistakes.why: An action completed before another past action requires the pluperfect.

mistakes.avoid: Hier, il faisait la demande et il a obtenu une réponse immédiate.
mistakes.prefer: Hier, il a fait la demande et il a obtenu une réponse immédiate.
mistakes.why: Both verbs are bounded events, so both take the compound past.

mistakes.avoid: J’ai dois envoyer le dossier hier, mais je ne l’ai pas fait.
mistakes.prefer: Je devais envoyer le dossier hier, mais je ne l’ai pas fait.
mistakes.why: `Devoir` in the imperfect expresses a plan that was not carried out; the compound past would state that the obligation was met.

vocabulary.example: Nous avions déménagé deux fois avant de trouver ce logement.
vocabulary.note: `-ger` verb; keeps the `e` before `a` and `o`.

vocabulary.example: J’avais déposé ma demande avant la date limite.
vocabulary.note: Regular `-er` verb; `déposer un dossier` is standard administrative usage.

vocabulary.example: Une entrevue d’embauche m’attendait le lendemain matin.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun used in Canada; `un entretien` in France.

vocabulary.example: Un guichet unique regroupe désormais toutes les démarches.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; `un guichet automatique` is a cash machine.

vocabulary.english: to have to, to be supposed to
vocabulary.example: Nous devions commencer à neuf heures, mais la salle n’était pas libre.
vocabulary.note: Imperfect `je devais` = was supposed to; compound past `j’ai dû` = had to, or must have.

practice.prompt: Complete with the right past tense: « Quand elle (arriver) à la réunion, tout le monde (partir) déjà. »
practice.hint: The second verb happened before the first.
practice.answer: Quand elle est arrivée à la réunion, tout le monde était déjà parti.

takeaways: Event equals compound past; scene equals imperfect.
Earlier than the past equals pluperfect: imperfect auxiliary plus participle.
The simple past is for reading, not for producing.
keywords: choosing a past tense and the pluperfect

lessons.title: Les formes du futur
lessons.summary: The simple future adds `-ai, -as, -a, -ons, -ez, -ont` to the infinitive, dropping the final `e` of an `-re` infinitive. Frequent irregular stems must be memorised: `être` gives `ser-`, `avoir` gives `aur-`, `faire` gives `fer-`, `aller` gives `ir-`, `venir` gives `viendr-`, `pouvoir` gives `pourr-`, `vouloir` gives `voudr-`, `voir` gives `verr-`, `devoir` gives `devr-`. The near future uses present `aller` plus an infinitive, and the negative wraps the conjugated `aller`.
objectives: Build the simple future from a regular or irregular stem.
Choose between the simple future and the near future.
Use the future after time conjunctions where English uses the present.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: The simple future is a single word: infinitive plus ending. `Parler` gives `je parlerai`, `finir` gives `je finirai`, and `attendre` drops its `e` to give `j’attendrai`. The endings are the present forms of `avoir` reduced, which is why every simple future ends in `-ai`, `-as`, `-a`, `-ons`, `-ez`, `-ont`. Irregular verbs change only the stem, never the endings.

The near future, `aller` plus infinitive, presents an action as planned or imminent and is very common in speech: `Nous allons présenter notre projet demain`. In the negative, only the conjugated `aller` is surrounded: `La ville ne va pas construire de logements`. One difference from English is decisive in writing: after `quand`, `lorsque`, `dès que`, and `aussitôt que`, French uses the future when the action is future, where English uses the present.
points: Add the endings straight to the infinitive for regular verbs.
Drop the final `e` of an `-re` infinitive before adding the ending.
Memorise the nine frequent irregular stems as a block.
Wrap only the conjugated `aller` when negating the near future.
Use the future, not the present, after `quand`, `lorsque`, and `dès que`.

examples.french: Nous réduirons nos déchets grâce à ce nouveau programme municipal.
examples.english: We will reduce our waste thanks to this new municipal program.
examples.note: Regular formation on an -re infinitive.

examples.french: Nous serons prêts et nous aurons tous les documents demandés.
examples.english: We will be ready and we will have all the requested documents.
examples.note: Irregular stems ser- and aur-.

examples.french: Je prendrai rendez-vous dès que le bureau ouvrira.
examples.english: I will make an appointment as soon as the office opens.
examples.note: French uses the future in both clauses after « dès que ».

examples.french: Nous allons présenter notre projet devant le comité demain.
examples.english: We are going to present our project to the committee tomorrow.
examples.note: Near future for a planned action.

examples.french: La ville ne va pas construire de logements sur ce terrain.
examples.english: The city is not going to build housing on this land.
examples.note: The negative surrounds « va », and « des » becomes « de ».

mistakes.avoid: Quand j’arrive au Canada, je chercherai un emploi.
mistakes.prefer: Quand j’arriverai au Canada, je chercherai un emploi.
mistakes.why: After `quand`, French uses the future for a future action, unlike English.

mistakes.avoid: Il ne va pas venir pas à la réunion.
mistakes.prefer: Il ne va pas venir à la réunion.
mistakes.why: In the near future the negative surrounds only the conjugated `aller`.

vocabulary.example: Nous réduirons la consommation d’énergie de vingt pour cent.
vocabulary.note: `-re` verb; the future drops the final `e`: `je réduirai`.

vocabulary.example: Vous pourrez suivre votre demande en ligne dès lundi.
vocabulary.note: Irregular future stem `pourr-`.

vocabulary.example: Un déchet mal trié complique tout le processus de recyclage.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun, usually used in the plural: `les déchets`.

vocabulary.example: Un terrain municipal sera transformé en parc de quartier.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; also means ground or field.

practice.prompt: Put into the simple future: « Je (faire) la demande dès que je (pouvoir). »
practice.hint: Both verbs have irregular stems, and French keeps the future after `dès que`.
practice.answer: Je ferai la demande dès que je pourrai.

takeaways: Infinitive plus `-ai, -as, -a, -ons, -ez, -ont`, with `-re` losing its `e`.
Nine irregular stems cover most of what you will need.
`Quand` plus future in French, where English uses the present.

lessons.title: Le conditionnel et les phrases avec « si »
lessons.summary: The present conditional uses the future stem with imperfect endings: `je postulerais`, `nous serions`. The past conditional uses the conditional of `avoir` or `être` plus a participle. Three condition patterns must be kept apart: `si` plus present with a future or imperative result; `si` plus imperfect with a present conditional; `si` plus pluperfect with a past conditional. Never place a future or a conditional directly after conditional `si`.
objectives: Form the present and past conditional from the future stem.
Match each type of condition to its pair of tenses.
Use the conditional alone for politeness and unconfirmed information.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: The conditional is built on the future stem, so any verb you can put in the future you can put in the conditional: `je serai` gives `je serais`, `il faudra` gives `il faudrait`. The endings are those of the imperfect. The past conditional adds a participle to a conditional auxiliary: `je serais parti`, `j’aurais postulé`.

Conditional sentences come in three fixed pairs. A real possibility uses `si` plus present, with a present, future, or imperative result: `Si vous avez des questions, appelez le service`. A hypothesis about now or later uses `si` plus imperfect with the present conditional: `Si j’avais plus d’expérience, je postulerais`. A counterfactual past uses `si` plus pluperfect with the past conditional: `Si j’avais connu ce programme, je me serais inscrit plus tôt`. Outside `si` clauses, the conditional alone softens a request (`Je voudrais un rendez-vous`) or marks unverified information (`Le service fermerait plus tôt`).
points: Take the future stem and add `-ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient`.
Keep the present after `si` when the condition is realistic.
Use the imperfect after `si` for a present or future hypothesis.
Use the pluperfect after `si` for a past that did not happen.
Use `je voudrais`, `pourriez-vous`, `j’aimerais` for polite requests.

examples.french: Si la ville améliore le service, davantage de résidents prendront le bus.
examples.english: If the city improves the service, more residents will take the bus.
examples.note: Real possibility: present plus future.

examples.french: Si vous avez des questions, appelez le service d’aide aux nouveaux arrivants.
examples.english: If you have questions, call the newcomer support service.
examples.note: Present plus imperative.

examples.french: Si j’avais plus d’expérience, je postulerais à ce poste.
examples.english: If I had more experience, I would apply for this position.
examples.note: Present hypothesis: imperfect plus present conditional.

examples.french: Si j’avais connu ce programme, je me serais inscrit plus tôt.
examples.english: If I had known about this program, I would have enrolled earlier.
examples.note: Past counterfactual: pluperfect plus past conditional.

examples.french: Je voudrais prendre rendez-vous avec une conseillère en emploi.
examples.english: I would like to make an appointment with an employment adviser.
examples.note: Conditional alone for a polite request.

mistakes.avoid: Si tu travaillerais, tu réussirais l’examen.
mistakes.prefer: Si tu travaillais, tu réussirais l’examen.
mistakes.why: The conditional never follows `si` directly; the condition takes the imperfect.

mistakes.avoid: Si j’aurais su, je serais venu plus tôt.
mistakes.prefer: Si j’avais su, je serais venu plus tôt.
mistakes.why: A past counterfactual requires the pluperfect after `si`.

vocabulary.example: Si la ville améliorait le service, davantage de résidents prendraient le bus.
vocabulary.note: Regular `-er` verb; the conditional stem is the full infinitive.

vocabulary.example: Je voudrais obtenir une attestation de résidence.
vocabulary.note: Conditional `je voudrais` is the standard polite request form.

vocabulary.example: Un délai de traitement plus court serait apprécié par tous les usagers.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun phrase; the gender comes from `délai`.

vocabulary.example: Une hypothèse raisonnable mérite d’être vérifiée avant la conclusion.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun beginning with a mute h.

practice.prompt: Complete: « Si le service (être) ouvert samedi, je (déposer) mon dossier ce week-end. »
practice.hint: This is a hypothesis about the present, not a real possibility.
practice.answer: Si le service était ouvert samedi, je déposerais mon dossier ce week-end.

takeaways: Future stem plus imperfect endings equals the conditional.
Present with future, imperfect with present conditional, pluperfect with past conditional.
`Si` is never followed by a future or a conditional.

lessons.title: Le subjonctif présent
lessons.summary: The subjunctive is a mood used in a `que` clause after a trigger expressing will, emotion, doubt, necessity, judgement, or purpose. Form it from the present `ils` form minus `-ent`, plus `-e, -es, -e, -ions, -iez, -ent`. Memorise `être`, `avoir`, `aller`, `faire`, `pouvoir`, `savoir`. Use an infinitive when the two subjects are the same and `que` plus subjunctive when they differ. `Après que` takes the indicative in careful standard French.
objectives: Recognise the trigger that requires a subjunctive.
Form regular and frequent irregular subjunctives.
Decide between an infinitive and a `que` clause.
Use `veiller à ce que`, `tenir à ce que`, and `s’attendre à ce que` with the full sequence.
Tell a decorative `ne` apart from a real negation in a subjunctive clause.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: A mood expresses how the speaker frames an event, not when it happens. The indicative presents an event as a fact; the subjunctive presents it as wanted, feared, doubted, required, judged, or aimed at. It therefore appears in a subordinate clause introduced by `que`, after a trigger in the main clause: `il faut que`, `je veux que`, `je doute que`, `je suis content que`, `il est important que`, `pour que`, `afin que`, `bien que`, `avant que`, `à condition que`, `jusqu’à ce que`.

Formation is regular for most verbs: take the present `ils` form, remove `-ent`, and add the subjunctive endings, so `ils réduisent` gives `que je réduise` and `que nous réduisions`. Six verbs are irregular and worth memorising in full: `sois/soyons`, `aie/ayons`, `aille/allions`, `fasse/fassions`, `puisse/puissions`, `sache/sachions`. The subject test decides the structure: same subject means an infinitive (`Je pars pour travailler`), different subjects mean `que` plus subjunctive (`Je pars pour que tu travailles`). One frequent trap: although `avant que` takes the subjunctive, `après que` takes the indicative in careful writing.

Three triggers built on `à` are especially useful in administrative writing and are often missed because English uses a plain infinitive: `veiller à ce que` (to make sure that), `tenir à ce que` (to insist that), and `s’attendre à ce que` (to expect that). All three keep the full sequence `à ce que` plus subjunctive: `Le service veille à ce que chaque demande soit traitée dans les délais`, `Nous tenons à ce que vous receviez une confirmation écrite`, `Je m’attends à ce qu’elle réponde avant vendredi`. Dropping `à ce` leaves an incorrect sentence.

After `avant que`, `à moins que`, `de peur que`, `de crainte que`, and `craindre que`, formal French may insert an optional, non-negative `ne`, called an expletive `ne`. `Je crains qu’elle ne soit déjà partie` means *I am afraid she has already left*. Do not identify this use merely by the absence of `pas`: a genuine negative can contain `jamais`, `plus`, `rien`, or `personne` instead. Compare `Je crains qu’elle ne soit pas informée` (*I am afraid she has not been informed*) and `Je crains qu’il ne revienne jamais` (*I am afraid he will never come back*). Read the whole clause and its meaning. Where `ne` is expletive, it can be omitted without changing the meaning: `avant que le délai expire` and `avant que le délai n’expire`.
points: Look for the trigger in the main clause before choosing the mood.
Build the stem from the present `ils` form minus `-ent`.
Learn the six irregular verbs as complete paradigms.
Use an infinitive when the subject does not change.
Keep the indicative after `après que`.
Add `souhaiter que` and `vouloir que` to the list of will triggers.
Keep the full sequence `à ce que` after `veiller`, `tenir`, and `s’attendre`.
Recognise the optional expletive `ne` after triggers such as `avant que` and `craindre que`.
Check the whole clause for real negation: `ne… pas`, `ne… jamais`, `ne… plus`, and other negative expressions.

examples.french: Il faut que nous réduisions la pollution dans les centres urbains.
examples.english: We must reduce pollution in urban centres.
examples.note: Regular formation from « ils réduisent ».

examples.french: Je suis heureuse que ma candidature ait été retenue.
examples.english: I am glad that my application was accepted.
examples.note: Emotion trigger with the irregular subjunctive of avoir.

examples.french: Je vous écris pour que vous connaissiez ma situation actuelle.
examples.english: I am writing so that you are aware of my current situation.
examples.note: Purpose with two different subjects.

examples.french: Je vous écris pour expliquer ma situation actuelle.
examples.english: I am writing to explain my current situation.
examples.note: Same subject, so an infinitive replaces the que clause.

examples.french: Bien que le dossier soit complet, il faut encore attendre la décision.
examples.english: Although the file is complete, we still have to wait for the decision.
examples.note: « Bien que » always takes the subjunctive.

examples.french: Le service veille à ce que chaque demande soit traitée dans les délais annoncés.
examples.english: The department makes sure that every application is processed within the announced deadlines.
examples.note: « Veiller » keeps the full sequence « à ce que » before the subjunctive.

examples.french: Nous tenons à ce que vous receviez une confirmation écrite, et je m’attends à ce qu’elle parte lundi.
examples.english: We insist that you receive a written confirmation, and I expect it to be sent on Monday.
examples.note: « Tenir à ce que » and « s’attendre à ce que » follow the same pattern.

examples.french: Je crains qu’elle ne soit déjà partie, mais je crains surtout qu’elle ne soit pas informée.
examples.english: I am afraid she has already left, but above all I am afraid she has not been informed.
examples.note: The first « ne » is decorative; the second is a real negation because « pas » is present.

examples.french: Nous partirons à moins qu’il ne pleuve, et déposez votre demande avant que le délai n’expire.
examples.english: We will leave unless it rains, and submit your application before the deadline expires.
examples.note: The optional « ne » adds a formal tone without changing the meaning.

examples.french: Je crains qu’il ne revienne jamais au bureau.
examples.english: I am afraid he will never come back to the office.
examples.note: « Ne… jamais » is a real negation even though there is no pas.

mistakes.avoid: Après qu’il soit parti, nous avons commencé la réunion.
mistakes.prefer: Après qu’il est parti, nous avons commencé la réunion.
mistakes.why: In careful standard French, `après que` introduces a fact and takes the indicative.

mistakes.avoid: Je veux que je parte plus tôt aujourd’hui.
mistakes.prefer: Je veux partir plus tôt aujourd’hui.
mistakes.why: When the two subjects are identical, French uses an infinitive rather than a `que` clause.

mistakes.avoid: Le responsable veille que tout soit prêt avant l’ouverture.
mistakes.prefer: Le responsable veille à ce que tout soit prêt avant l’ouverture.
mistakes.why: `Veiller` governs `à ce que` before a clause; the sequence cannot be shortened to `que`.

mistakes.avoid: Nous veillons à ce que le dossier est complet avant l’envoi.
mistakes.prefer: Nous veillons à ce que le dossier soit complet avant l’envoi.
mistakes.why: `Veiller à ce que` expresses a precaution rather than a fact, so the clause takes the subjunctive.

mistakes.avoid: Déposez votre demande avant qu’il ne vient au guichet.
mistakes.prefer: Déposez votre demande avant qu’il ne vienne au guichet.
mistakes.why: The optional `ne` does not change the mood: `avant que` still requires the subjunctive.

vocabulary.example: Il faut que vous fournissiez une preuve de résidence.
vocabulary.note: Impersonal verb, used only with `il`; followed by an infinitive or by `que` plus subjunctive.

vocabulary.example: Il faut que j’aille au bureau des permis avant midi.
vocabulary.note: Irregular subjunctive: `que j’aille`, `que nous allions`.

vocabulary.example: Nous devons décider avant que le délai expire.
vocabulary.note: Takes the subjunctive, unlike `après que`, which takes the indicative.

vocabulary.example: Une décision favorable a été communiquée par courriel.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; the ending -sion is a feminine hint.

vocabulary.english: to wish that, to hope that
