vocabulary.example: Nous souhaitons que chaque famille reçoive une réponse avant l’été.
vocabulary.note: Trigger of will, so it takes the subjunctive; `souhaiter` plus infinitive when the subject is the same.

vocabulary.example: Veillez à ce que rien ne soit oublié dans le dossier.
vocabulary.note: The sequence `à ce que` is obligatory and is followed by the subjunctive.

vocabulary.example: Je m’attends à ce que la réponse arrive avant la fin du mois.
vocabulary.note: Same pattern as `tenir à ce que`; the plain `s’attendre à` takes a noun.

vocabulary.example: Nous craignons que le délai soit trop court pour rassembler les pièces.
vocabulary.note: Takes the subjunctive and may have an optional expletive `ne`; distinguish genuine negatives such as `ne… jamais`.

practice.prompt: Choose the mood: « Je reste jusqu’à ce que le guichet (fermer). » and « Après que le guichet (fermer), je suis rentré. »
practice.hint: One conjunction takes the subjunctive, the other the indicative.
practice.answer: Je reste jusqu’à ce que le guichet ferme. Après que le guichet a fermé, je suis rentré.

takeaways: The trigger, not the meaning of the verb, calls the subjunctive.
Stem from `ils` minus `-ent`; six irregular verbs to memorise.
Same subject equals infinitive; `après que` keeps the indicative.
`Veiller`, `tenir`, and `s’attendre` all keep `à ce que`.
An expletive `ne` is optional and non-negative; the absence of `pas` alone does not identify it.

lessons.title: Les constructions infinitives de temps et de but
lessons.summary: Use `avant de` plus infinitive for an action that comes first, and `après` plus past infinitive (`avoir` or `être` plus participle) for an action already completed. With a reflexive verb the past infinitive is `après s’être` plus participle. For purpose, use `pour` or `afin de` plus infinitive when both verbs share a subject, and `pour que` or `afin que` plus subjunctive when they do not.
objectives: Build a past infinitive with the correct auxiliary.
Choose between an infinitive and a subjunctive clause for purpose.
Avoid the bare `après` plus infinitive pattern.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: An infinitive names an action without marking a subject or a tense, which is why French uses it whenever the subject is already clear. `Avant de` is always followed by a simple infinitive: `Avant de signer le bail, elle a vérifié les conditions`. `Après` requires the past infinitive, because the action is already finished: `Après avoir rempli le formulaire, je l’ai envoyé`. Choose the auxiliary exactly as in the compound past, so movement and reflexive verbs use `être`: `après être arrivée`, `après s’être installée`.

Purpose works on the subject test. One subject allows an infinitive: `Je suis cette formation pour améliorer mon français`. Two subjects require a conjunction plus the subjunctive: `Je vous écris afin que vous compreniez ma situation`. Writing `après` directly in front of a simple infinitive is not standard; in careful French it must be the past infinitive.
points: Use `avant de` plus a simple infinitive for the earlier action.
Use `après` plus `avoir` or `être` plus participle for a completed action.
Choose the past-infinitive auxiliary with the compound-past rules.
Use `après s’être` plus participle with a reflexive verb, agreeing where required.
Switch to `pour que` or `afin que` plus subjunctive as soon as the subject changes.
Put both negative words in front of the whole past infinitive: `après ne pas avoir dormi`.

examples.french: Après avoir rempli le formulaire, je l’ai envoyé au ministère.
examples.english: After completing the form, I sent it to the ministry.
examples.note: Past infinitive with avoir.

examples.french: Après s’être installée à Montréal, elle a cherché un emploi bilingue.
examples.english: After settling in Montreal, she looked for a bilingual job.
examples.note: Reflexive past infinitive; the participle agrees with the subject.

examples.french: Avant de signer le bail, elle a vérifié toutes les conditions.
examples.english: Before signing the lease, she checked all the conditions.
examples.note: « Avant de » takes a simple infinitive.

examples.french: Je suis cette formation pour améliorer mon français professionnel.
examples.english: I am taking this course to improve my professional French.
examples.note: One subject, so an infinitive is enough.

examples.french: La ville a modifié l’horaire afin que les familles puissent participer.
examples.english: The city changed the schedule so that families could take part.
examples.note: Two subjects, so a conjunction plus the subjunctive.

examples.french: Après ne pas avoir dormi de la nuit, elle a reporté son entrevue.
examples.english: After not having slept all night, she postponed her interview.
examples.note: The negation stands in front of the entire past infinitive, auxiliary included.

mistakes.avoid: Après courir, je me repose quelques minutes.
mistakes.prefer: Après avoir couru, je me repose quelques minutes.
mistakes.why: `Après` requires the past infinitive when the action is already completed.

mistakes.avoid: J’ai écrit une lettre pour que je clarifie ma situation.
mistakes.prefer: J’ai écrit une lettre pour clarifier ma situation.
mistakes.why: With a single subject French uses `pour` plus infinitive, not `pour que`.

mistakes.avoid: Après avoir ne pas dormi, elle a reporté son entrevue.
mistakes.prefer: Après ne pas avoir dormi, elle a reporté son entrevue.
mistakes.why: With an infinitive, `ne pas` stays together and precedes the auxiliary rather than splitting the verb group.

vocabulary.example: Après s’être installés, ils ont inscrit les enfants à l’école du quartier.
vocabulary.note: Reflexive verb; the past infinitive is `après s’être installé(e)(s)`.

vocabulary.example: Avant de signer, vérifiez la durée du bail et le montant du loyer.
vocabulary.note: Regular `-er` verb; frequent in administrative instructions.

vocabulary.example: Un bail signé engage le locataire pour douze mois.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; irregular plural `des baux`.

vocabulary.example: Un ministère provincial gère les demandes de reconnaissance de diplôme.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; not to be confused with `une ministre`, the person.

vocabulary.example: Il regrette de ne pas avoir joint toutes les pièces.
vocabulary.note: Negative past infinitive; both negative words precede the auxiliary.

practice.prompt: Rewrite with a past infinitive: « Elle est arrivée, puis elle a téléphoné au bureau. »
practice.hint: `Arriver` takes `être`, so the participle agrees.
practice.answer: Après être arrivée, elle a téléphoné au bureau.

takeaways: `Avant de` plus infinitive, `après` plus past infinitive.
The past infinitive follows the compound-past auxiliary rules.
One subject equals `pour`; two subjects equal `pour que` plus subjunctive.
keywords: infinitive constructions for sequence and purpose

lessons.title: Le participe présent et le gérondif
lessons.summary: Form the present participle from the present `nous` form minus `-ons` plus `-ant`: `nous travaillons` gives `travaillant`. Three verbs are irregular: `ayant`, `étant`, `sachant`. Adding `en` gives the gerund, which expresses simultaneity, manner, or means and requires the same understood subject as the main verb. The present participle without `en` can instead express cause or a relative-like description.
objectives: Form the present participle, including the three irregular verbs.
Use `en` plus participle for simultaneity, manner, or means.
Keep the subject of the gerund identical to the subject of the main verb.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: The present participle is the `-ant` form. It is built on the present `nous` stem, so it inherits any spelling change from that form: `nous commençons` gives `commençant`, `nous mangeons` gives `mangeant`. Only `avoir`, `être`, and `savoir` are irregular, giving `ayant`, `étant`, and `sachant`.

Adding `en` produces the gerund, which places two actions of the same subject side by side. It can express simultaneity (`En travaillant, elle a appris beaucoup de vocabulaire`), manner or means (`Elle a trouvé un logement en consultant les annonces`). The constraint is strict: the subject of the gerund must be the subject of the main verb, so a sentence like `En arrivant, le dossier était prêt` is faulty because a file cannot arrive. Without `en`, the participle instead gives a cause or a description: `Ayant acquis une solide expérience, elle a dirigé le projet`.
points: Take the present `nous` form and replace `-ons` with `-ant`.
Keep the spelling change of the `nous` form: `commençant`, `mangeant`.
Memorise `ayant`, `étant`, `sachant`.
Add `en` for simultaneity, manner, or means.
Check that the gerund and the main verb share the same subject.

examples.french: En travaillant avec une équipe bilingue, elle a enrichi son vocabulaire.
examples.english: By working with a bilingual team, she expanded her vocabulary.
examples.note: Gerund of means, same subject as the main verb.

examples.french: Elle a trouvé un logement en consultant les annonces du quartier.
examples.english: She found housing by looking through the local listings.
examples.note: Gerund of manner.

examples.french: En arrivant au bureau, j’ai remarqué que la file était déjà longue.
examples.english: On arriving at the office, I noticed that the queue was already long.
examples.note: Simultaneity; the subject of both verbs is « je ».

examples.french: Ayant acquis une solide expérience, elle a dirigé le projet avec assurance.
examples.english: Having gained solid experience, she led the project confidently.
examples.note: Participle without « en »: cause rather than simultaneity.

examples.french: Ne sachant pas où déposer le dossier, il a téléphoné à la mairie.
examples.english: Not knowing where to submit the file, he phoned the town hall.
examples.note: Irregular participle « sachant » in a causal construction.

mistakes.avoid: En arrivant au guichet, le dossier était déjà complet.
mistakes.prefer: En arrivant au guichet, j’avais déjà un dossier complet.
mistakes.why: The gerund must share the subject of the main verb, and a file cannot arrive.

mistakes.avoid: En sachant la réponse, elle a levé la main.
mistakes.prefer: Sachant la réponse, elle a levé la main.
mistakes.why: `Savoir` expresses a state, so the causal participle without `en` is the natural form.

vocabulary.example: Ayant acquis de l’expérience à l’étranger, elle a été retenue immédiatement.
vocabulary.note: Irregular verb; participle `acquis`, present participle `acquérant`.

vocabulary.example: En consultant le site du ministère, j’ai trouvé la liste des documents.
vocabulary.note: Regular `-er` verb; very useful with the gerund of means.

vocabulary.example: Un stage en milieu bilingue complète utilement une formation.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; `un stagiaire` is the intern.

vocabulary.example: Une équipe bilingue répond aux appels du lundi au vendredi.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; takes a singular verb in French.

practice.prompt: Join with a gerund: « Elle prépare son entrevue. Elle relit les annonces. »
practice.hint: Both actions belong to the same subject.
practice.answer: Elle prépare son entrevue en relisant les annonces.

takeaways: `Nous` form minus `-ons` plus `-ant`, with three irregular verbs.
`En` plus participle equals simultaneity, manner, or means.
Different subjects make the gerund ungrammatical.
keywords: the present participle and en + participle

lessons.title: La voix passive et les tournures pronominales
lessons.summary: The passive is `être` plus past participle, and the participle agrees with the subject: `les demandes ont été traitées`. The agent, when named, is introduced by `par`. French often prefers two alternatives: a pronominal construction with `se` for a general process (`Cette démarche se fait en ligne`), and `on` plus an active verb for an unspecified human agent (`On m’a informé`).
objectives: Build a passive sentence with the correct agreement.
Replace a heavy passive with a pronominal construction where it is idiomatic.
Use `on` for an unnamed human agent.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: In a passive sentence the grammatical subject receives the action instead of performing it. French forms it with `être` in the required tense plus the past participle, which agrees with that subject: `Le formulaire a été envoyé`, `Les demandes ont été traitées`. If the agent is mentioned, `par` introduces it: `Le rapport a été rédigé par le comité`.

French uses the passive less than English and has two natural alternatives. A pronominal construction with `se` describes a general process or property, with no agent in view: `Cette démarche se fait entièrement en ligne`, `Ce produit se vend bien`. The pronoun `on` plus an active verb covers an unspecified but human agent and is the usual spoken equivalent of an English passive: `On m’a indiqué que le service fermerait plus tôt`.
points: Conjugate `être` in the tense you need, then add the participle.
Agree the participle with the subject, not with the agent.
Introduce a named agent with `par`.
Use `se` plus verb for a general process with no agent.
Use `on` plus an active verb when the agent is human but unnamed.
Use the pronominal passive for what is normally done, sold, or said: `se vendre`, `se dire`, `s’écrire`, `se manger`.

examples.french: Le formulaire a été envoyé par voie électronique.
examples.english: The form was sent electronically.
examples.note: Passive with a masculine singular subject.

examples.french: Les demandes ont été traitées en priorité cette semaine.
examples.english: The applications were processed as a priority this week.
examples.note: The participle agrees with the feminine plural subject.

examples.french: Le rapport a été rédigé par le comité de quartier.
examples.english: The report was written by the neighbourhood committee.
examples.note: The agent is introduced by « par ».

examples.french: Cette démarche se fait entièrement en ligne.
examples.english: This procedure is completed entirely online.
examples.note: Pronominal construction for a general process.

examples.french: On m’a indiqué que le service fermerait plus tôt aujourd’hui.
examples.english: I was told that the service would close earlier today.
examples.note: « On » replaces an English passive with an unnamed agent.

examples.french: Ce produit local se vend très bien, et cela ne se dit pas dans une lettre officielle.
examples.english: This local product sells very well, and that is not said in an official letter.
examples.note: The pronominal passive states a general norm with no agent in view.

mistakes.avoid: Les demandes ont été traité la semaine dernière.
mistakes.prefer: Les demandes ont été traitées la semaine dernière.
mistakes.why: In the passive the participle agrees with the subject, here feminine plural.

mistakes.avoid: Le formulaire a été envoyer par voie électronique.
mistakes.prefer: Le formulaire a été envoyé par voie électronique.
mistakes.why: The passive is built with a past participle, `envoyé`, not with the infinitive `envoyer`, which sounds identical.

vocabulary.example: Les dossiers sont traités dans l’ordre d’arrivée.
vocabulary.note: Regular `-er` verb; `le traitement` is the related noun.

vocabulary.english: to be done, to take place
vocabulary.example: L’inscription se fait en ligne jusqu’au 30 juin.
vocabulary.note: Pronominal construction used instead of a passive with no agent.

vocabulary.example: Un avis officiel a été publié sur le site de la municipalité.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; identical in the plural.

vocabulary.example: Un comité consultatif examine les projets de rénovation.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; the ending -té is usually feminine, so this one must be learned.

vocabulary.example: Les billets se vendent en ligne à partir du 1er mars.
vocabulary.note: Pronominal passive; the subject is the thing sold, not the seller.

vocabulary.english: to be said, to be the usual way of saying
vocabulary.example: « Bonne journée » se dit couramment à la fin d’un échange.
vocabulary.note: Frequently used to comment on usage and register.

practice.prompt: Rewrite without a passive: « Les décisions sont prises par une commission. » and « The forms are filled in online. »
practice.hint: One keeps a named agent, the other has none.
practice.answer: Une commission prend les décisions. Les formulaires se remplissent en ligne.

takeaways: `Être` plus participle, agreeing with the subject; agent after `par`.
`Se` plus verb for a process with no agent.
`On` plus active verb is the everyday equivalent of an English passive.

lessons.title: La construction causative « faire + infinitif »
lessons.summary: `Faire` plus an infinitive expresses causing an action: `Je fais réparer mon ordinateur` means I am having my computer repaired. Object pronouns normally precede `faire` (`Je le fais réparer`), but follow it in an affirmative imperative (`Faites-le réparer`). Adverbs can come between the verbs. The performer can be a direct object (`Je fais venir Paul`) or follow `à/par` when the infinitive already has a direct object (`Je fais réparer la porte par Paul`). `Fait` stays unchanged before an infinitive, including in `Elle s’est fait rembourser`.
objectives: Express an action carried out by someone else.
Place object pronouns with `faire`, accounting for the affirmative imperative.
Use `se faire + infinitif` and leave its participle unchanged.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: A causative construction says that the subject causes an action rather than necessarily performing it. French builds it with `faire` plus an infinitive: `Je fais réparer mon ordinateur` means I am having my computer repaired. Keep the noun object after the infinitive, not between the two verbs. This does not prohibit adverbs: `Cela fait souvent rire les enfants` is correct. `Laisser` plus an infinitive expresses permission instead: `Le gardien laisse entrer les visiteurs`; it also allows the order `Le gardien laisse les visiteurs entrer`.

Object pronouns normally precede `faire`: `Je le fais réparer`, `Elle nous a fait remplir un formulaire`. In an affirmative imperative, they follow it: `Faites-le réparer`. The performer’s construction depends on the infinitive: `Je fais venir Paul` has no separate direct object for `venir`, so `Paul` is direct. When the infinitive already has a direct object, introduce the performer with `à` or `par`: `J’ai fait signer le contrat à la directrice`, `J’ai fait traduire le document par un traducteur agréé`. The pronominal `se faire` plus an infinitive presents the subject as someone who benefits or suffers: `Elle s’est fait rembourser ses frais`, `Il s’est fait voler son vélo`. The participle `fait` stays unchanged before an infinitive.
points: Do not insert the noun object between `faire` and the infinitive; adverbs can intervene.
Place object pronouns before `faire`, except in affirmative commands: `Je le fais réparer`, `Faites-le réparer`.
Use a direct performer with an intransitive infinitive (`faire venir Paul`); use `à/par` when the infinitive already has a direct object.
Use `laisser + infinitif` when the meaning is to let rather than to make.
Use `se faire + infinitif` for an action done for or to the subject.
Leave the participle `fait` unchanged in `elle s’est fait rembourser`.

examples.french: Je fais réparer mon ordinateur avant la reprise des cours.
examples.english: I am having my computer repaired before classes start again.
examples.note: The subject causes the action; someone else performs it.

examples.french: Ce formulaire est illisible, alors je le fais refaire.
examples.english: This form is illegible, so I am having it redone.
examples.note: The pronoun goes before « faire », never between the two verbs.

examples.french: La municipalité a fait construire une passerelle par une entreprise locale.
examples.english: The city had a footbridge built by a local company.
examples.note: « Par » names the performer and avoids any ambiguity.

examples.french: J’ai fait signer le contrat à la directrice avant l’échéance.
examples.english: I had the director sign the contract before the deadline.
examples.note: The thing is the direct object; the person takes « à ».

examples.french: Elle s’est fait rembourser ses frais de déplacement.
examples.english: She got her travel expenses reimbursed.
examples.note: « Se faire » plus infinitive; the participle « fait » stays invariable.

examples.french: Le gardien laisse entrer les visiteurs à partir de huit heures.
examples.english: The security guard lets visitors in from eight o’clock.
examples.note: « Laisser + infinitif » means to let, not to make.

examples.french: Ce jeu fait souvent rire les enfants.
examples.english: This game often makes the children laugh.
examples.note: An adverb can intervene; with intransitive rire, the children are the direct performer.

examples.french: Votre ordinateur est en panne ? Faites-le réparer avant lundi.
examples.english: Is your computer broken? Have it repaired before Monday.
examples.note: In an affirmative imperative, le follows faire and precedes the infinitive.

mistakes.avoid: Je fais mon ordinateur réparer cette semaine.
mistakes.prefer: Je fais réparer mon ordinateur cette semaine.
mistakes.why: `Faire` and its infinitive form one block; the object cannot be inserted between them.

mistakes.avoid: Elle s’est faite rembourser ses frais.
mistakes.prefer: Elle s’est fait rembourser ses frais.
mistakes.why: In `se faire + infinitif` the participle `fait` is invariable, so it never agrees with the subject.

vocabulary.example: Nous avons fait réparer la porte d’entrée la semaine dernière.
vocabulary.note: Model of the causative; object pronouns attach to `faire`, not to `réparer`.

vocabulary.example: Elle s’est fait rembourser le titre de transport.
vocabulary.note: The participle `fait` never agrees in this construction.

vocabulary.example: L’agent laisse entrer les candidats dès l’ouverture.
vocabulary.note: `Laisser + infinitif` expresses permission, unlike causative `faire`.

vocabulary.example: Une passerelle relie le parc au quartier voisin.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; also used figuratively for a link between two services.

vocabulary.example: Un traducteur agréé doit certifier les diplômes étrangers.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun phrase; feminine `une traductrice agréée`.

practice.prompt: Say that you are having your diplomas translated, then replace the object with a pronoun.
practice.hint: The pronoun goes in front of `faire`.
practice.answer: Je fais traduire mes diplômes. Je les fais traduire.

takeaways: `Faire + infinitif` equals having something done by someone else.
Pronouns normally precede `faire`, but follow it in affirmative imperatives; adverbs can intervene before the infinitive.
The performer is direct with `faire venir Paul`, but follows `à/par` when the infinitive already has a direct object.
`Se faire + infinitif` keeps `fait` invariable.

lessons.title: Le passé récent
lessons.summary: The recent past is the fixed pattern `venir de` plus infinitive: it states that an action has just happened. Only `venir` is conjugated, and `de` is obligatory. In the present it means has just; in the imperfect (`je venais de`) it means had just. Do not confuse it with `venir` plus infinitive without `de`, which expresses movement in order to do something.
objectives: Conjugate `venir` correctly for each subject.
Keep `de` before the infinitive in every person.
Distinguish the recent past from `venir` used as a movement verb.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: The recent past is a periphrasis: a fixed group of words replacing a single tense. `Venir` carries the person and the tense, `de` links the two verbs, and the second verb stays in the infinitive: `Je viens de terminer`, `Nous venons de recevoir`, `Le ministère vient d’annoncer`. `De` elides to `d’` before a vowel.

Two contrasts matter. First, tense: `je viens de déposer` means I have just submitted, while `je venais de déposer` means I had just submitted and situates the action before another past moment. Second, structure: without `de`, `venir` plus infinitive keeps its movement meaning, so `Je viens terminer la réunion` means I am coming in order to finish the meeting. A time expression can specify how recent the action is: `Je viens de terminer la réunion, il y a deux minutes`. With an explicit time marker, `J’ai terminé la réunion il y a deux minutes` is a concise alternative, not a grammatical correction.
points: Conjugate `venir` for the subject: `je viens`, `nous venons`, `ils viennent`.
Insert `de` or `d’` before the infinitive, without exception.
Leave the second verb in the infinitive, never in a participle.
Use the imperfect `venais de` for had just.
Read `venir` plus bare infinitive as movement, not as recent past.

examples.french: Je viens de terminer mon entrevue d’embauche.
examples.english: I have just finished my job interview.
examples.note: Present of venir plus de plus infinitive.

examples.french: Le ministère vient d’annoncer une nouvelle mesure de soutien.
examples.english: The ministry has just announced a new support measure.
examples.note: « De » elides before a vowel.

examples.french: Nous venons de recevoir votre demande de logement.
examples.english: We have just received your housing application.
examples.note: Only venir changes for the subject.

examples.french: Je venais de déposer le dossier quand le guichet a fermé.
examples.english: I had just submitted the file when the counter closed.
examples.note: Imperfect of venir for an action just completed in the past.

examples.french: Je viens terminer la réunion avec vous, puis je repars.
examples.english: I am coming to finish the meeting with you, then I am leaving again.
examples.note: Without « de », venir keeps its movement meaning.

examples.french: Je viens de terminer la réunion, il y a deux minutes.
examples.english: I have just finished the meeting, two minutes ago.
examples.note: The time expression specifies how recent the event is; using the compound past would be a more concise alternative.

mistakes.avoid: Je vient de terminer la réunion.
mistakes.prefer: Je viens de terminer la réunion.
mistakes.why: With `je`, the present of `venir` is `viens`, not the third-person form `vient`.

mistakes.avoid: Nous venons de reçu votre demande.
mistakes.prefer: Nous venons de recevoir votre demande.
mistakes.why: The recent past takes an infinitive, never a past participle.

vocabulary.example: Elle vient de recevoir sa confirmation d’inscription.
vocabulary.note: Fixed pattern; only `venir` is conjugated and `de` is obligatory.

vocabulary.example: La ville vient d’annoncer la gratuité des transports le dimanche.
vocabulary.note: `-cer` verb: cedilla before `a` and `o`.

vocabulary.example: Une réunion d’information vient de se terminer dans la grande salle.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; `se réunir` is the related verb.

vocabulary.example: Une mesure de soutien temporaire aide les familles à faible revenu.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun phrase; the gender comes from `mesure`.

practice.prompt: Say in French that the service has just closed, and that it had just closed when you arrived.
practice.hint: Present of `venir` first, then the imperfect.
practice.answer: Le service vient de fermer. Le service venait de fermer quand je suis arrivé.

takeaways: `Venir de` plus infinitive equals has just.
`Venais de` plus infinitive equals had just.
Dropping `de` turns the sentence back into movement.

lessons.title: L’action en cours : « être en train de »
lessons.summary: French does not form a continuous tense with `être` plus a present participle. The simple present can already describe an ongoing action. To emphasise progress at a reference moment, use `être en train de` plus an infinitive. Only `être` is conjugated, and `de` is required. The reference moment may be now, in the past, in the future, or repeated: `Tous les matins à huit heures, je suis en train de déjeuner`. For an ordinary habit without that focus, use the simple present.
objectives: Build `être en train de` plus infinitive in the present, the imperfect, and the future.
Explain why French cannot translate *I am filling in* with a present participle.
Distinguish an ordinary habit from an action in progress at a recurring reference moment.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: English marks a continuous aspect inside the verb: *I fill in* versus *I am filling in*. French has no such tense. The simple present covers both readings, and `Je remplis le formulaire` is already the normal translation of *I am filling in the form*. When you need to insist that the action is under way at the moment you are describing, French adds a separate phrase instead of changing the verb: `être en train de` plus an infinitive. `Je suis en train de remplir le formulaire` states explicitly that the action is happening right now.

Three details make the construction reliable. Only `être` carries person and tense, so the second verb stays in the infinitive. `Je suis remplissant` cannot express the English continuous. `De` belongs to the fixed phrase. Finally, the tense of `être` sets the reference point: now (`Le conseiller est en train de vérifier votre dossier`), a past moment (`Elle était en train de garer la voiture quand l’agent est arrivé`), or a future moment (`À dix heures, nous serons en train de passer l’entretien`). Repetition is compatible with this focus: `Tous les matins à huit heures, je suis en train de déjeuner` describes what is in progress at that time each day. For a plain habit, `Tous les matins, je prends l’autobus` is the simpler choice.
points: Conjugate only `être`; leave the second verb in the infinitive.
Keep `de` or `d’` between `en train` and the infinitive.
Use the present of `être` for an action under way now.
Use the imperfect of `être` for an action under way at a past moment, typically interrupted by a compound past.
Use the simple present for an unmarked habit; the progressive can describe what is under way at a recurring moment.
Remember that the plain present already translates the English continuous when no insistence is needed.

examples.french: Je suis en train de remplir ma demande de logement social.
examples.english: I am in the middle of filling in my social housing application.
examples.note: Present of « être »; the action is under way at the moment of speaking.

examples.french: Nous sommes en train de faire traduire les documents pour l’inscription.
examples.english: We are in the middle of having the documents translated for the registration.
examples.note: The infinitive after « de » can itself be a causative « faire » construction.

examples.french: Elle était en train de garer la voiture quand l’agent est arrivé.
examples.english: She was in the middle of parking the car when the officer arrived.
examples.note: Imperfect of « être » for the ongoing action, compound past for the interruption.

examples.french: Le conseiller est en train de vérifier votre dossier ; veuillez patienter quelques minutes.
examples.english: The adviser is checking your file right now; please wait a few minutes.
examples.note: Typical counter formula justifying a wait.

examples.french: À dix heures, nous serons en train de passer l’entretien d’embauche.
examples.english: At ten o’clock we will be in the middle of the job interview.
examples.note: Future of « être » for an action under way at a coming moment.

examples.french: Tous les matins, je prends l’autobus de sept heures pour aller au travail.
examples.english: Every morning I take the seven o’clock bus to go to work.
examples.note: The simple present states the habit without focusing on an action in progress.

examples.french: Tous les matins à huit heures, je suis en train de déjeuner.
examples.english: Every morning at eight, I am in the middle of eating breakfast.
examples.note: The action is in progress at the same reference time each day.

mistakes.avoid: Je suis remplissant le formulaire en ligne.
mistakes.prefer: Je suis en train de remplir le formulaire en ligne.
mistakes.why: French cannot place a present participle after `être` to build a continuous tense; the fixed phrase `être en train de` plus infinitive does that job.

mistakes.avoid: À huit heures, je suis en train de prends l’autobus.
mistakes.prefer: À huit heures, je suis en train de prendre l’autobus.
mistakes.why: The verb after `de` must be the infinitive `prendre`, not the conjugated form `prends`.

mistakes.avoid: Nous sommes en train remplir le dossier.
mistakes.prefer: Nous sommes en train de remplir le dossier.
mistakes.why: `De` belongs to the fixed phrase and is never omitted before the infinitive.

vocabulary.english: to be in the middle of doing
vocabulary.example: Je suis en train de préparer les pièces justificatives demandées.
vocabulary.note: Only `être` is conjugated; the following verb stays in the infinitive.

vocabulary.example: Une demande de logement peut prendre plusieurs mois à être traitée.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun phrase; the gender comes from `demande`.

vocabulary.example: Veuillez patienter dans la salle d’attente jusqu’à l’appel de votre nom.
vocabulary.note: More formal than `attendre` and used with no object.

vocabulary.example: Il est interdit de garer sa voiture devant l’entrée de l’immeuble.
vocabulary.note: `Se garer` is the pronominal form used when no object is named.

vocabulary.example: Un entretien d’embauche dure rarement plus d’une heure.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun phrase; `une entrevue` is the usual Canadian equivalent.

practice.prompt: Rewrite twice: « Je remplis le formulaire. » — once to insist that it is happening right now, once to say it was happening when the counter closed.
practice.hint: Only the tense of `être` changes; the infinitive stays.
practice.answer: Je suis en train de remplir le formulaire. / J’étais en train de remplir le formulaire quand le guichet a fermé.

takeaways: French has no continuous tense; `être en train de` plus infinitive supplies the meaning.
The tense of `être` sets the moment; the second verb never changes.
Use the plain present for an ordinary habit; the progressive can focus on an action at a repeated reference moment.

modules.title: Les pronoms, les questions et la négation
modules.description: Track references, place pronouns correctly, ask questions, and form natural negation.

lessons.title: Les pronoms compléments directs et indirects
lessons.summary: A direct object follows the verb with no preposition and is replaced by `me, te, le, la, nous, vous, les`. A person introduced by `à` is replaced by `me, te, lui, nous, vous, leur`. The pronoun goes before the conjugated verb or auxiliary, and before the infinitive it belongs to. When two pronouns meet, the order is fixed: `me/te/nous/vous` before `le/la/les`, and `le/la/les` before `lui/leur`.
objectives: Test a verb’s construction before choosing a pronoun.
Position a single pronoun correctly in simple, compound, and infinitive structures.
Apply the fixed order when two pronouns appear together.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: The pronoun is decided by the French verb, not by the English translation. `Voir quelqu’un` and `regarder quelque chose` take a direct object, so they use `le`, `la`, `les`. `Parler à quelqu’un`, `téléphoner à quelqu’un`, `répondre à quelqu’un`, and `envoyer quelque chose à quelqu’un` take an indirect object, so they use `lui` and `leur`. Several verbs that are direct in English are indirect in French, and that mismatch is the main source of error.

Placement follows the verb group. Before a single conjugated verb: `Elle nous reçoit`. Before the auxiliary in a compound tense: `Elle nous a reçus`. Before the infinitive when the pronoun belongs to it: `Je dois le remplir`. For pronouns placed before a verb, use these ordered slots: `me/te/se/nous/vous`, then `le/la/les`, then `lui/leur`, then `y`, then `en`. Not every slot must or can be filled in every construction. Thus `Je les lui remettrai` combines a direct and an indirect object; `Oui, elle les y a posées` combines a direct object and a place. A preceding direct object still controls agreement with `avoir`: `posées` agrees with `les` when it replaces `les clés`. Affirmative commands use a different order after the verb: `Donnez-le-moi`; negative commands return the pronouns before it: `Ne me le donnez pas`.
points: Check whether the French verb takes a direct object or `à` plus a person.
Use `le`, `la`, `les` for a direct object and `lui`, `leur` for a person after `à`.
Place the pronoun before the conjugated verb, or before the auxiliary in a compound tense.
Attach the pronoun to the infinitive it completes: `Je vais le remplir`.
Follow the fixed sequence `me/te/nous/vous`, then `le/la/les`, then `lui/leur`.
Remember that `attendre` and `écouter` are direct in French, with no preposition at all.
Follow the full five-slot order when several pronouns meet: `me/te/nous/vous`, `le/la/les`, `lui/leur`, `y`, `en`.
Agree the participle with the direct-object pronoun standing in front of it.

examples.french: La conseillère nous reçoit à neuf heures.
examples.english: The adviser is meeting us at nine o’clock.
examples.note: « Recevoir quelqu’un » is direct.

examples.french: Je leur envoie les documents demandés dès ce soir.
examples.english: I am sending them the requested documents this evening.
examples.note: « Envoyer à quelqu’un » is indirect, so « leur ».

examples.french: Ce formulaire est long, mais je dois le remplir avant vendredi.
examples.english: This form is long, but I have to complete it before Friday.
examples.note: The pronoun goes before the infinitive it belongs to.

examples.french: Les documents ? Je les lui remettrai demain matin.
examples.english: The documents? I will hand them to him tomorrow morning.
examples.note: Direct pronoun before indirect pronoun.

examples.french: Elle m’a téléphoné hier pour confirmer le rendez-vous.
examples.english: She phoned me yesterday to confirm the appointment.
examples.note: « Téléphoner à quelqu’un » is indirect in French, unlike its English equivalent.

examples.french: J’attends la conseillère depuis vingt minutes ; je l’attends devant le guichet.
examples.english: I have been waiting for the adviser for twenty minutes; I am waiting for her in front of the counter.
examples.note: « Attendre quelqu’un » is direct in French, so the pronoun is « la », not « lui ».

examples.french: Les clés du local ? Oui, elle les y a posées ce matin.
examples.english: The keys to the room? Yes, she put them there this morning.
examples.note: When replacing the keys with a pronoun, les precedes y and triggers agreement. Keeping the noun is also correct: « Elle y a posé les clés ».

examples.french: Elle me les a envoyés par courriel, mais ne le leur transmettez pas avant la vérification.
examples.english: She sent them to me by email, but do not forward it to them before the check.
examples.note: « Me » before « les »; in a negative command the pronouns keep their normal order before the verb.

mistakes.avoid: Je l’ai téléphoné pour confirmer.
mistakes.prefer: Je lui ai téléphoné pour confirmer.
mistakes.why: `Téléphoner à quelqu’un` takes an indirect object, so the pronoun is `lui`.

mistakes.avoid: Je vais remplir le demain.
mistakes.prefer: Je vais le remplir demain.
mistakes.why: The pronoun stands before the infinitive it completes, not after it.

mistakes.avoid: J’attends pour la conseillère depuis vingt minutes.
mistakes.prefer: J’attends la conseillère depuis vingt minutes.
mistakes.why: `Attendre` takes a direct object in French; the English preposition for has no equivalent here.

mistakes.avoid: Je lui le remettrai demain matin au guichet.
mistakes.prefer: Je le lui remettrai demain matin au guichet.
mistakes.why: `Le/la/les` always comes before `lui/leur` in the fixed sequence.

mistakes.avoid: Oui, elle y les a posées ce matin.
mistakes.prefer: Oui, elle les y a posées ce matin.
mistakes.why: When both pronouns are used, the direct object `les` precedes `y`. Repeating the noun instead is also grammatical.

vocabulary.example: J’ai téléphoné à la conseillère, puis je lui ai envoyé un courriel.
vocabulary.note: Indirect in French even though the English verb is direct.

vocabulary.example: Je les lui remettrai avant la fin de la semaine.
vocabulary.note: Follows `mettre`; participle `remis`.

vocabulary.example: Un document numérisé est accepté pour la première étape.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; `un justificatif` is the narrower administrative term.

vocabulary.example: Un rendez-vous en personne reste nécessaire pour la signature.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; invariable in the plural.

vocabulary.example: Nous attendons la décision du comité depuis trois semaines.
vocabulary.note: Direct object with no preposition, so the pronoun is `le`, `la`, or `les`.

practice.prompt: Replace the underlined groups: « J’envoie le dossier à la conseillère. »
practice.hint: Direct pronoun first, then indirect.
practice.answer: Je le lui envoie.

takeaways: The French verb decides: direct object or `à` plus person.
`Lui` and `leur` are for people introduced by `à`.
Fixed order: `me/te/nous/vous`, `le/la/les`, `lui/leur`, `y`, `en`.
Five slots in order: `me/te/nous/vous`, `le/la/les`, `lui/leur`, `y`, `en`.

lessons.title: Les pronoms « y » et « en »
lessons.summary: `Y` replaces a place or a non-person complement introduced by `à`: `Je vais au bureau` gives `J’y vais`; `Je pense au projet` gives `J’y pense`. `En` replaces a complement introduced by `de`, a partitive phrase, or a counted noun: `Je parle du projet` gives `J’en parle`; `J’ai deux dossiers` gives `J’en ai deux`. Stressed forms make personal references clear (`Je pense à elle`, `Je parle d’elle`), while `en` can also count people (`Des collègues ? J’en connais plusieurs`).
objectives: Find the preposition of the phrase you want to replace.
Keep the quantity expression when using `en`.
Use stressed pronouns for clear personal reference and recognise that `en` can also count people.
Place `y` correctly inside a pronominal verb in a compound tense.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: `Y` and `en` are adverbial pronouns: they stand for a whole prepositional phrase rather than for a noun alone. The preposition of the original phrase decides which one you need. Anything built with `à` and referring to a thing or a place becomes `y`; anything built with `de` and referring to a thing becomes `en`. `En` also covers the partitive (`du café` gives `j’en bois`) and any counted noun (`deux formations` gives `j’en ai suivi deux`).

A quantity word stays in the sentence after `en`: `J’en veux deux`, `Il y en a beaucoup`. To refer clearly to a particular person, stressed forms are useful: `Je pense à elle`, `Je parle de lui`. This is not a blanket exclusion of people from `en`: `Des collègues ? J’en connais plusieurs` is correct. Placement follows the verb group: before the conjugated verb or auxiliary, and before the infinitive the pronoun belongs to.

`S’habituer à` illustrates placement with a pronominal verb. `Je m’habitue à la nouvelle procédure` can become `Je m’y habitue`; in a compound tense, `y` sits between the reflexive pronoun and the auxiliary: `Je m’y suis habitué`. Keeping `à ça` is also grammatical: `Je me suis habitué à ça`. With `s’habituer`, the reflexive pronoun is direct, so the participle agrees: a woman writes `Je m’y suis habituée`. Do not generalise this agreement to every pronominal verb: `elles se sont parlé` stays unchanged because `se` is indirect.
points: Identify the preposition before choosing between `y` and `en`.
Use `y` for `à` plus a thing or a place, `en` for `de` plus a thing.
Use `en` for a partitive article and for any counted noun.
Repeat the number or quantity after `en`.
Use `à elle`, `de lui`, and other stressed forms for clear personal reference; quantified `en` can also refer to people.
Place `y` between the reflexive pronoun and the auxiliary: `je m’y suis habitué`.
With `s’habituer`, agree with the direct reflexive pronoun: `je m’y suis habituée` for a woman; other pronominal verbs need their own agreement analysis.

examples.french: Vous allez au centre de services ? Oui, j’y vais cet après-midi.
examples.english: Are you going to the service centre? Yes, I am going there this afternoon.
examples.note: « Y » replaces « au centre de services ».

examples.french: Avez-vous besoin de renseignements ? Oui, j’en ai besoin.
examples.english: Do you need information? Yes, I need some.
examples.note: « Avoir besoin de » becomes « en ».

examples.french: Elle a suivi deux formations cette année ; elle en a suivi deux.
examples.english: She took two training courses this year; she took two of them.
examples.note: The number stays after « en ».

examples.french: Ce projet est important : nous y pensons depuis des mois.
examples.english: This project is important: we have been thinking about it for months.
examples.note: « Penser à » plus a thing gives « y ».

examples.french: Ma conseillère est excellente ; je pense souvent à elle.
examples.english: My adviser is excellent; I often think about her.
examples.note: With a person, a stressed pronoun replaces « y ».

examples.french: Le froid me surprenait au début, mais je m’y suis habituée en quelques mois.
examples.english: The cold surprised me at first, but I got used to it within a few months.
examples.note: « Y » sits before the auxiliary; the participle agrees with a female subject.

examples.french: La nouvelle procédure est plus longue, mais nous nous y sommes habitués rapidement.
examples.english: The new procedure takes longer, but we got used to it quickly.
examples.note: Same structure in the plural, with agreement on « habitués ».

mistakes.avoid: J’en vais à l’école chaque matin.
mistakes.prefer: J’y vais chaque matin.
mistakes.why: A place introduced by `à` is replaced by `y`, not by `en`.

mistakes.avoid: Ma sœur habite ici ; je pense souvent à la.
mistakes.prefer: Ma sœur habite ici ; je pense souvent à elle.
mistakes.why: After the preposition `à`, use the stressed pronoun `elle`, not the object pronoun `la`.

mistakes.avoid: C’était difficile au début, mais je me suis y habitué.
mistakes.prefer: C’était difficile au début, mais je m’y suis habitué.
mistakes.why: When using `y`, place it before the auxiliary and elide `me` to `m’`. The alternative `je me suis habitué à ça` is also correct.

vocabulary.example: Nous parlons du projet en réunion, et nous en parlons aussi entre nous.
vocabulary.note: Built with `de`, so the complement is replaced by `en`.

vocabulary.example: Je pense à ma prochaine entrevue, et j’y pense chaque soir.
vocabulary.note: `Y` for a thing, but `à lui` or `à elle` for a person.

vocabulary.example: Un renseignement précis évite un déplacement inutile.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun, frequently used in the plural: `des renseignements`.

vocabulary.example: Un centre de services regroupe plusieurs démarches administratives.
vocabulary.note: Masculine compound noun; learn it as one unit.

practice.prompt: Answer with `y` or `en`: « Combien de dossiers avez-vous déposés ? » (three) and « Allez-vous à la mairie ? » (yes).
practice.hint: One answer keeps a number.
practice.answer: J’en ai déposé trois. Oui, j’y vais.

takeaways: `À` plus thing gives `y`; `de` plus thing gives `en`.
`En` also covers partitives and counted nouns, and the number stays.
Stressed pronouns clarify personal references (`à elle`, `de lui`); `en` can also count people.
`Y` precedes the auxiliary in `je m’y suis habitué`; it does not determine the participle’s agreement rule.

lessons.title: Les pronoms toniques, réfléchis et emphatiques
lessons.summary: Stressed pronouns (`moi, toi, lui, elle, nous, vous, eux, elles`) are used after a preposition, in a coordinated subject, after `c’est`, and for emphasis. Naming yourself last is a courtesy convention, not a grammar requirement. `Lui et toi avez répondu` and `Toi et lui, vous avez répondu` are both correct. Reflexive pronouns (`me, te, se, nous, vous, se`) belong to the verb and refer back to its subject. `Soi` is useful with an indefinite or general subject.
objectives: Use a stressed pronoun in each of its four contexts.
Distinguish courtesy conventions from grammatical agreement in a coordinated subject.
Choose `soi` and `soi-même` with an indefinite subject.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: A stressed pronoun stands on its own, away from the verb. French requires it in four situations: after any preposition (`avec lui`, `chez elle`, `pour eux`), in a coordinated subject (`Elle et moi participerons`), after `c’est` (`C’est moi`), and for contrast or emphasis (`Moi, je préfère attendre`). Adding `-même` reinforces it: `moi-même`, `eux-mêmes`.

A coordinated subject does not have a compulsory order by person. Naming yourself last is courteous (`Ma collègue et moi`), but reversing the order is not ungrammatical. Repeating the group with a subject pronoun is also optional: `Lui et toi avez répondu` and `Toi et lui, vous avez répondu` are both correct. Agreement depends on the people included, not their order: a group including `moi` takes the `nous` form; without a first person, a group including `toi` takes the `vous` form. Reflexive pronouns instead belong to the verb: `elle se prépare`, `nous nous inscrivons`. With an indefinite or general subject, `soi` is useful: `Il vaut mieux vérifier le formulaire soi-même`.
points: Use a stressed pronoun immediately after any preposition.
Naming yourself last (`Elle et moi`) is a courtesy convention, not a required word order.
Agree by the people included: `Lui et moi avons répondu`, `Lui et toi avez répondu`.
Repeat the group with a matching subject pronoun if desired: `Toi et lui, vous avez répondu`.
Use `c’est moi`, `c’est lui`, `ce sont eux` to identify.
Add `-même` for emphasis, agreeing in number: `nous-mêmes`, `eux-mêmes`.
Use `soi` and `soi-même` when the subject is `on`, `chacun`, or unspecified.

examples.french: Elle et moi participerons à la consultation publique de jeudi.
examples.english: She and I will take part in Thursday’s public consultation.
examples.note: Naming yourself last is courteous; the verb takes the nous form because moi is included.

examples.french: Le rendez-vous a lieu chez elle, pas au bureau.
examples.english: The appointment is at her place, not at the office.
examples.note: Stressed pronoun after a preposition.

examples.french: Ils ont préparé le dossier eux-mêmes, sans aide extérieure.
examples.english: They prepared the file themselves, without outside help.
examples.note: Emphatic form agreeing in number.

examples.french: Il vaut mieux vérifier le formulaire soi-même avant de l’envoyer.
examples.english: It is better to check the form oneself before sending it.
examples.note: « Soi » with an impersonal subject.

examples.french: Moi, je préfère déposer le dossier en personne.
examples.english: Personally, I prefer to submit the file in person.
examples.note: Stressed pronoun in front for contrast.

examples.french: Toi et lui, vous présenterez le projet devant le conseil de quartier.
examples.english: You and he will present the project to the neighbourhood council.
examples.note: Second person before third, resumed by « vous ».

examples.french: Ma femme et toi, vous êtes les meilleures amies du monde.
examples.english: You and my wife are the best of friends.
examples.note: The coordinated subject is resumed by « vous »; the attribute agrees in the feminine plural.

mistakes.avoid: Ma collègue et je avons rédigé le rapport.
mistakes.prefer: Ma collègue et moi avons rédigé le rapport.
mistakes.why: Use the stressed form `moi`, not `je`, in this coordinated subject.

mistakes.avoid: Ils ont préparé le dossier eux-même.
mistakes.prefer: Ils ont préparé le dossier eux-mêmes.
mistakes.why: The emphatic form agrees in number: plural `eux-mêmes`.

mistakes.avoid: Lui et toi a rempli les mêmes formulaires.
mistakes.prefer: Lui et toi avez rempli les mêmes formulaires.
mistakes.why: This coordinated subject includes `toi` and no first person, so it takes the second-person plural verb `avez`. Its order is grammatical without a repeated `vous`.

vocabulary.example: Une consultation publique permet à chacun de s’exprimer sur le projet.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun phrase; the gender comes from `consultation`.

vocabulary.example: Elle se prépare seule pour l’entrevue de mardi.
vocabulary.note: Reflexive verb; the pronoun changes with the subject.

vocabulary.example: Il vaut mieux relire son dossier soi-même avant de l’envoyer.
vocabulary.note: Used with `on`, `chacun`, or an impersonal construction.

vocabulary.example: Ma collègue et moi partageons le même bureau.
vocabulary.note: Feminine form; the masculine is `un collègue`, with the same spelling.

practice.prompt: Rewrite politely: « Moi et lui avons déposé la demande. »
practice.hint: Only the order changes; the original is grammatical, but naming yourself last is courteous.
practice.answer: Lui et moi avons déposé la demande.

takeaways: Preposition, coordination, `c’est`, emphasis: four homes for stressed pronouns.
Subject order is flexible; agreement follows the people included, and a repeated subject pronoun is optional.
Indefinite subject equals `soi` and `soi-même`.

lessons.title: Les indéfinis « tout », « quelqu’un », « chacun », « n’importe » et « autre »
lessons.summary: `Tout` agrees when it determines a noun (`tout le dossier`, `toutes les candidates`) but is invariable as an adverb (`tout simplement`). `Quelqu’un` and `quelque chose` take `de` before an adjective: `quelqu’un d’autre`, `quelque chose d’important`. `Chacun` and `chacune` are singular and take `de` or `d’entre`. `N’importe qui`, `n’importe quoi`, and `n’importe quel` express free choice in positive sentences; the negative counterparts are `personne` and `rien`. `Autre` varies with specificity: `un autre`, `l’autre`, `les autres`, `d’autres`.
objectives: Agree `tout` correctly and recognise its invariable adverbial use.
Insert `de` before an adjective after `quelqu’un` and `quelque chose`.
Select the right form of `autre` and of the `n’importe` series.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: An indefinite word refers without identifying a precise person or thing. `Tout` has four determiner forms — `tout`, `toute`, `tous`, `toutes` — and is normally followed by another determiner: `tout le dossier`, `toutes les candidates`. As a pronoun it means everything (`Tout est prêt`), and before an adjective or adverb it becomes an invariable intensifier: `tout simplement`, `tout près`.

`Quelqu’un` and `quelque chose` are singular and insert `de` before any adjective: `quelqu’un de disponible`, `quelque chose d’utile`, `quelqu’un d’autre`. `Chacun` and `chacune` are always singular and take `de` or `d’entre` before a group: `chacune des candidates`, `chacun d’entre vous`. The `n’importe` series expresses free choice and is used in positive sentences only: `n’importe qui`, `n’importe quoi`, `n’importe quel formulaire`; the negatives are `personne` and `rien`. Finally, `autre` is graded by specificity: `un autre` (another one), `l’autre` (the other specific one), `les autres` (the others), `d’autres` (some others).

Three quantifiers are often mixed up because English uses *some* and *many* for all of them. `Quelques` introduces a small number and is always plural: `J’habite à quelques rues de la station de métro`. `Plusieurs` means several, is a determiner in its own right, and never changes form: `Plusieurs organismes offrent des cours de français gratuits`. `De nombreux` and `de nombreuses` mean many and do agree with the noun: `De nombreuses familles attendent encore un logement abordable`. Note the article in that last one: the plural indefinite `des` reduces to `de` in front of a plural adjective placed before the noun, which is why it is `de nombreux services` and never `des nombreux services`. The definite article `les` is never affected by that rule.
points: Agree `tout` with the noun group it introduces, and leave it invariable before an adjective.
Add `de` between `quelqu’un` or `quelque chose` and any adjective.
Keep `chacun` and `chacune` singular, followed by `de` or `d’entre`.
Use the `n’importe` series only in positive sentences.
Choose among `un autre`, `l’autre`, `les autres`, and `d’autres` by specificity.
Use `plusieurs` for an unspecified number greater than one, and `quelque part` for an unidentified place.
Pronounce the final `s` of `tous` when it is a pronoun (`ils sont tous venus`) and keep it silent in the determiner (`tous les dossiers`).
Use `tout ce que`, `tout ce qui`, and `tout ce dont` to mean everything that.
Use `quelques` for a small plural number and `plusieurs` for several; the pronoun can introduce a subset with `de`: `plusieurs de mes collègues`.
Agree `de nombreux` and `de nombreuses` with the noun, and keep `de` rather than `des` before them.

examples.french: Toutes les candidates ont reçu les mêmes consignes écrites.
examples.english: All the candidates received the same written instructions.
examples.note: « Tout » agrees with the noun group it introduces.

examples.french: Quelqu’un d’autre pourra-t-il m’expliquer cette démarche ?
examples.english: Will someone else be able to explain this procedure to me?
examples.note: « De » is required before the adjective.

examples.french: Chacun d’entre vous peut proposer une solution concrète.
examples.english: Each of you can suggest a concrete solution.
examples.note: « Chacun » stays singular and takes « d’entre ».

examples.french: Prenez n’importe quel formulaire vert ; les autres sont périmés.
examples.english: Take any green form at all; the others are out of date.
examples.note: Free choice in a positive sentence, then « les autres » for a known group.

examples.french: Personne n’a répondu et rien n’a été décidé pendant la réunion.
examples.english: Nobody answered and nothing was decided during the meeting.
examples.note: Negative counterparts of the n’importe series.

examples.french: Plusieurs candidats attendent encore une réponse, et le dossier manquant est quelque part dans les archives.
examples.english: Several applicants are still waiting for an answer, and the missing file is somewhere in the archives.
examples.note: « Plusieurs » is invariable in form and always plural; « quelque part » names an unidentified place.

examples.french: Tout ce que vous avez fourni est conforme, et les candidats sont tous convoqués lundi.
examples.english: Everything you provided is compliant, and the candidates are all summoned on Monday.
examples.note: « Tout ce que » for everything that; in « tous convoqués » the pronoun « tous » is pronounced with its final s.

examples.french: J’habite à quelques rues de la station de métro, et plusieurs organismes offrent des cours de français gratuits dans le secteur.
examples.english: I live a few streets from the subway station, and several organisations offer free French courses in the area.
examples.note: « Quelques » for a small number, invariable « plusieurs » for several.

examples.french: De nombreuses familles attendent encore un logement abordable dans ce quartier.
examples.english: Many families are still waiting for affordable housing in this neighbourhood.
examples.note: « De » instead of « des » before the preposed plural adjective « nombreuses ».

examples.french: Plusieurs de mes collègues suivent ce cours du soir.
examples.english: Several of my colleagues take this evening course.
examples.note: As a pronoun, plusieurs can take de before the group from which a subset is selected.

mistakes.avoid: Je cherche quelqu’un disponible cet après-midi.
mistakes.prefer: Je cherche quelqu’un de disponible cet après-midi.
mistakes.why: `Quelqu’un` requires `de` before an adjective.

mistakes.avoid: Chacune des candidates ont reçu une réponse.
mistakes.prefer: Chacune des candidates a reçu une réponse.
mistakes.why: `Chacune` is singular, so the verb stays in the singular.

mistakes.avoid: Tout que vous avez envoyé est arrivé ce matin.
mistakes.prefer: Tout ce que vous avez envoyé est arrivé ce matin.
mistakes.why: `Tout` needs the relative group `ce que`, `ce qui`, or `ce dont` before a clause.

mistakes.avoid: Des nombreux services sont offerts gratuitement aux nouveaux arrivants.
mistakes.prefer: De nombreux services sont offerts gratuitement aux nouveaux arrivants.
mistakes.why: The plural indefinite `des` reduces to `de` before a plural adjective that comes in front of the noun.

mistakes.avoid: Plusieurs personne attend encore une réponse du service.
mistakes.prefer: Plusieurs personnes attendent encore une réponse du service.
mistakes.why: `Plusieurs` is invariable but the noun and the verb that follow it are plural.

vocabulary.example: Une consigne claire évite beaucoup d’erreurs pendant l’épreuve.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; `suivre les consignes` means to follow instructions.

vocabulary.example: Une candidate motivée pose des questions précises en entrevue.
vocabulary.note: Feminine form; the masculine is `un candidat`.

vocabulary.example: N’importe quelle pièce d’identité officielle est acceptée.
vocabulary.note: Determiner form; it agrees with the noun that follows.

vocabulary.example: Chacun d’entre nous doit relire son dossier avant l’envoi.
vocabulary.note: Always singular, even when the group is plural.

vocabulary.example: Plusieurs mesures ont été annoncées lors de la consultation.
vocabulary.note: Invariable and plural; determiner in `plusieurs personnes`, pronoun in `plusieurs de mes collègues`.

vocabulary.example: J’ai rangé l’attestation quelque part dans ce classeur.
vocabulary.note: Invariable; the negative counterpart is `nulle part`.

vocabulary.example: Tout ce que vous déposez avant midi est traité le jour même.
vocabulary.note: Use `tout ce qui` when the element is the subject of the clause.

vocabulary.example: La consigne est claire, et nos valises sont à la consigne de la gare.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun with two meanings decided by context; `les consignes` are usually instructions.

vocabulary.example: De nombreuses demandes ont été déposées avant la date limite.
vocabulary.note: Agrees with the noun; `de` replaces `des` because the adjective comes first.

practice.prompt: Complete: « ___ les documents sont prêts, mais il manque ___ d’important : ___ des candidats doit signer. »
practice.hint: Agreement, then `de` before an adjective, then a singular indefinite.
practice.answer: Tous les documents sont prêts, mais il manque quelque chose d’important : chacun des candidats doit signer.

takeaways: `Tout` agrees as a determiner and is invariable as an intensifier.
`Quelqu’un` and `quelque chose` need `de` before an adjective.
`N’importe` for free choice, `personne` and `rien` for negation.
`Quelques` a few, `plusieurs` several and invariable, `de nombreux` many and agreeing.
keywords: tout, quelqu’un, chacun, n’importe, and autre

lessons.title: La négation et la place des pronoms
lessons.summary: In careful written French, `ne` precedes the verb group and words such as `pas`, `jamais`, and `plus` follow the conjugated verb or auxiliary. Object and reflexive pronouns sit between `ne` and the verb; an object `personne` follows the past participle. Before an infinitive, place `ne pas` together: `ne pas déranger`. Signs may use either an infinitive or an imperative (`Ne dérangez pas`). Keep `ne` in formal prose; its omission belongs to informal usage. `Si` contradicts a negative statement or question.
objectives: Position both negative elements in simple and compound tenses.
Place `ne pas` before an infinitive and recognise the imperative as another valid sign format.
Judge when the spoken omission of `ne` is acceptable.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: French negation has two parts. `Ne` attaches to the left of the verb group and the second word follows the conjugated verb: `Nous ne pouvons pas venir ce soir`, `Je ne t’attends pas`. In a compound tense the second word comes after the auxiliary, not after the participle: `Je n’ai pas mangé`, `Je n’ai pas marché dans la forêt`, `Je ne suis pas allé en France le mois dernier`. Object and reflexive pronouns belong inside the frame, immediately after `ne`.

Before an infinitive, `ne pas` stays together: `Ne pas déranger`, `Ne pas fumer`. An imperative is equally grammatical on a sign: `Ne dérangez pas`, `Ne fumez pas`. The choice is a matter of presentation, not a rule banning commands from signs. An object `personne` follows the past participle: `Je n’ai vu personne`. The more formal `ne… guère` means hardly, and `ne… nullement` means not at all. Dropping `ne` is common in relaxed speech and informal messages, but keep it in formal letters and exam prose. Finally, use `si` to contradict a negative question or statement.
points: Write `ne` before the pronouns and the conjugated verb.
Place `pas`, `jamais`, `plus`, `guère`, or `nullement` after the conjugated verb or the auxiliary.
Keep `ne pas` together in front of an infinitive: `Ne pas déranger`, `Ne pas fumer`.
Place `personne` after the past participle when it is the object.
Keep `ne` in formal writing; distinguish that register choice from informal speech or messages.
Use `si` when contradicting a negative question or statement.

examples.french: Nous ne pouvons pas venir ce soir, et je ne t’attends pas après dix-huit heures.
examples.english: We cannot come this evening, and I am not waiting for you after six o’clock.
examples.note: Simple tenses, with the object pronoun inside the negation.

examples.french: Je n’ai pas mangé et je ne suis pas allé en France le mois dernier.
examples.english: I have not eaten and I did not go to France last month.
examples.note: In compound tenses the second element follows the auxiliary, whatever the auxiliary.

examples.french: Sur la porte, on lit « Ne pas déranger » et, dans le hall, « Ne pas fumer ».
examples.english: On the door it reads “Do not disturb” and, in the lobby, “No smoking”.
examples.note: Before an infinitive the two negative words stand together.

examples.french: Le service n’a guère de personnel cette semaine et n’accepte nullement les retards.
examples.english: The department has hardly any staff this week and does not tolerate lateness at all.
examples.note: « Ne… guère » and « ne… nullement » belong to a formal register.

examples.french: Dans une lettre officielle, j’écris « Je ne parle pas français » ; dans un message familier, on peut lire « Je parle pas français ».
examples.english: In an official letter, I write “Je ne parle pas français”; in an informal message, you may read “Je parle pas français”.
examples.note: The distinction is formal versus informal usage, not simply writing versus speech.

examples.french: Vous n’avez pas encore soumis le formulaire ? Si, je l’ai soumis ce matin.
examples.english: Have you not submitted the form yet? Yes, I submitted it this morning.
examples.note: « Si » contradicts a negative question.

mistakes.avoid: Je le ne connais pas et je ne l’ai jamais vu.
mistakes.prefer: Je ne le connais pas et je ne l’ai jamais vu.
mistakes.why: The object pronoun belongs between `ne` and the verb, not before `ne`.

mistakes.avoid: Il a ne pas répondu à ma demande.
mistakes.prefer: Il n’a pas répondu à ma demande.
mistakes.why: In a compound tense, `ne` precedes the auxiliary and `pas` follows it.

mistakes.avoid: Sur la porte, on lit « Ne pas dérangez » comme consigne générale.
mistakes.prefer: Sur la porte, on lit « Ne pas déranger » comme consigne générale.
mistakes.why: Use the infinitive after `ne pas`: `Ne pas déranger`. The imperative `Ne dérangez pas` is another correct option.

vocabulary.example: Je ne connais pas encore la décision du comité.
vocabulary.note: Basic frame; `ne` precedes the verb group, `pas` follows the conjugated verb.

vocabulary.example: Elle n’a jamais manqué une séance de formation.
vocabulary.note: Rules out every occurrence; same placement as `ne… pas`.

vocabulary.example: Le guichet n’accepte plus les paiements en espèces.
vocabulary.note: Marks a situation that has stopped.

vocabulary.example: Ce rapport n’apporte guère d’éléments nouveaux.
vocabulary.note: Formal register; close in meaning to `presque pas`.

vocabulary.english: not at all, in no way
vocabulary.example: La municipalité n’est nullement responsable de ce retard.
vocabulary.note: Formal register; stronger than `pas du tout` in writing.

vocabulary.example: Un portail sécurisé permet de suivre l’état de sa demande.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; also means a gate.

practice.prompt: Write the sign meaning “no smoking”, then say formally that you did not walk in the forest.
practice.hint: An infinitive sign, then a compound tense.
practice.answer: Ne pas fumer. Je n’ai pas marché dans la forêt.

takeaways: `Ne` hugs the verb group; the second word follows the conjugated verb.
`Ne pas` stands together in front of an infinitive, as on signs.
Keep `ne` in formal prose; both infinitive and imperative instructions are valid on signs.
`Si` is the yes that contradicts a negative.

lessons.title: L’accord avec une phrase affirmative ou négative
lessons.summary: To echo someone, match the polarity of their statement. After a positive statement use `moi aussi`, `lui aussi`, `nous aussi`. After a negative statement use `moi non plus`, `elle non plus`. `Non plus` also adds a second excluded element: `Elle n’utilise pas la voiture, et son conjoint non plus`. Using `aussi` after a negative is one of the most audible learner errors.
objectives: Identify whether the first statement is positive or negative.
Respond with the matching stressed pronoun and particle.
Add a second excluded element with `non plus`.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: Polarity is simply whether a sentence affirms or denies. French marks agreement with a previous speaker by copying that polarity: a positive statement is echoed with `aussi`, a negative statement with `non plus`. The person is expressed by a stressed pronoun placed first: `moi aussi`, `toi non plus`, `eux aussi`.

The same particle works inside a single sentence when you add a second element to what has already been said. After a positive clause: `Elle participe à l’atelier, et son conjoint aussi`. After a negative clause: `Elle n’utilise pas la voiture, et son conjoint non plus`. English uses too and either, and English speakers regularly transfer too into a negative context, which produces the incorrect `moi aussi` after a denial.
points: Read the first statement and label it positive or negative.
Echo a positive statement with `aussi`.
Echo a negative statement with `non plus`.
Start with the stressed pronoun: `moi`, `toi`, `lui`, `elle`, `nous`, `vous`, `eux`, `elles`.
Use `non plus` to add a second excluded element after a negative clause.

examples.french: Je participe à l’atelier du samedi. — Moi aussi !
examples.english: I go to the Saturday workshop. — So do I!
examples.note: Positive statement echoed with « aussi ».

examples.french: Je ne peux pas travailler dimanche. — Moi non plus !
examples.english: I cannot work on Sunday. — Neither can I!
examples.note: Negative statement echoed with « non plus ».

examples.french: Elle n’utilise pas la voiture, et son conjoint non plus.
examples.english: She does not use the car, and neither does her partner.
examples.note: A second excluded element inside the same sentence.

examples.french: Il a déposé sa demande en ligne, et sa sœur aussi.
examples.english: He submitted his application online, and so did his sister.
examples.note: A second included element after a positive clause.

examples.french: Nous n’avons pas reçu la confirmation. — Nous non plus.
examples.english: We have not received the confirmation. — Neither have we.
examples.note: The stressed pronoun comes first.

mistakes.avoid: Je n’ai pas compris la consigne. — Moi aussi.
mistakes.prefer: Je n’ai pas compris la consigne. — Moi non plus.
mistakes.why: A negative statement is echoed with `non plus`, never with `aussi`.

mistakes.avoid: Elle n’aime pas les longues réunions, et son collègue aussi.
mistakes.prefer: Elle n’aime pas les longues réunions, et son collègue non plus.
mistakes.why: The added element is also excluded, so it takes `non plus`.

vocabulary.example: Je ne travaille pas le dimanche. — Moi non plus.
vocabulary.note: Reply used only after a negative statement.

vocabulary.example: Je suis un cours du soir. — Moi aussi.
vocabulary.note: Reply used only after a positive statement.

vocabulary.example: Un conjoint peut accompagner le demandeur à l’entrevue.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; feminine `une conjointe`.

vocabulary.example: Un horaire de fin de semaine ne convient pas à tout le monde.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun despite its final -e.

practice.prompt: Reply agreeing: « Je n’ai pas encore reçu ma carte. » then « J’ai déjà pris rendez-vous. »
practice.hint: Opposite polarities require opposite particles.
practice.answer: Moi non plus. / Moi aussi.

takeaways: Positive equals `aussi`; negative equals `non plus`.
The stressed pronoun always comes first.
`Non plus` also adds a second excluded element.
keywords: agreeing with positive and negative statements

lessons.title: Les formes de la question
lessons.summary: French questions can use statement order with questioning intonation, `est-ce que`, or inversion. Their register depends on the wording and context; inversion is often formal but is not obligatory in writing. Question words include `où`, `quand`, `pourquoi`, `comment`, `combien`, `qui`, `que`, `quel`, and `lequel`. For things, `qu’est-ce qui` asks about the subject and `qu’est-ce que` about the object. Some present-tense inversions with `je` are restricted, but many are valid: `ai-je`, `suis-je`, `dois-je`, `puis-je`, `sais-je`, `vais-je`, and future forms such as `pourrai-je`.
objectives: Match a question structure to the register of the situation.
Choose the right question word for a person, a thing, a quantity, or a choice.
Recognise common inversions with `je` without treating a short example list as exhaustive.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: Register is the level of formality suited to the audience. Statement-order questions (`Vous avez un rendez-vous ?`) are common in conversation and written dialogue; final question words (`Tu habites où ?`) often sound informal. `Est-ce que` is a useful neutral choice. Inversion often sounds more formal (`Où habitez-vous ?`), but some inverted questions are ordinary everyday language (`Combien coûte ce service ?`). Writing does not require inversion in every question. Compare `Tu pars quand ?`, `Quand est-ce que tu pars ?`, and `Quand pars-tu ?`.

For a person, `qui` can appear alone or after a preposition: `Qui vous a reçu ?`, `Avec qui travaillez-vous ?`, `À qui dois-je m’adresser ?`; the long subject form `qui est-ce qui` also exists. For a thing, `qu’est-ce qui` marks the subject and `qu’est-ce que` the object; inverted `que` is another object form. `Quel` agrees with its noun (`quel formulaire`, `quelles conditions`, `Quelles sont vos disponibilités ?`), while `lequel` selects from a known set (`Lequel de ces documents faut-il joindre ?`). It contracts with `à` and `de` to give forms such as `auquel` and `duquel`. `N’est-ce pas` asks for confirmation. Inversion with `je` depends on the verb and tense: familiar forms include `ai-je`, `suis-je`, `dois-je`, `puis-je`, `sais-je`, and `vais-je`, while `Pourrai-je venir ?` uses an ordinary future form. These examples are not an exhaustive list. In the present of `pouvoir`, use `puis-je`, not `peux-je`.
points: Use statement-order questions in conversation and written dialogue; a final question word often sounds informal.
Use `est-ce que` as a neutral way to form a direct question.
Choose inversion when it suits the wording and register, not merely because the question is written.
Use `qui` for a person in any role, including after a preposition: `avec qui`, `à qui`.
Choose `qu’est-ce qui` for an unknown subject and `qu’est-ce que` for an unknown object.
Agree `quel` with its noun, and use `lequel` to ask which one of a known set.
Recognise forms such as `Que sais-je ?`, `Où vais-je ?`, and `Pourrai-je venir ?`; use `puis-je` for present-tense `pouvoir`.
For the full `lequel` system and its contracted forms, see the dedicated lesson on `lequel`.

examples.french: Tu pars quand ? — Quand est-ce que tu pars ? — Quand partez-vous ?
examples.english: When are you leaving? (informal, neutral, formal)
examples.note: One question word across the three registers.

examples.french: Avec qui travaillez-vous sur ce dossier, et à qui dois-je m’adresser ?
examples.english: Who are you working with on this file, and who should I speak to?
examples.note: « Qui » after a preposition, and the fixed inversion « dois-je ».

examples.french: Qu’est-ce qui bloque la demande, et qu’est-ce que le service recommande ?
examples.english: What is holding up the application, and what does the department recommend?
examples.note: Subject form, then object form.

examples.french: Quelles conditions faut-il remplir, et lequel de ces formulaires dois-je joindre ?
examples.english: Which conditions have to be met, and which of these forms should I attach?
examples.note: « Quelles » determines a noun; « lequel » selects from a known set.

examples.french: Combien coûte le permis, et combien de pièces justificatives faut-il fournir ?
examples.english: How much does the permit cost, and how many supporting documents must be provided?
examples.note: « Combien » alone before a verb, « combien de » before a noun.

examples.french: Puis-je déposer mon dossier en ligne ? Vous acceptez les copies numérisées, n’est-ce pas ?
examples.english: May I submit my file online? You accept scanned copies, don’t you?
examples.note: « Puis-je » is the accepted inversion; « n’est-ce pas » asks for confirmation.

examples.french: Pourrai-je retirer mon attestation demain ?
examples.english: Will I be able to collect my certificate tomorrow?
examples.note: Future-tense inversion with je is not limited to the short list of common present forms.

mistakes.avoid: Qu’est-ce que se passe au guichet ?
mistakes.prefer: Qu’est-ce qui se passe au guichet ?
mistakes.why: The missing element is the subject of `se passe`, which requires `qui`.

mistakes.avoid: Quel mesures avez-vous prises ?
mistakes.prefer: Quelles mesures avez-vous prises ?
mistakes.why: `Quel` is a determiner and agrees with the feminine plural noun `mesures`.

mistakes.avoid: Peux-je déposer ma demande aujourd’hui ?
mistakes.prefer: Puis-je déposer ma demande aujourd’hui ?
mistakes.why: For the present-tense inversion of `pouvoir` with `je`, the standard form is `puis-je`, not `peux-je`.

vocabulary.example: Est-ce que vous acceptez les documents numérisés ?
vocabulary.note: Neutral question opener; elides to `est-ce qu’` before a vowel.

vocabulary.example: Combien de pièces justificatives faut-il joindre ?
vocabulary.note: `Combien` alone stands before a verb; `combien de` stands before a noun.

vocabulary.example: Puis-je obtenir une attestation aujourd’hui ?
vocabulary.note: Fixed formal inversion; `peux-je` does not exist.

vocabulary.example: Le dossier est complet, n’est-ce pas ?
vocabulary.note: Invariable tag placed at the end of a statement.

vocabulary.example: Un prix affiché comprend toutes les taxes.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; identical in the plural.

practice.prompt: Ask formally: how much the service costs, who you should contact, and which of two forms to sign.
practice.hint: Use inversion, `qui` after a preposition, and `lequel`.
