vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; feminine `une résidente`.

vocabulary.example: Un argument précis renforce la conclusion du texte.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; it does not mean a quarrel.

vocabulary.example: Les résidents trouvent la nouvelle procédure plus claire que l’ancienne.
vocabulary.note: The adjective agrees with the direct object, not with the subject.

practice.prompt: Rewrite with `plaire`: « The volunteers like this project. » then react: « I do not mind. »
practice.hint: Subject and object swap; the reaction uses `ça`.
practice.answer: Ce projet plaît aux bénévoles. Ça ne me dérange pas.

takeaways: `Plaire à` puts the liked thing first and the person after.
`Ça me plaît`, `ça m’est égal`, `ça ne me dérange pas` are ready-made reactions.
Affirmative opinion equals indicative; denied opinion equals subjunctive.
`Trouver` plus object plus adjective judges the object, with agreement.

lessons.title: Nuancer un propos : « peut-être », « sans doute » et le doute
lessons.summary: `Peut-être` has three positions: after the verb (`Il viendra peut-être`), at the head of the sentence followed by `que` (`Peut-être qu’il viendra`), or at the head with inversion in a formal register (`Peut-être viendra-t-il`). Never leave it sentence-initial without `que` or inversion. The short negative answer is `peut-être pas`. `Sans doute` means probably, not without doubt. `Douter de` means to doubt something, while `se douter de` means to suspect that it is true, and `il se peut que` takes the subjunctive.
objectives: Place `peut-être` in all three accepted positions.
Separate `douter de` from `se douter de`.
Grade certainty with `sans doute` and `il se peut que`.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: Hedging softens a claim without abandoning it, which is exactly what an opinion paragraph needs. `Peut-être` is the most frequent device, and its placement is the difficulty. The neutral position is after the conjugated verb: `Le service rouvrira peut-être la semaine prochaine`. At the head of the sentence it needs one of two supports: the conjunction `que` (`Peut-être que le service rouvrira`) or subject-verb inversion in a formal register (`Peut-être le service rouvrira-t-il`). A sentence-initial `peut-être` with neither is not standard. As a short answer, French says `peut-être pas`, not a bare negative.

Two neighbours are worth grading against it. `Sans doute` is weaker than its English look-alike: it means probably, not without any doubt, and `sans aucun doute` is the form that means certainly. `Il se peut que` introduces a possibility and takes the subjunctive: `Il se peut que le délai soit prolongé`. Finally, two verbs that share a root mean opposite things: `douter de quelque chose` is to be unsure of it (`Je doute de l’exactitude de ce chiffre`), while `se douter de quelque chose` is to suspect that it is true (`Je m’en doutais`, I thought as much).
points: Place `peut-être` after the conjugated verb for the neutral form.
Add `que` when `peut-être` opens the sentence, or invert in a formal register.
Answer with `peut-être pas` rather than a bare negative.
Read `sans doute` as probably, and `sans aucun doute` as certainly.
Use `il se peut que` plus the subjunctive for an open possibility.
Separate `douter de` (to be unsure) from `se douter de` (to suspect it is true).

examples.french: La demande sera peut-être traitée avant vendredi.
examples.english: The application will perhaps be processed before Friday.
examples.note: Neutral position, after the conjugated verb.

examples.french: Peut-être que le service rouvrira la semaine prochaine.
examples.english: Perhaps the service will reopen next week.
examples.note: Sentence-initial « peut-être » requires « que ».

examples.french: Peut-être viendra-t-il en personne déposer le dossier.
examples.english: He may well come in person to submit the file.
examples.note: Formal alternative: inversion instead of « que ».

examples.french: — Le bureau est-il ouvert samedi ? — Peut-être pas ; je vous conseille d’appeler.
examples.english: “Is the office open on Saturday?” “Perhaps not; I would advise you to call.”
examples.note: « Peut-être pas » is the fixed short negative answer.

examples.french: Il se peut que le délai soit prolongé, mais ce retard est sans doute temporaire.
examples.english: The deadline may be extended, but this delay is probably temporary.
examples.note: « Il se peut que » takes the subjunctive; « sans doute » means probably.

examples.french: Je doute de l’exactitude de ce chiffre, mais je me doutais déjà du résultat.
examples.english: I doubt this figure is accurate, but I already suspected the result.
examples.note: « Douter de » to be unsure, « se douter de » to suspect it is true.

mistakes.avoid: Peut-être il viendra demain matin.
mistakes.prefer: Peut-être qu’il viendra demain matin.
mistakes.why: A sentence-initial `peut-être` needs `que`, or inversion as in `peut-être viendra-t-il`.

mistakes.avoid: Le bureau est-il ouvert samedi ? — Peut-être non.
mistakes.prefer: Le bureau est-il ouvert samedi ? — Peut-être pas.
mistakes.why: The fixed short answer is `peut-être pas`; `peut-être non` is not idiomatic.

mistakes.avoid: Je me doute de ce chiffre : il me semble trop élevé.
mistakes.prefer: Je doute de ce chiffre : il me semble trop élevé.
mistakes.why: `Se douter de` means to suspect something is true; being unsure of it is `douter de`.

vocabulary.example: Peut-être que la décision sera annoncée cette semaine.
vocabulary.note: Required when `peut-être` opens the sentence, unless you use inversion.

vocabulary.example: Ce retard est sans doute lié au nombre de demandes.
vocabulary.note: Weaker than English `without doubt`; `sans aucun doute` means certainly.

vocabulary.example: Il se peut que le guichet ferme plus tôt aujourd’hui.
vocabulary.note: Always followed by the subjunctive.

vocabulary.english: to doubt, to be unsure of
vocabulary.example: Je doute de la fiabilité de cette source.
vocabulary.note: `Douter que` also takes the subjunctive.

vocabulary.example: Je me doutais de sa réponse avant même de lire le courriel.
vocabulary.note: Opposite meaning to `douter de`, despite the shared root.

practice.prompt: Hedge the claim three ways: the office will perhaps close earlier today.
practice.hint: Neutral position, `peut-être que`, and formal inversion.
practice.answer: Le bureau fermera peut-être plus tôt aujourd’hui. Peut-être que le bureau fermera plus tôt aujourd’hui. Peut-être le bureau fermera-t-il plus tôt aujourd’hui.

takeaways: `Peut-être` after the verb, or first with `que` or inversion.
`Peut-être pas` is the short negative; `sans doute` means probably.
`Douter de` equals unsure; `se douter de` equals suspecting it is true.

lessons.title: Les verbes « savoir », « connaître », « croire » et « penser »
lessons.summary: `Savoir` takes a fact, a clause, a question word, or an infinitive expressing an acquired ability: `Je sais nager`, `Je ne sais pas où déposer ma demande`. `Connaître` always takes a noun phrase and means to be acquainted with a person, place, or field; it never takes an infinitive or a clause. `Croire à` means to accept something as true, `croire en` expresses trust or faith, and `penser à` means to have something in mind.
objectives: Split `savoir` and `connaître` by the type of complement.
Use `savoir` with a question word for information.
Distinguish `croire à`, `croire en`, and `penser à`.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: The dividing line is grammatical rather than semantic. `Connaître` is followed by a noun phrase and nothing else: `Je connais bien les services offerts`, `Je connais cette conseillère`, `Je connais Montréal`. `Savoir` is followed by a fact, a `que` clause, a question word, or an infinitive: `Je sais que le bureau ferme à midi`, `Je ne sais pas où déposer ma demande`, `Je sais remplir ce formulaire`. If an infinitive or a clause follows, `connaître` is impossible.

`Croire` and `penser` are separated by their prepositions. `Croire à` means to consider something real or effective: `Je crois à l’efficacité de cette mesure`. `Croire en` expresses trust or faith in a person or a value: `Je crois en l’importance de l’éducation publique`. `Penser à` means to have someone or something in mind: `Je pense à ma prochaine entrevue`; with a thing the complement can be replaced by `y`, but with a person French keeps `à lui`, `à elle`.
points: Use `connaître` only in front of a noun phrase.
Use `savoir` before a clause, a question word, or an infinitive.
Read `savoir` plus infinitive as an acquired ability, not as permission.
Use `croire à` for effectiveness and `croire en` for trust.
Replace `à` plus thing with `y`, but keep `à elle` and `à lui` for people.
Use `se demander` for an internal question and `croire à` for accepting that something is real or effective.
Use `croire quelqu’un` with no preposition when you believe what a person says.

examples.french: Savez-vous remplir ce formulaire en ligne ?
examples.english: Do you know how to complete this form online?
examples.note: « Savoir » plus infinitive: an acquired ability.

examples.french: Je ne sais pas où déposer ma demande de logement.
examples.english: I do not know where to submit my housing application.
examples.note: « Savoir » plus a question word.

examples.french: Je connais bien les services offerts aux nouveaux arrivants.
examples.english: I am familiar with the services offered to newcomers.
examples.note: « Connaître » plus a noun phrase.

examples.french: Je crois en l’importance de l’éducation publique et j’y crois depuis longtemps.
examples.english: I believe in the importance of public education and I have believed in it for a long time.
examples.note: « Croire en » for a value, then « y » replacing the complement.

examples.french: Je pense à ma prochaine entrevue et je pense souvent à elle depuis notre rencontre.
examples.english: I am thinking about my next interview, and I often think about her since we met.
examples.note: « Y » for a thing, a stressed pronoun for a person.

examples.french: Je me demande si le service est ouvert le samedi, mais je crois à l’efficacité du portail en ligne.
examples.english: I wonder whether the service is open on Saturdays, but I believe the online portal is effective.
examples.note: « Se demander si » introduces an indirect question; « croire à » accepts something as real or effective.

examples.french: Je le crois : son explication est cohérente et vérifiable.
examples.english: I believe him: his explanation is coherent and verifiable.
examples.note: Believing what a person says is direct, so the pronoun is « le », not « lui ».

mistakes.avoid: Je connais parler français depuis trois ans.
mistakes.prefer: Je sais parler français depuis trois ans.
mistakes.why: An acquired ability expressed by an infinitive requires `savoir`.

mistakes.avoid: Je sais cette conseillère depuis longtemps.
mistakes.prefer: Je connais cette conseillère depuis longtemps.
mistakes.why: Acquaintance with a person is expressed by `connaître` plus a noun phrase.

mistakes.avoid: Son explication est claire : je lui crois.
mistakes.prefer: Son explication est claire : je le crois.
mistakes.why: `Croire quelqu’un` is transitive, so the pronoun is `le` or `la`; `lui` would require a preposition the verb does not take.

vocabulary.english: to know (a fact), to know how to
vocabulary.example: Je sais où se trouve le bureau et je sais remplir la demande.
vocabulary.note: Followed by a clause, a question word, or an infinitive.

vocabulary.english: to know, to be familiar with
vocabulary.example: Elle connaît bien le quartier et ses services de proximité.
vocabulary.note: Always followed by a noun phrase; never by an infinitive.

vocabulary.example: Nous croyons en la valeur de ce programme d’intégration.
vocabulary.note: `Croire à` instead expresses belief in the reality or effectiveness of something.

vocabulary.example: Une procédure clairement expliquée réduit le nombre de questions.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; `une démarche` is the step you take within it.

vocabulary.example: Elle se demande combien de temps prendra le traitement du dossier.
vocabulary.note: Pronominal; followed by `si` or by a question word, never by `que`.

vocabulary.english: to believe in (the reality or effectiveness of)
vocabulary.example: Nous croyons à l’utilité de cette mesure pour le quartier.
vocabulary.note: `Croire en` expresses trust in a person or a value instead.

vocabulary.example: Les membres du comité l’ont crue sans hésiter.
vocabulary.note: Direct object; distinct from `croire à` (effectiveness) and `croire en` (trust).

practice.prompt: Choose the verb: « Je ___ cette procédure, mais je ne ___ pas comment la commencer. »
practice.hint: A noun phrase, then a question word.
practice.answer: Je connais cette procédure, mais je ne sais pas comment la commencer.

takeaways: Noun phrase equals `connaître`; clause, question word, or infinitive equals `savoir`.
`Croire à` for effectiveness, `croire en` for trust.
`Penser à` plus thing becomes `y`, plus person stays stressed.

lessons.title: Les verbes « arriver », « parvenir » et « se passer »
lessons.summary: `Arriver` means both to arrive and to happen: `Le train arrive`, `Un changement est arrivé`. With `à` plus infinitive, `arriver à` and the more formal `parvenir à` both mean to manage to do something, and `y arriver` resumes a goal already mentioned. `Se passer` describes what happens or happened: `Qu’est-ce qui s’est passé ?`.
objectives: Read `arriver` correctly as arrival or as occurrence.
Use `arriver à` and `parvenir à` for successful effort.
Ask and answer about what happened with `se passer`.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: `Arriver` has two readings and the context decides. With a person or a vehicle it means to arrive: `Elle est arrivée au Canada l’an dernier`. With an event or with an indirect pronoun it means to happen: `Un changement important est arrivé dans mon quartier`, `Ça m’est arrivé une fois`. In both readings the auxiliary is `être`.

Followed by `à` plus an infinitive, `arriver` shifts again and expresses success after effort: `Je suis arrivé à joindre le service`. `Parvenir à` is the more formal equivalent: `Je suis parvenu à trouver un logement`. When the goal has already been mentioned, `y` replaces it and gives the very frequent `y arriver`: `C’était difficile, mais j’y suis arrivé`. `Se passer` is impersonal in questions and is the standard way of asking about an event: `Qu’est-ce qui s’est passé ?` or, more formally, `Que s’est-il passé ?`.
points: Use `être` as the auxiliary for `arriver` in every meaning.
Read `arriver` plus a place as arrival, and `arriver` plus an event or pronoun as occurrence.
Use `arriver à` or `parvenir à` plus infinitive for success after effort.
Use `y arriver` when the goal is already known.
Ask about an event with `Qu’est-ce qui s’est passé ?` or `Que s’est-il passé ?`.

examples.french: Je suis parvenu à trouver un logement près de mon travail.
examples.english: I managed to find housing near my workplace.
examples.note: Formal register for a goal reached after effort.

examples.french: C’était difficile au début, mais j’y suis arrivé.
examples.english: It was difficult at first, but I managed it.
examples.note: « Y arriver » resumes a goal already mentioned.

examples.french: Un changement important est arrivé dans mon quartier cette année.
examples.english: An important change happened in my neighbourhood this year.
examples.note: « Arriver » in its occurrence reading, with the auxiliary être.

examples.french: Qu’est-ce qui s’est passé pendant la réunion de quartier ?
examples.english: What happened during the neighbourhood meeting?
examples.note: Standard question with « se passer ».

examples.french: Ça m’est arrivé une fois, et depuis je vérifie toujours mes documents.
examples.english: It happened to me once, and since then I always check my documents.
examples.note: Occurrence with an indirect pronoun.

mistakes.avoid: Que s’est passé pendant la réunion de quartier ?
mistakes.prefer: Que s’est-il passé pendant la réunion de quartier ?
mistakes.why: In the inverted question, `se passer` keeps its impersonal subject `il`, which is inverted after the verb.

mistakes.avoid: J’ai arrivé à joindre le service ce matin.
mistakes.prefer: Je suis arrivé à joindre le service ce matin.
mistakes.why: `Arriver` always takes the auxiliary `être` in the compound past.

vocabulary.english: to manage to, to succeed in
vocabulary.example: Elle est parvenue à obtenir un rendez-vous en moins d’une semaine.
vocabulary.note: Formal register; conjugated like `venir` and taking `être`.

vocabulary.example: La démarche était longue, mais nous y sommes arrivés.
vocabulary.note: `Y` stands for a goal already mentioned.

vocabulary.example: La consultation s’est bien passée malgré le nombre de participants.
vocabulary.note: Pronominal verb; the auxiliary is `être`.

vocabulary.example: Un événement imprévu a interrompu la cérémonie d’accueil.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; also written `un évènement`.

practice.prompt: Ask what happened, then answer that you managed to finish the file anyway.
practice.hint: The question needs a subject form; the answer can use `y arriver`.
practice.answer: Qu’est-ce qui s’est passé ? Malgré tout, j’y suis arrivé et le dossier est terminé.

takeaways: `Arriver` equals to arrive and to happen, always with `être`.
`Arriver à` and `parvenir à` equal to manage to.
`Qu’est-ce qui s’est passé ?` is the standard question.
keywords: arriver, parvenir, y arriver, and se passer

lessons.title: Les distinctions entre des verbes proches
lessons.summary: Learn verbs with their construction and intended meaning. Bring a document with `apporter`, take a child somewhere with `amener`, and use `rendre visite à` for an ordinary social visit. `Quitter` takes a direct object in `quitter le bureau`, while `partir du bureau` uses a preposition. `Laisser` can mean to leave behind, `croiser quelqu’un` to run into someone, and `disposer de` to have something available. `Inclure` and `comprendre` overlap in the sense include; only `comprendre` means understand. `Devoir` can mean have to or owe, without requiring an explicit creditor.
objectives: Store each verb together with the complement it accepts.
Separate leaving a place, leaving a person, and leaving something behind.
Read `disposer de` and `disposer` as two different verbs.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: Two criteria settle most of these pairs. The first is whether the complement is a thing or a person: you `apporter` a document but you `amener` a child; you `visiter` a museum but you `rendre visite à` a friend. The second is the preposition, which belongs to the verb and must be memorised with it: `manquer` alone means to miss, but `manquer de` means to lack. `Convaincre quelqu’un de` and `persuader quelqu’un de` share the same structure, so the difference is one of emphasis: evidence for the first, winning someone over for the second.

Departure splits three ways. `Partir` is intransitive: `Je pars à huit heures`. `Quitter` takes a direct object in `Je quitte le bureau à dix-sept heures` and `Elle a quitté son emploi`; this construction does not mean that every use requires an explicitly named object. `Laisser` means to leave something or someone behind, and it also means to let: `J’ai laissé mon dossier à l’accueil`, `Laissez-moi vérifier`. `Croiser quelqu’un` is to run into someone by chance: `J’ai croisé ma voisine au marché`. `Disposer de` means to have something available (`Le centre dispose de deux salles`), while `disposer` with a direct object means to arrange (`Elle a disposé les chaises en cercle`). `S’équiper de` means to equip oneself with something: `Il faut s’équiper de bonnes bottes pour l’hiver`. For remembering a thing expressed by a noun, compare `Je me souviens de cette réunion` / `Je m’en souviens` with the careful French construction `Je me rappelle cette réunion` / `Je me la rappelle`.

`Devoir` followed directly by an infinitive can express obligation or probability: `Je dois déposer ma demande avant vendredi`. With a thing or amount owed, it means to owe: `Il doit 200 $`, `Tu dois de l’argent depuis le mois dernier`. Naming the creditor is optional: add `à la banque`, or use an indirect pronoun in `Tu me dois de l’argent`, when that information is relevant. `Patrick me doit une faveur` shows that the object need not be money. Another useful overlap concerns inclusion: both `Le prix inclut les taxes` and `Le prix comprend les taxes` are correct. `Inclure` can describe incorporating an item or what a whole includes; `comprendre` also means to understand.
points: Use `apporter` for a thing and `amener` for a person.
Use `rendre visite à` for ordinary social visits; `visiter` also takes people in contexts such as visiting patients or prisoners.
Use `partir` with no object, `quitter` with an object, and `laisser` for what stays behind.
Use `croiser quelqu’un` for an unplanned meeting.
Read `disposer de` as to have available and `disposer` as to arrange.
Use `s’équiper de` for acquiring the equipment you need.
Use either `inclure` or `comprendre` for what a whole includes; use `comprendre` for understanding.
Before a noun naming what is remembered, use `se souvenir de`; in careful French, `se rappeler` takes that noun directly.
Read `devoir` plus an infinitive as a modal use and `devoir` plus something owed as owing; naming the creditor is optional.

examples.french: J’amène ma fille à la garderie et j’apporte son dossier médical.
examples.english: I take my daughter to daycare and bring her medical file.
examples.note: A person is « amenée », a thing is « apportée ».

examples.french: J’ai rendu visite à une famille nouvellement installée dans le quartier.
examples.english: I visited a family that has recently settled in the neighbourhood.
examples.note: Rendre visite à is the usual expression for a social visit.

examples.french: Je quitte le bureau à dix-sept heures, mais je laisse mon dossier à l’accueil.
examples.english: I leave the office at five, but I leave my file at reception.
examples.note: « Quitter » takes an object; « laisser » names what stays behind.

examples.french: J’ai croisé ma voisine au marché et elle m’a parlé du nouveau service.
examples.english: I ran into my neighbour at the market and she told me about the new service.
examples.note: « Croiser » marks an unplanned meeting.

examples.french: Le centre dispose de deux salles, et la bénévole a disposé les chaises en cercle.
examples.english: The centre has two rooms available, and the volunteer arranged the chairs in a circle.
examples.note: « Disposer de » to have available, « disposer » to arrange.

examples.french: Il faut s’équiper de bonnes bottes avant le premier verglas.
examples.english: You need to get yourself a good pair of boots before the first ice.
examples.note: « S’équiper de » is always followed by « de ».

examples.french: Le tarif comprend l’assurance, et nous avons inclus une copie du bail dans le dossier.
examples.english: The price includes insurance, and we included a copy of the lease in the file.
examples.note: These examples illustrate containing and incorporating; both inclure and comprendre can describe what a price includes.

examples.french: Je me souviens de l’entrevue, mais je ne me rappelle plus le nom du recruteur.
examples.english: I remember the interview, but I no longer remember the recruiter’s name.
examples.note: « Se souvenir » keeps « de »; « se rappeler » takes a direct object.

examples.french: Je dois déposer ma demande avant vendredi, et je dois encore 200 $ à la coopérative.
examples.english: I have to submit my application before Friday, and I still owe $200 to the co-op.
examples.note: Modal « devoir » plus infinitive, then lexical « devoir » plus amount plus « à ».

examples.french: Je dois encore deux mois de loyer.
examples.english: I still owe two months’ rent.
examples.note: The creditor can remain unexpressed; the amount owed is the direct object.

mistakes.avoid: J’ai rendu visite ma sœur pendant les vacances.
mistakes.prefer: J’ai rendu visite à ma sœur pendant les vacances.
mistakes.why: In `rendre visite à quelqu’un`, the person is introduced by `à`.

mistakes.avoid: Je pars le bureau à dix-sept heures.
mistakes.prefer: Je quitte le bureau à dix-sept heures.
mistakes.why: Use the direct construction `quitter le bureau`, or the prepositional alternative `partir du bureau`.

mistakes.avoid: Le centre dispose deux salles de réunion.
mistakes.prefer: Le centre dispose de deux salles de réunion.
mistakes.why: In the sense of having something available, the verb is `disposer de`; without `de` it means to arrange.

mistakes.avoid: Le prix inclut les taxes, mais je ne inclus pas votre question.
mistakes.prefer: Le prix inclut les taxes, mais je ne comprends pas votre question.
mistakes.why: `Le prix inclut les taxes` is correct. To mean understand in the second clause, use `comprendre`, not `inclure`.

mistakes.avoid: Je me rappelle de notre conversation de mardi.
mistakes.prefer: Je me rappelle notre conversation de mardi.
mistakes.why: `Se rappeler` takes a direct object in careful French; only `se souvenir` keeps `de`.

mistakes.avoid: Je dois de partir avant la fin de la réunion.
mistakes.prefer: Je dois partir avant la fin de la réunion.
mistakes.why: Modal `devoir` is followed directly by the infinitive, with no preposition.

mistakes.avoid: Tu doit de l’argent depuis le mois dernier.
mistakes.prefer: Tu dois de l’argent depuis le mois dernier.
mistakes.why: The present form with `tu` is `dois`, not `doit`. No explicit creditor is required.

vocabulary.example: J’amène mon fils au centre communautaire chaque mercredi.
vocabulary.note: Used with people; `apporter` is used with things.

vocabulary.english: to leave (a place or a person)
vocabulary.example: Elle a quitté son emploi pour suivre une formation à temps plein.
vocabulary.note: Takes a direct object in quitter son emploi or quitter le bureau; partir du bureau uses de.

vocabulary.example: J’ai laissé une copie du formulaire à l’accueil.
vocabulary.note: Also used for permission: `laissez-moi vérifier`.

vocabulary.example: Nous avons croisé la conseillère devant la bibliothèque.
vocabulary.note: Marks an unplanned meeting; `rencontrer` is neutral.

vocabulary.example: Nous disposons de trois semaines pour compléter le dossier.
vocabulary.note: Without `de`, `disposer` means to arrange or lay out.

vocabulary.example: Les bénévoles se sont équipés de vestes réfléchissantes.
vocabulary.note: Always followed by `de`; `équiper quelqu’un de` is the non-reflexive form.

vocabulary.example: Ce quartier manque de places en garderie.
vocabulary.note: Without `de`, `manquer` means to miss an event or a vehicle.

vocabulary.example: Veuillez inclure une preuve de résidence dans votre envoi.
vocabulary.note: Participle `inclus`, feminine `incluse`; also describes inclusion in `Le prix inclut les taxes`.

vocabulary.english: to comprise, to include (of a whole)
vocabulary.example: Le forfait comprend le transport et les repas.
vocabulary.note: Overlaps with `inclure` for what a whole includes; `comprendre` also means to understand.

vocabulary.example: Je me souviens de la date limite indiquée sur la lettre.
vocabulary.note: Always keeps `de`; the synonym `se rappeler` takes a direct object instead.

vocabulary.example: Le locataire doit encore deux mois de loyer à la propriétaire.
vocabulary.note: Lexical use; the creditor after à can be left understood. Modal devoir is followed directly by an infinitive.

vocabulary.example: Une offre d’emploi bilingue a été publiée hier sur le site du centre.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; `une proposition` is a proposal put forward, not a commercial offer.

practice.prompt: Complete: « Je ___ le bureau à midi, je ___ le dossier à l’accueil et j’ai ___ un collègue dans l’ascenseur. »
practice.hint: Object of departure, what stays behind, an unplanned meeting.
practice.answer: Je quitte le bureau à midi, je laisse le dossier à l’accueil et j’ai croisé un collègue dans l’ascenseur.

takeaways: Thing equals `apporter`; person equals `amener` and `rendre visite à`.
`Partir` without an object, `quitter` with one, `laisser` for what stays.
`Disposer de` equals to have available; `s’équiper de` equals to get equipped.
`Se souvenir de` keeps the preposition; `se rappeler` does not.
`Devoir` plus infinitive is modal; with something owed it means owe, whether or not the creditor is named.

lessons.title: L’impératif et les pronoms
lessons.summary: The imperative exists only for `tu`, `nous`, and `vous`, and the subject pronoun is not written. Regular `-er` verbs drop the final `-s` in the `tu` form (`parle`, `remplis` for `-ir` verbs keeps it), but the `-s` returns before `y` and `en` (`vas-y`, `manges-en`). In an affirmative command, pronouns follow the verb with a hyphen and `me` becomes `moi`; in a negative command, they return to their usual place before the verb.
objectives: Form the three imperative persons from the present tense.
Attach pronouns correctly in an affirmative command.
Restore the normal order in a negative command.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: The imperative is the mood of instructions, advice, and encouragement. It borrows the present-tense forms of `tu`, `nous`, and `vous` and simply drops the subject: `Remplis le formulaire`, `Remplissons le formulaire`, `Remplissez le formulaire`. One spelling rule applies to `-er` verbs, including `aller`: the `tu` form loses its final `-s`, giving `parle` and `va`. That `-s` comes back for pronunciation before `y` and `en`: `vas-y`, `manges-en`.

Pronoun placement is the main difficulty. In an affirmative command the pronouns follow the verb, joined by hyphens, and the stressed forms `moi` and `toi` replace `me` and `te`: `Donnez-moi le formulaire`, `Envoyez-lui une copie`, `Asseyez-vous`. In a negative command everything returns to the ordinary pre-verbal order: `Ne le leur transmettez pas`, `Ne t’inquiète pas`. For a very formal written instruction, French often prefers `veuillez` plus an infinitive: `Veuillez signer le formulaire`.
points: Take the present form and delete the subject pronoun.
Drop the final `-s` in the `tu` form of `-er` verbs and of `aller`.
Restore that `-s` before `y` and `en`: `vas-y`, `parles-en`.
Attach pronouns after the verb with hyphens in an affirmative command, using `moi` and `toi`.
Put the pronouns back before the verb in a negative command.
Read product and safety notices as imperatives addressed to `vous`: `Agitez bien avant emploi`.

examples.french: Prépare tes documents, puis vas-y sans attendre.
examples.english: Get your documents ready, then go ahead without waiting.
examples.note: « Prépare » loses the -s; « vas-y » gets it back before y.

examples.french: Donnez-moi le formulaire, s’il vous plaît.
examples.english: Give me the form, please.
examples.note: Affirmative command: pronoun after the verb, « me » becomes « moi ».

examples.french: Envoyez-lui une copie du dossier avant vendredi.
examples.english: Send him or her a copy of the file before Friday.
examples.note: Indirect pronoun joined by a hyphen.

examples.french: Ne le leur transmettez pas avant la vérification finale.
examples.english: Do not send it to them before the final check.
examples.note: Negative command: ordinary pre-verbal order returns.

examples.french: Veuillez signer le formulaire et le retourner par courriel.
examples.english: Please sign the form and return it by email.
examples.note: Formal written instruction with « veuillez » plus infinitive.

examples.french: Agitez bien avant emploi et conservez le flacon à l’abri de la lumière.
examples.english: Shake well before use and keep the bottle away from light.
examples.note: Product notices use the « vous » imperative with no subject pronoun.

mistakes.avoid: Me donnez le formulaire, s’il vous plaît.
mistakes.prefer: Donnez-moi le formulaire, s’il vous plaît.
mistakes.why: In an affirmative command the pronoun follows the verb and `me` becomes `moi`.

mistakes.avoid: Ne donnez-le pas avant la vérification.
mistakes.prefer: Ne le donnez pas avant la vérification.
mistakes.why: A negative command restores the ordinary order, with the pronoun before the verb.

vocabulary.example: Signez le formulaire au bas de la dernière page.
vocabulary.note: Regular `-er` verb; the `tu` imperative is `signe`, without `-s`.

vocabulary.example: Veuillez joindre une copie de votre pièce d’identité.
vocabulary.note: Formal imperative of `vouloir`, always followed by an infinitive.

vocabulary.example: Une vérification supplémentaire retarde parfois l’envoi du dossier.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; the ending -tion is a feminine hint.

vocabulary.example: Une copie numérisée est acceptée pour la première étape.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; `un exemplaire` refers to a printed copy of a document.

vocabulary.example: Agitez la bouteille avant de servir.
vocabulary.note: Regular `-er` verb; frequent on product labels in the imperative.

practice.prompt: Give the same instruction affirmatively and then negatively: send the file to them.
practice.hint: The pronoun order changes with the polarity.
practice.answer: Envoyez-le-leur. Ne le leur envoyez pas.

takeaways: Three persons only, no written subject.
`-er` verbs lose the `-s`, and recover it before `y` and `en`.
Affirmative equals pronouns after with hyphens; negative equals pronouns before.

lessons.title: Les différents emplois de « on »
lessons.summary: `On` is an indefinite subject pronoun and always takes a third-person singular verb. It has three everyday readings: we in conversation, people in general, and someone unspecified. It is also the natural French replacement for an English passive with an unnamed human agent. In formal writing, prefer `nous` when the reference must be explicit.
objectives: Keep the verb in the third-person singular after `on`.
Interpret `on` from the context of the sentence.
Choose between `on` and `nous` according to register.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: `On` is grammatically singular, whatever it means: `On y va`, `On a annoncé une consultation`. Its meaning is supplied by the context. In conversation it usually replaces `nous`: `On part à huit heures`. In a general statement it means people as a whole: `Au Canada, on peut recevoir certains services en français`. In a report about an unidentified person it means someone: `On a frappé à la porte`.

Because `on` names a human agent without identifying one, it is the most idiomatic French equivalent of many English passives: `I was told` becomes `On m’a indiqué`, and `The decision was announced` becomes `On a annoncé la décision`. Register matters in writing: an exam text or a formal letter normally uses `nous` when the writer means themselves and their group, keeping `on` for genuinely general statements. Note that adjectives after `on` meaning we are commonly written in the plural: `On est prêts`.
points: Conjugate the verb in the third-person singular after `on`.
Read `on` as we in conversation and as people in a general statement.
Use `on` plus an active verb instead of an English passive.
Prefer `nous` in formal writing when the reference is specific.
Write a following adjective in the plural when `on` means we.

examples.french: Au Canada, on peut recevoir certains services en français.
examples.english: In Canada, people can receive certain services in French.
examples.note: General statement; the verb stays singular.

examples.french: On a annoncé une consultation publique pour lundi prochain.
examples.english: A public consultation was announced for next Monday.
examples.note: « On » replaces an English passive with an unnamed agent.

examples.french: Dans ce quartier, on organise souvent des activités gratuites.
examples.english: In this neighbourhood, people often organise free activities.
examples.note: People in general.

examples.french: On est prêts à déposer le dossier dès demain matin.
examples.english: We are ready to submit the file as early as tomorrow morning.
examples.note: « On » meaning we, with a plural adjective.

examples.french: Nous avons examiné la demande et nous vous répondrons sous huit jours.
examples.english: We have reviewed the application and we will reply within eight days.
examples.note: Formal writing prefers « nous » when the reference is explicit.

mistakes.avoid: On sont arrivés en retard à la réunion.
mistakes.prefer: On est arrivés en retard à la réunion.
mistakes.why: `On` always takes a third-person singular verb, even when the participle is plural in meaning.

mistakes.avoid: Dans notre lettre de motivation, on demande un rendez-vous.
mistakes.prefer: Dans notre lettre de motivation, nous demandons un rendez-vous.
mistakes.why: A formal letter uses `nous` when the writer refers explicitly to themselves.

vocabulary.example: Un usager peut déposer une plainte directement en ligne.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; feminine `une usagère`.

vocabulary.example: Un service bilingue accueille les usagers du lundi au vendredi.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; `un service public` is a public service.

vocabulary.example: Une activité gratuite est proposée chaque samedi à la bibliothèque.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; the ending -té is a feminine hint.

vocabulary.example: On organise une séance d’information chaque premier lundi du mois.
vocabulary.note: Regular `-er` verb; frequently used with `on` in general statements.

practice.prompt: Rewrite without a passive: « The forms were sent yesterday. » then make it formal with `nous`.
practice.hint: The agent is human but unnamed in the first version.
practice.answer: On a envoyé les formulaires hier. Nous avons envoyé les formulaires hier.

takeaways: `On` is always singular, whatever it means.
Context decides between we, people, and someone.
`On` replaces an English passive; `nous` belongs to formal writing.

lessons.title: Verbes transitifs et formes pronominales : « terminer », « asseoir » et leurs paires
lessons.summary: Compare a verb’s constructions rather than assuming that every pronominal form removes its object. `Terminer le rapport` names what is completed, while `J’ai terminé` can leave it understood and `La séance se termine` describes an event ending. `Asseoir quelqu’un` means to seat another person; `s’asseoir` means to sit down. Other pairs include `ouvrir/s’ouvrir` and `arrêter/s’arrêter`, but their possible uses must be learned individually.
objectives: Decide whether an agent or the affected subject drives the sentence.
Use `asseoir` for seating someone else and `s’asseoir` for sitting down.
Transfer the pattern to comparable verb pairs.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: A direct-transitive construction links a verb to a direct object: `Je termine le rapport`. The object can also be understood from context, so `J’ai terminé` is a complete, correct sentence. In `La séance se termine à dix-sept heures`, the event itself is the subject. Do not turn this pair into a universal rule: pronominal verbs can also have an object, as in `Elle se lave les mains`.

`Asseoir quelqu’un` means to seat another person: `L’infirmière assoit le patient dans le fauteuil`. `S’asseoir` means to sit down: `Asseyez-vous, je vous en prie`. The pronominal form takes `être` (`elle s’est assise`, with agreement), while the transitive form takes `avoir` (`elle a assis l’enfant`). Learn other pairs in context: `Le conducteur arrête le bus` versus `Le bus s’arrête`. Some verbs also have non-pronominal intransitive uses: `Le guichet ouvre à neuf heures` is correct without an object or a reflexive pronoun.
points: Name the object when needed, but allow it to be understood in expressions such as `J’ai terminé`.
Learn each pronominal construction separately; some still take a direct object.
Use `asseoir quelqu’un` for seating someone else and `s’asseoir` for sitting down.
Compare `ouvrir/s’ouvrir` and `arrêter/s’arrêter` in full sentences rather than applying one universal object rule.
Remember that the pronominal form takes `être` and usually agrees in compound tenses.
Separate the action `s’asseoir` from the resulting state `être assis(e)`, which uses the participle as an adjective.

examples.french: Je termine le rapport avant la réunion de quinze heures.
examples.english: I am finishing the report before the three o’clock meeting.
examples.note: Transitive use with a direct object.

examples.french: La séance se termine à dix-sept heures précises.
examples.english: The session ends at five o’clock sharp.
examples.note: The event itself is the subject.

examples.french: L’infirmière assoit le patient dans le fauteuil avant l’examen.
examples.english: The nurse seats the patient in the chair before the examination.
examples.note: « Asseoir » with a direct object: someone seats someone else.

examples.french: Asseyez-vous, je vous en prie ; elle s’est assise près de la fenêtre.
examples.english: Please sit down; she sat down near the window.
examples.note: « S’asseoir » for sitting down, with agreement in the compound past.

examples.french: Le bus s’arrête devant la mairie, puis le conducteur arrête le moteur.
examples.english: The bus stops in front of the town hall, then the driver switches off the engine.
examples.note: The same contrast with « arrêter ».

examples.french: Le guichet ouvre à neuf heures et la porte s’ouvre automatiquement.
examples.english: The counter opens at nine o’clock and the door opens automatically.
examples.note: Ouvre is intransitive here; s’ouvre is pronominal. Neither sentence needs a direct object.

examples.french: Elle s’assoit à côté de la fenêtre ; dix minutes plus tard, elle est toujours assise au même endroit.
examples.english: She sits down next to the window; ten minutes later, she is still sitting in the same place.
examples.note: « S’asseoir » is the action of sitting down; « être assis(e) » is the state that follows.

examples.french: Avez-vous terminé le rapport ? — Oui, j’ai terminé.
examples.english: Have you finished the report? — Yes, I have finished.
examples.note: The answer leaves the object understood instead of repeating it.

mistakes.avoid: La réunion se termines à midi.
mistakes.prefer: La réunion se termine à midi.
mistakes.why: The third-person singular present is `termine`, not the second-person form `termines`.

mistakes.avoid: Asseyez-se dans le fauteuil, s’il vous plaît.
mistakes.prefer: Asseyez-vous dans le fauteuil, s’il vous plaît.
mistakes.why: The vous imperative takes the matching reflexive pronoun `vous`, not third-person `se`.

vocabulary.example: Je termine la lettre de motivation avant la date limite.
vocabulary.note: Takes a direct object here; the object can be understood in `J’ai terminé`.

vocabulary.english: to end, to come to an end
vocabulary.example: La formation se termine par une évaluation écrite.
vocabulary.note: Pronominal; takes `être` in compound tenses.

vocabulary.example: L’agent assoit les visiteurs dans la salle d’attente.
vocabulary.note: Transitive; two accepted present forms, `il assoit` and `il assied`.

vocabulary.example: Les candidats s’assoient dès que leur nom est appelé.
vocabulary.note: Pronominal; imperative `assieds-toi`, `asseyez-vous`.

vocabulary.example: Un fauteuil confortable est réservé aux personnes à mobilité réduite.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; `un siège` is the general word for a seat.

vocabulary.english: to be seated, to be sitting
vocabulary.example: Les candidats sont assis dans la salle depuis huit heures.
vocabulary.note: State resulting from `s’asseoir`; the participle agrees like an adjective.

practice.prompt: Say that the receptionist seats the visitors, then invite one visitor to sit down.
practice.hint: Transitive first, pronominal imperative second.
practice.answer: La réceptionniste assoit les visiteurs. Asseyez-vous, s’il vous plaît.

takeaways: A transitive object can be understood; a pronominal verb can also have an object.
`Asseoir quelqu’un` seats another person; `s’asseoir` is sitting down.
Learn the possible constructions of `ouvrir`, `fermer`, and `arrêter` individually.
keywords: transitive verbs and their pronominal pairs

lessons.title: Les constructions de « cacher » et de « rapporter »
lessons.summary: `Cacher quelque chose à quelqu’un` means to hide something from someone, so French uses `à` where English uses from. `Se cacher de quelqu’un` means to hide oneself from that person. `Rapporter` has three readings: to bring back, to report information, and to yield a return. `Se rapporter à` means to relate or refer to.
objectives: Use `à` after `cacher` where English would use from.
Distinguish the pronominal and non-pronominal forms.
Read `rapporter` correctly from its complement.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: The preposition belongs to the French verb, not to the English translation. `Cacher` is built as `cacher quelque chose à quelqu’un`, so `The company must not hide this information from employees` becomes `L’entreprise ne doit pas cacher cette information aux employés`. Adding the reflexive pronoun changes both the meaning and the preposition: `se cacher de quelqu’un` means to hide oneself from that person.

`Rapporter` is decided by its complement. With a concrete object it means to bring back: `Rapportez le formulaire signé`. With information it means to report: `Le témoin a rapporté les faits`. With money or an investment it means to yield: `Ce placement rapporte peu`. The pronominal `se rapporter à` is different again and means to relate to, typically used for a text, a statistic, or a rule: `Cette statistique se rapporte au marché du travail canadien`.
points: Build `cacher` as `cacher quelque chose à quelqu’un`.
Use `se cacher de quelqu’un` when the subject hides itself.
Read `rapporter` plus object as bring back.
Read `rapporter` plus information as report.
Use `se rapporter à` for a reference or a relationship between ideas.

examples.french: L’entreprise ne doit pas cacher cette information aux employés.
examples.english: The company must not hide this information from employees.
examples.note: French uses « à » where English uses from.

examples.french: Il se cachait de ses créanciers depuis plusieurs mois.
examples.english: He had been hiding from his creditors for several months.
examples.note: Pronominal form with « de ».

examples.french: Rapportez le formulaire signé au guichet avant seize heures.
examples.english: Bring the signed form back to the counter before four o’clock.
examples.note: « Rapporter » plus a concrete object.

examples.french: Le journal a rapporté les propos de la porte-parole sans les commenter.
examples.english: The newspaper reported the spokesperson’s words without commenting on them.
examples.note: « Rapporter » plus information.

examples.french: Cette statistique se rapporte au marché du travail canadien.
examples.english: This statistic relates to the Canadian labour market.
examples.note: « Se rapporter à » for a relationship between ideas.

mistakes.avoid: Il cache la vérité de ses collègues.
mistakes.prefer: Il cache la vérité à ses collègues.
mistakes.why: `Cacher quelque chose à quelqu’un` uses `à`, even though English uses from.

mistakes.avoid: Ce chapitre rapporte à la question du logement.
mistakes.prefer: Ce chapitre se rapporte à la question du logement.
mistakes.why: In the sense of relating to, the verb is pronominal: `se rapporter à`.

vocabulary.example: Elle n’a rien caché à son employeur au sujet de son horaire.
vocabulary.note: The person is introduced by `à`, never by `de`.

vocabulary.english: to relate to, to refer to
vocabulary.example: Ce paragraphe se rapporte aux conditions d’admission.
vocabulary.note: Pronominal; the complement is introduced by `à`.

vocabulary.example: Un employé à temps partiel a droit aux mêmes protections.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; feminine `une employée`.

vocabulary.example: Une statistique récente montre une hausse du nombre de demandes.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; usually plural when it names the discipline.

practice.prompt: Translate: « She did not hide the delay from the committee, and this note refers to the same file. »
practice.hint: One `à` after `cacher`, one pronominal verb.
practice.answer: Elle n’a pas caché le retard au comité, et cette note se rapporte au même dossier.

takeaways: `Cacher quelque chose à quelqu’un`, not `de`.
`Se cacher de` for hiding oneself.
`Se rapporter à` equals to relate to.
keywords: cacher, se cacher, rapporter, and se rapporter

lessons.title: La famille du verbe « rendre »
lessons.summary: `Rendre quelque chose` means to give something back. `Rendre visite à quelqu’un` means to visit a person. `Se rendre quelque part` means to go somewhere, in a formal register. `Se rendre compte de` plus a noun and `se rendre compte que` plus a clause both mean to realise. `Rendre compte de`, without the reflexive pronoun, means to report on or account for something.
objectives: Separate the five frequent constructions built on `rendre`.
Choose between `se rendre compte de` and `se rendre compte que`.
Keep `rendre compte de` apart from its reflexive counterpart.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: `Rendre` means to give back in `Je rends le formulaire à la conseillère`, with a direct object and an indirect recipient. Adding a fixed noun changes the meaning. `Rendre visite à quelqu’un` is the usual expression for an ordinary social visit. `Visiter` often takes a place, but it can also take people, notably in `visiter les malades` or `visiter les prisonniers`. This is a distinction of usage, not an absolute ban on visiting a person with `visiter`. `Rendre service à quelqu’un` means to do someone a favour.

The reflexive forms are a second family. `Se rendre` plus a place means to go there and belongs to a formal or administrative register: `Veuillez vous rendre au guichet 4`. `Se rendre compte` means to realise, and its complement decides the structure: `de` plus a noun (`Je me rends compte de la difficulté`) or `que` plus a clause (`Je me rends compte que le délai est court`). Dropping the reflexive pronoun gives a different verb again: `rendre compte de` means to report on or to account for, as in `Le comité doit rendre compte de ses dépenses`. Note that in `se rendre compte`, `compte` is invariable and the past participle never agrees: `elle s’est rendu compte`.
points: Use `rendre` plus a direct object for giving something back.
Prefer `rendre visite à` for a social visit; recognise accepted uses of `visiter` with people.
Use `se rendre` plus a place in formal instructions.
Use `se rendre compte de` before a noun and `se rendre compte que` before a clause.
Use `rendre compte de` when the meaning is to report on something.
Leave the participle unchanged in `elle s’est rendu compte`.

examples.french: Je rends le formulaire à la conseillère avant midi.
examples.english: I am giving the form back to the adviser before noon.
examples.note: Basic meaning: to give something back.

examples.french: J’ai rendu visite à une famille nouvellement arrivée dans le quartier.
examples.english: I visited a family that has recently arrived in the neighbourhood.
examples.note: Rendre visite à is the ordinary expression for a social visit.

examples.french: Veuillez vous rendre au guichet 4 avec votre pièce d’identité.
examples.english: Please go to counter 4 with your identification.
examples.note: « Se rendre » plus a place, in a formal instruction.

examples.french: Je me rends compte de la difficulté et je me rends compte que le délai est très court.
examples.english: I realise how difficult it is and I realise that the deadline is very short.
examples.note: « De » before a noun, « que » before a clause.

examples.french: Le comité doit rendre compte de ses dépenses devant le conseil.
examples.english: The committee has to account for its spending before the council.
examples.note: Without the reflexive pronoun, the meaning is to report on.

examples.french: Elle s’est rendu compte de l’erreur en relisant son dossier.
examples.english: She realised the mistake while rereading her file.
examples.note: The participle stays unchanged in this fixed expression.

examples.french: Les bénévoles visitent les malades à l’hôpital.
examples.english: The volunteers visit patients at the hospital.
examples.note: Visiter can take people; this accepted usage does not describe touring a place.

mistakes.avoid: Je me rends compte que la difficulté de cette démarche.
mistakes.prefer: Je me rends compte de la difficulté de cette démarche.
mistakes.why: `Que` introduces a clause; before a noun phrase the expression takes `de`.

mistakes.avoid: Elle s’est rendue compte de son erreur trop tard.
mistakes.prefer: Elle s’est rendu compte de son erreur trop tard.
mistakes.why: In `se rendre compte`, the direct object is `compte`, which follows the verb, so the participle does not agree.

vocabulary.example: Nous nous rendons compte de l’ampleur du problème.
vocabulary.note: `De` before a noun, `que` before a clause; the participle never agrees.

vocabulary.english: to go (formal), to make one’s way
vocabulary.example: Les candidats doivent se rendre à la salle B avant huit heures.
vocabulary.note: Formal register; `aller` is the neutral equivalent.

vocabulary.english: to report on, to account for
vocabulary.example: La directrice rend compte de ses décisions chaque trimestre.
vocabulary.note: Without the reflexive pronoun the meaning changes completely.

vocabulary.example: Ce nouveau service rend service à toutes les familles du quartier.
vocabulary.note: Fixed expression; the person is introduced by `à`.

vocabulary.example: Une dépense imprévue doit être justifiée dans le rapport annuel.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; `dépenser` is the related verb.

practice.prompt: Translate: « She realised that the office was closed, so she went to the other counter and gave the form back. »
practice.hint: Three different members of the `rendre` family.
practice.answer: Elle s’est rendu compte que le bureau était fermé ; elle s’est donc rendue à l’autre guichet et elle a rendu le formulaire.

takeaways: `Rendre` alone equals to give back.
`Rendre visite à` a person, `se rendre` to a place.
`Se rendre compte de` a noun, `que` a clause; `rendre compte de` equals to report on.

lessons.title: S’habiller : « mettre », « essayer » et « aller à »
lessons.summary: `Mettre` is the ordinary verb for putting clothes on: `Je mets une veste`. `Essayer` is trying a garment on before buying it, often after seeing it `en vitrine`. `Aller à` expresses suitability, and the roles are the reverse of English: the item is the subject and the person is an indirect object (`Cette veste lui va bien`). `Aller avec` matches two items, and `convenir à` is the more formal way of saying that something suits a person or a situation.
objectives: Use `mettre` and `essayer` in a shopping or dressing situation.
Put the item, not the person, in subject position with `aller à`.
Choose between `aller à`, `aller avec`, and `convenir à`.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: Three verbs cover the everyday clothing situation. `Mettre` means to put on and takes a direct object: `Je mets un manteau`, `Elle a mis une tenue sobre pour l’entrevue`. `Porter` is the state that follows: `Elle porte un manteau`. `Essayer` is trying a garment on: `Puis-je essayer cette veste ?`, typically after noticing it `en vitrine`, in the shop window.

`Aller à` expresses suitability and reverses the English word order: the clothing, the colour, or the hairstyle is the subject, and the person is an indirect object introduced by `à` or replaced by `me`, `te`, `lui`, `nous`, `vous`, `leur`. English says She looks good in that jacket; French says `Cette veste lui va bien`. Two neighbours must be kept apart: `aller avec` links two items rather than an item and a person (`Cette cravate va bien avec la chemise bleue`), and `convenir à` is the more formal equivalent of `aller à`, usable for people and also for situations (`Cette tenue convient à un entretien`, `Cet horaire ne me convient pas`). The adverbs `bien`, `très bien`, and `mal` grade the judgement.
points: Use `mettre` plus a direct object for putting a garment on.
Use `porter` for the state of wearing it.
Use `essayer` for trying on, and `en vitrine` for what is displayed in the window.
Make the item the subject of `aller à` and the person an indirect object.
Use `aller avec` between two items and `convenir à` in a formal register.

examples.french: Je mets une veste sobre pour l’entrevue de demain.
examples.english: I am putting on an understated jacket for tomorrow’s interview.
examples.note: « Mettre » takes a direct object.

examples.french: J’ai vu ce manteau en vitrine ; puis-je l’essayer ?
examples.english: I saw this coat in the window; may I try it on?
examples.note: « En vitrine » for the display, « essayer » for trying on.

examples.french: Cette veste sobre va bien à la candidate.
examples.english: This understated jacket suits the candidate.
examples.note: The item is the subject; the person follows « à ».

examples.french: Le rose pâle lui va très bien, mais le vert foncé lui va mal.
examples.english: Pale pink suits her very well, but dark green does not suit her.
examples.note: « Aller mal à quelqu’un » means it does not suit them; a flat refusal would need « pas du tout ».

examples.french: Cette cravate va bien avec la chemise bleue.
examples.english: This tie goes well with the blue shirt.
examples.note: « Aller avec » links two items.

examples.french: Cette tenue convient à un entretien, mais cet horaire ne me convient pas.
examples.english: This outfit is suitable for an interview, but this schedule does not suit me.
examples.note: « Convenir à » works for a situation as well as a person.

mistakes.avoid: Elle va bien cette veste pour l’entrevue.
mistakes.prefer: Cette veste lui va bien pour l’entrevue.
mistakes.why: The item that suits is the subject and the person is an indirect object.

mistakes.avoid: Je porte mon manteau avant de sortir, puis je pars.
mistakes.prefer: Je mets mon manteau avant de sortir, puis je pars.
mistakes.why: `Mettre` names the action of putting a garment on; `porter` describes the state of wearing it.

vocabulary.example: Elle met un manteau léger dès que la température monte.
vocabulary.note: Direct object; participle `mis`, present `je mets`, `nous mettons`.

vocabulary.example: Puis-je essayer ce manteau en taille moyenne ?
vocabulary.note: `-yer` verb: `j’essaie` or `j’essaye`, both accepted.

vocabulary.english: to suit, to be suitable for
vocabulary.example: Cet horaire ne convient pas aux parents de jeunes enfants.
vocabulary.note: Formal equivalent of `aller à`; also used for situations.

vocabulary.example: Une vitrine bien éclairée attire les passants le soir.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; `en vitrine` means on display.

vocabulary.example: Une veste sobre convient à un entretien d’embauche.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; `un veston` is used in Canada for a suit jacket.

vocabulary.example: Une tenue soignée fait bonne impression dès l’accueil.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; `être en tenue de travail` means to be in work clothes.

vocabulary.example: Elle porte une veste bleue et elle porte aussi un dossier volumineux.
vocabulary.note: Durative: the state of wearing, unlike the punctual `mettre`; it also means to carry.

practice.prompt: Say that you saw a coat in the window, ask to try it on, and say it suits you.
practice.hint: Three different verbs, and the item is the subject of the last one.
practice.answer: J’ai vu ce manteau en vitrine. Puis-je l’essayer ? Il me va très bien.

takeaways: `Mettre` puts on, `porter` wears, `essayer` tries on.
With `aller à`, the item is the subject and the person is indirect.
`Aller avec` matches two items; `convenir à` is the formal equivalent.

modules.title: Le vocabulaire du quotidien
modules.description: Use practical vocabulary for daily life, health, food, weather, travel, and culture.

lessons.title: La météo et les moments de la journée
lessons.summary: Weather is impersonal in French: the subject `il` refers to nothing. Four frames cover almost everything. `Il fait` plus an adjective gives a general condition (`il fait beau`, `il fait froid`); an impersonal weather verb stands alone (`il pleut`, `il neige`, `il gèle`); `il y a` plus a weather noun names a phenomenon (`il y a du vent`, `il y a des nuages`, `il y a du verglas`); and `le temps est` plus an adjective gives a description (`le temps est nuageux`). Ask about it with `Quel temps fait-il ?`. For times of day, `le soir` is the recurring period, `une soirée` an evening as an event, and `la nuit` the night-time hours.
objectives: Ask and answer a question about the weather with the standard formula.
Choose among the four impersonal frames before naming the weather.
Separate `le soir`, `une soirée`, and `la nuit`.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: An impersonal construction has a grammatical subject that refers to nothing at all. The standard question is `Quel temps fait-il ?`, and the answer picks one of four frames. `Il fait` takes an adjective or a temperature: `il fait beau`, `il fait mauvais`, `il fait froid`, `il fait moins dix`. Some weather verbs are impersonal on their own and need nothing after them: `il pleut`, `il neige`, `il gèle`, `il grêle`. `Il y a` takes a weather noun with its article: `il y a du vent`, `il y a de la pluie`, `il y a des nuages`, `il y a du verglas`. `Le temps est` takes a descriptive adjective: `le temps est ensoleillé`, `le temps est nuageux`.

Two of these overlap in everyday speech. `C’est nuageux` is a common conversational variant of `le temps est nuageux`, and `il y a des nuages` says the same thing with a noun; all three are correct, and the `le temps est` form is the safest in writing. The parts of the day are distinguished by aspect: `le soir` names the recurring period and is used adverbially (`Le soir, nous écoutons la radio`), while `une soirée` presents the evening as an event or a measured span, which is why greetings use it. The same pair exists for `le jour` and `une journée`, `le matin` and `une matinée`.
points: Ask with `Quel temps fait-il ?` and answer with one of the four frames.
Use `il fait` plus an adjective or a temperature.
Use an impersonal verb alone: `il pleut`, `il neige`, `il gèle`.
Use `il y a` plus an article and a weather noun: `du vent`, `des nuages`, `du verglas`.
Use `le temps est` plus a descriptive adjective, and treat `c’est nuageux` as its conversational variant.
Use `le soir` for the recurring period and `une soirée` for the event.

examples.french: — Quel temps fait-il ce matin ? — Il fait froid, mais le temps est ensoleillé.
examples.english: “What is the weather like this morning?” “It is cold, but the weather is sunny.”
examples.note: The standard question, then two different frames in the answer.

examples.french: Il pleut depuis hier soir, alors prends un parapluie.
examples.english: It has been raining since yesterday evening, so take an umbrella.
examples.note: « Pleuvoir » is impersonal and needs nothing after it.

examples.french: Il y a des nuages et du vent ; c’est nuageux sur toute la région.
examples.english: There are clouds and wind; it is cloudy across the whole region.
examples.note: A weather noun with « il y a », then the conversational « c’est nuageux ».

examples.french: Il y avait du verglas toute la matinée, alors les autobus étaient en retard.
examples.english: There was black ice all morning, so the buses were late.
examples.note: « Verglas » is ice on the ground; freezing rain is « la pluie verglaçante ».

examples.french: Les inondations et les glissements de terrain ont coupé deux routes régionales.
examples.english: The floods and landslides cut off two regional roads.
examples.note: Vocabulary for weather events reported in the news.

examples.french: Passez une bonne soirée après la cérémonie d’accueil !
examples.english: Have a good evening after the welcome ceremony!
examples.note: A greeting presents the evening as a span, so it uses « soirée ».

mistakes.avoid: Il fait du vent et il y a froid aujourd’hui.
mistakes.prefer: Il y a du vent et il fait froid aujourd’hui.
mistakes.why: A weather noun goes with `il y a`, and an adjective goes with `il fait`.

mistakes.avoid: Il fait pleuvoir depuis ce matin.
mistakes.prefer: Il pleut depuis ce matin.
mistakes.why: `Pleuvoir` is already an impersonal verb, so it is not combined with `il fait`.

mistakes.avoid: Bonne soir et à demain !
mistakes.prefer: Bonne soirée et à demain !
mistakes.why: A greeting presents the evening as a span, which requires `soirée`.

vocabulary.example: Le verglas rend les trottoirs dangereux en février.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; freezing rain is `la pluie verglaçante`.

vocabulary.example: Un nuage épais cache le soleil depuis midi.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; `il y a des nuages` is the usual plural form.

vocabulary.example: Un parapluie solide est utile pendant tout le mois de novembre.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; regular plural `des parapluies`.

vocabulary.example: Une soirée conviviale a réuni tous les nouveaux voisins.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; `le soir` names the recurring period instead.

vocabulary.example: Les inondations du printemps ont endommagé plusieurs maisons.
vocabulary.note: Feminine plural noun; the singular `une inondation` also exists.

vocabulary.example: Un glissement de terrain a bloqué la route pendant deux jours.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun phrase; the gender comes from `glissement`.

vocabulary.example: Deux personnes disparues ont été retrouvées en fin de journée.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun phrase; the adjective agrees, giving `des personnes disparues`.

practice.prompt: Ask about the weather, then answer using three different frames: cold, raining, and windy.
practice.hint: One adjective frame, one impersonal verb, one weather noun.
practice.answer: Quel temps fait-il ? Il fait froid, il pleut et il y a du vent.

takeaways: `Quel temps fait-il ?` opens the topic.
Four frames: `il fait` plus adjective, impersonal verb alone, `il y a` plus noun, `le temps est` plus adjective.
`Le soir` recurs; `une soirée` is an event.
keywords: weather and parts of the day

lessons.title: Le corps, la douleur, les odeurs et les sensations
lessons.summary: Pain uses `avoir mal à` plus a definite article, contracted where required: `j’ai mal à la tête`, `au dos`, `aux dents`. `Avoir mal au cœur` is idiomatic and means to feel nauseous, not to have a heart problem. `Sentir` covers giving off a smell and perceiving physically; `se sentir` reports how a person feels. `Faire mal à` names who is hurting: `Le dos me fait mal`.
objectives: Build `avoir mal à` with the correct contracted article.
Separate `sentir`, `se sentir`, and `faire mal`.
Interpret `avoir mal au cœur` correctly.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: With `avoir mal à`, the body part takes a definite article, never a possessive, because the subject already identifies the owner: `J’ai mal à la tête`, `Il a mal au dos`, `Elle a mal aux dents`. The contraction rules apply exactly as elsewhere: `à + le` gives `au`, `à + les` gives `aux`. An alternative structure reverses the roles: `Le dos me fait mal`, where the body part is the subject and the person is an indirect pronoun.

Three verbs must be kept apart. `Sentir` with a direct object means to smell or to perceive something: `Je ne sens rien dans la main gauche`. `Sentir` with an adjective or a noun means to give off a smell: `Ce plat sent très bon`, `La salle sent la peinture`. `Se sentir` plus an adjective reports a state: `Comment est-ce que vous vous sentez ?`. Finally, `avoir mal au cœur` is an idiom meaning to feel sick or nauseous; a heart condition would be `un problème cardiaque`.
points: Use `avoir mal à` plus the definite article of the body part.
Contract to `au` and `aux` where the gender and number require it.
Use `faire mal à` when the body part is the subject.
Use `sentir` for smelling or perceiving, `se sentir` for a personal state.
Read `avoir mal au cœur` as nausea.
Note that fixed body-part idioms also keep the definite article: `avoir les mains dans les poches`.

examples.french: J’ai mal à la tête depuis le début de mon quart de travail.
examples.english: I have had a headache since the start of my shift.
examples.note: Definite article, no possessive.

examples.french: Il a mal au dos et aux épaules après cette journée de déménagement.
examples.english: His back and shoulders hurt after this day of moving.
examples.note: Contractions « au » and « aux ».

examples.french: Comment est-ce que vous vous sentez depuis votre traitement ?
examples.english: How have you been feeling since your treatment?
examples.note: « Se sentir » reports a personal state.

examples.french: Je ne sens rien dans la main gauche depuis l’accident.
examples.english: I cannot feel anything in my left hand since the accident.
examples.note: « Sentir » in its perception meaning.

examples.french: Ce plat sent très bon, mais j’ai mal au cœur depuis ce matin.
examples.english: This dish smells very good, but I have been feeling sick since this morning.
examples.note: « Sentir » for a smell, and the idiom « avoir mal au cœur ».

examples.french: Il regardait les autres travailler, les mains dans les poches.
examples.english: He watched the others work, with his hands in his pockets.
examples.note: Fixed idiom with the definite article; it suggests standing idle rather than helping.

mistakes.avoid: J’ai mal à mon dos depuis hier.
mistakes.prefer: J’ai mal au dos depuis hier.
mistakes.why: French uses the definite article with a body part in this construction, and `à + le` contracts.

mistakes.avoid: Je sens fatigué après cette journée.
mistakes.prefer: Je me sens fatigué après cette journée.
mistakes.why: Reporting one’s own state requires the pronominal `se sentir`.

vocabulary.example: La tête du patient reste immobile pendant l’examen.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; `avoir mal à la tête` means to have a headache.

vocabulary.example: Le dos me fait mal après une longue journée debout.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; contracts to `au dos` after `avoir mal à`.

vocabulary.example: Je me sens beaucoup mieux depuis le début du traitement.
vocabulary.note: Pronominal; followed by an adjective or an adverb.

vocabulary.example: Un quart de travail de nuit demande une bonne organisation du sommeil.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun phrase used in Canada; `un poste` is used in France.

vocabulary.example: Un traitement de six semaines a été prescrit par la clinique.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; the ending -ment is a masculine hint.

vocabulary.example: Une épaule douloureuse limite les mouvements du bras.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; `avoir mal à l’épaule` for the pain construction.

vocabulary.example: Après son opération, il marche avec une canne pendant six semaines.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; the same word appears in `une canne à pêche`, a fishing rod.

vocabulary.french: avoir les mains dans les poches
vocabulary.english: to stand idle, to do nothing to help
vocabulary.example: Personne n’avait les mains dans les poches pendant le déménagement.
vocabulary.note: Fixed idiom keeping the definite article, like other body-part expressions.

practice.prompt: Say in French: my teeth hurt, I feel tired, and this room smells of paint.
practice.hint: Three different structures, one of them with a contraction.
practice.answer: J’ai mal aux dents, je me sens fatigué et cette salle sent la peinture.

takeaways: `Avoir mal à` plus a definite article, contracted as needed.
`Sentir` perceives or gives off a smell; `se sentir` reports a state.
`Avoir mal au cœur` equals nausea.
keywords: the body, pain, smell, and feeling

lessons.title: Les sports, les activités et les instruments
lessons.summary: Learn `jouer à` for games such as `jouer au tennis`, `jouer de` for instruments such as `jouer de la guitare`, and `faire` plus a partitive article for activities: `faire de la natation`, `faire du ski`. The partitive presents an activity without counting individual outings; it does not require a habit. Contrast `faire du vélo` with a counted ride, `faire un tour à vélo`, and `faire de la randonnée` with `faire une randonnée`.
objectives: Learn the preposition with jouer and the partitive article with faire.
Separate an uncounted activity from a counted outing or session.
Use tense and context to distinguish a habit from a particular event.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: Learn the construction with the activity. Games use `jouer à`: `jouer au soccer`, `jouer au hockey`, `jouer aux échecs`. Instruments use `jouer de`: `jouer de la guitare`, `jouer du violon`. With jouer, prepositions contract with definite articles where required: `à + le → au`, `de + le → du`. With faire, the activity instead takes a partitive article: `faire de la natation`, `faire du vélo`, `faire de la randonnée`. Do not describe this as adding a second `de` before a partitive.

The article contrasts uncounted activity with counted units, not necessarily habit with a single event. `Je fais du vélo` may mean that I cycle regularly or that I am cycling now. `J’ai fait du vélo ce matin` describes past cycling with the same partitive. A countable noun identifies an outing or a unit: `faire un tour à vélo`, `faire une randonnée`, `faire une séance de yoga`, `faire quelques longueurs`, `faire une partie de tennis`. These can recur too: `Je fais une randonnée chaque dimanche`. Tense and context establish when and how often the activity happens.
points: Use `jouer à` for games and sports with rules.
Use `jouer de` for a musical instrument.
Use `faire` plus a partitive article to name an activity, whether habitual or particular.
Use a countable noun to count outings or units: `un tour à vélo`, `une randonnée`, `une partie de tennis`.
Use tense and time expressions, not the partitive alone, to identify a habit or a particular event.
Read `la batterie` from its context: the drum kit, a car battery, or a set of equipment.

examples.french: Il joue au tennis au centre communautaire et fait une partie avec sa voisine le samedi.
examples.english: He plays tennis at the community centre and plays a game with his neighbour on Saturdays.
examples.note: « Jouer au tennis » for the sport, « une partie » for one match.

examples.french: Je joue de la guitare pendant le festival francophone.
examples.english: I play the guitar during the Francophone festival.
examples.note: « Jouer de » for an instrument.

examples.french: Je fais du vélo toute l’année, mais hier j’ai simplement fait un tour à vélo.
examples.english: I cycle all year round, but yesterday I just went for a bike ride.
examples.note: General practice, then one occasion.

examples.french: Elle fait de la randonnée depuis dix ans et elle a fait une randonnée facile dimanche.
examples.english: She has been hiking for ten years and she did an easy hike on Sunday.
examples.note: The countable noun marks a single outing.

examples.french: Un débutant peut faire quelques longueurs avant de s’inscrire aux cours de natation.
examples.english: A beginner can swim a few lengths before signing up for swimming lessons.
examples.note: Quelques longueurs counts lengths of the pool rather than naming the activity as an uncounted whole.

examples.french: J’ai fait du yoga ce matin, mais je ne fais pas de yoga régulièrement.
examples.english: I did yoga this morning, but I do not do yoga regularly.
examples.note: A completed time marker bounds the event, even with the partitive.

examples.french: L’orchestre répète la partition, et le chef d’orchestre reprend le refrain plus lentement.
examples.english: The orchestra is rehearsing the score, and the conductor goes over the chorus more slowly.
examples.note: Core music vocabulary for describing a rehearsal or a concert.

examples.french: En ce moment, je fais du vélo ; d’habitude, je fais une randonnée chaque dimanche.
examples.english: Right now I am cycling; usually, I go for a hike every Sunday.
examples.note: A partitive can describe current activity, and a countable outing can belong to a habit.

mistakes.avoid: Elle joue le piano depuis trois ans.
mistakes.prefer: Elle joue du piano depuis trois ans.
mistakes.why: An instrument requires `jouer de`, with the article contracted.

mistakes.avoid: Nous jouons à la natation le mardi.
mistakes.prefer: Nous faisons de la natation le mardi.
mistakes.why: The activity is expressed with `faire` plus the partitive `de la`: `faire de la natation`, not `jouer à la natation`.

mistakes.avoid: Hier après-midi, j’ai fait de la randonnée de trois heures.
mistakes.prefer: Hier après-midi, j’ai fait une randonnée de trois heures.
mistakes.why: Use `une randonnée de trois heures` to describe the duration of one hike. The partitive is also possible with `pendant`: `J’ai fait de la randonnée pendant trois heures`.

mistakes.avoid: Il joue à la batterie dans un groupe du quartier.
mistakes.prefer: Il joue de la batterie dans un groupe du quartier.
mistakes.why: An instrument takes `jouer de`; `jouer à` is reserved for games and sports.

vocabulary.example: Le tennis demande de la précision et une bonne endurance.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; `jouer au tennis`, but `faire une partie de tennis` for one match.

vocabulary.example: La guitare acoustique accompagne doucement la chanteuse.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; `jouer de la guitare`.

vocabulary.example: Une randonnée de deux heures suffit pour découvrir le parc.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; `faire une randonnée` counts a hike, while `faire de la randonnée` names the activity without counting outings.

vocabulary.example: Un tour à vélo le long du canal prend environ une heure.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun phrase naming a counted ride; `faire du vélo` names the activity and can also refer to one occasion.

vocabulary.example: Les jeux de société occupent les enfants pendant l’atelier.
vocabulary.note: Masculine plural of `un jeu`, which takes -x.

vocabulary.example: Un débutant est accueilli dans le groupe du mardi soir.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; feminine `une débutante`.

vocabulary.example: Un orchestre communautaire donne un concert gratuit en juin.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun despite its final -e.

vocabulary.example: Un chef d’orchestre invité dirigera le concert de fin d’année.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun phrase; the gender comes from `chef`.

vocabulary.example: Une partition annotée circule entre les musiciens.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; not to be confused with `une partie`.

vocabulary.example: Un refrain simple aide la classe à retenir la chanson.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; `un couplet` is a verse.

vocabulary.example: La batterie du groupe est installée au fond de la salle, et la batterie de la voiture est déchargée.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun with several meanings decided by context: drums, a car battery, or a set of equipment.

practice.prompt: Say that you swim regularly, then that you swam a few lengths this morning.
practice.hint: Use the partitive to name swimming and régulièrement to express the habit; count pool lengths with quelques longueurs.
practice.answer: Je fais de la natation régulièrement, et ce matin j’ai fait quelques longueurs.

takeaways: Learn `jouer à` with games, `jouer de` with instruments, and `faire` plus a partitive article with activities.
The partitive names uncounted activity; a countable noun identifies outings or units.
Tense and context establish habit or a particular event; either article pattern can occur with a habit.
