lessons.title: La nourriture, les quantités et les portions
lessons.summary: Use a partitive article for an unmeasured amount of food: `du pain`, `de la farine`, `des légumes`. As soon as the quantity is measured, the article disappears and only `de` remains: `un kilo de pommes`, `beaucoup de pain`, `une tranche de fromage`. `La moitié de` names half of a specific whole, and a definite article expresses a rate: `trois dollars le kilo`.
objectives: Use partitive articles for unmeasured food.
Drop the article after any expression of quantity.
Express a unit price with a definite article.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: A partitive article presents an unmeasured portion of something uncountable: `du lait`, `de la farine`, `de l’eau`, and the plural `des légumes`. It answers the question some what, and English usually leaves it out, which is why it is easy to forget: `Je prends du café` is I have coffee, not I have the coffee.

The moment a quantity is stated, the article vanishes and only `de` remains. That applies to weights and containers (`un kilo de pommes`, `une bouteille d’eau`, `une tranche de pain`), to adverbs of quantity (`beaucoup de légumes`, `peu de sel`, `assez de temps`), and after a negation (`Je n’ai pas de pain`). Two related structures complete the topic: `la moitié de` for half of a specific whole (`la moitié des repas`), and the definite article for a unit price (`trois dollars le kilo`, `deux dollars la pièce`).
points: Use `du`, `de la`, `de l’`, `des` for an unspecified amount.
Reduce to `de` alone after a weight, a container, or an adverb of quantity.
Reduce to `de` alone after a negation.
Use `la moitié de` plus a determined noun for half of a specific whole.
Use `le`, `la`, or `les` before the unit when giving a rate.
Check the meal names by region: in Canada, `le déjeuner` is breakfast, `le dîner` lunch, and `le souper` dinner; in France, `le petit déjeuner`, `le déjeuner`, and `le dîner`.

examples.french: La banque alimentaire distribue du lait, de la farine et des légumes frais.
examples.english: The food bank distributes milk, flour, and fresh vegetables.
examples.note: Three partitive forms for unmeasured amounts.

examples.french: J’ai acheté un kilo de pommes et beaucoup de légumes au marché.
examples.english: I bought a kilo of apples and a lot of vegetables at the market.
examples.note: After a quantity, only « de » remains.

examples.french: Le centre communautaire a gardé la moitié des repas pour les bénévoles.
examples.english: The community centre kept half of the meals for the volunteers.
examples.note: « La moitié de » plus a determined noun.

examples.french: Les pommes locales coûtent trois dollars le kilo cette semaine.
examples.english: Local apples cost three dollars per kilo this week.
examples.note: The definite article expresses a rate.

examples.french: Il n’y a plus de café, mais il reste de la soupe et du pain.
examples.english: There is no coffee left, but there is still soup and bread.
examples.note: Negation reduces to « de »; the positive clause keeps the partitive.

examples.french: Au Québec, je prends du café au déjeuner et de la soupe au dîner.
examples.english: In Quebec, I have coffee at breakfast and soup at lunch.
examples.note: Canadian meal names: déjeuner is breakfast and dîner is lunch.

mistakes.avoid: J’ai acheté beaucoup des légumes au marché.
mistakes.prefer: J’ai acheté beaucoup de légumes au marché.
mistakes.why: An adverb of quantity is followed by `de` alone, without an article.

mistakes.avoid: Je voudrais le pain et la confiture, s’il vous plaît.
mistakes.prefer: Je voudrais du pain et de la confiture, s’il vous plaît.
mistakes.why: An unmeasured amount takes a partitive article, not a definite one.

vocabulary.example: Le pain frais est distribué chaque matin à la banque alimentaire.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; `du pain` for an unspecified amount.

vocabulary.example: La confiture de fraises est préparée avec les fruits du jardin.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; `de la confiture` for an unspecified amount.

vocabulary.example: Les céréales complètes apportent davantage de fibres au petit déjeuner.
vocabulary.note: Feminine plural noun; normally used in the plural in this sense.

vocabulary.example: La moitié des participants a choisi la visite guidée.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; `la moitié de` plus a determined noun.

vocabulary.example: Une banque alimentaire soutient les familles à faible revenu du quartier.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun phrase; the gender comes from `banque`.

vocabulary.example: Le déjeuner est servi de sept heures à neuf heures.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; the meal it names depends on the region.

vocabulary.example: Le souper communautaire réunit les voisins le premier vendredi du mois.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun used in Canada; `le dîner` names the evening meal in France.

vocabulary.example: Le raisin local arrive sur les marchés à la fin de l’été.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun, usually singular for the fruit as a food: `du raisin`.

vocabulary.example: Le restaurant propose un menu végétarien et une option végétalienne.
vocabulary.note: Doubles the `n` in the feminine, like `canadien / canadienne`.

practice.prompt: Complete: « Je voudrais ___ eau, un litre ___ lait et ___ pommes ; il n’y a plus ___ sucre. »
practice.hint: Partitive, quantity, partitive, negation.
practice.answer: Je voudrais de l’eau, un litre de lait et des pommes ; il n’y a plus de sucre.

takeaways: Unmeasured food takes `du`, `de la`, `de l’`, `des`.
Any stated quantity or a negation reduces the article to `de`.
A rate uses the definite article: `trois dollars le kilo`.

lessons.title: La maison, les voyages et les services
lessons.summary: Everyday service situations rely on fixed phrases that are faster to reuse than to build word by word: `Où se trouve…, s’il vous plaît ?`, `au rez-de-chaussée`, `au premier étage`, `au fond du couloir`, `réserver une voiture de location`, `faire les courses`. Note that `faire les courses` means grocery shopping, while leisure shopping is `faire du shopping` or `faire les magasins`.
objectives: Ask where a service is located in a polite, ready-made form.
Understand floor and direction indications.
Separate grocery shopping from leisure shopping.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: A lexical chunk is a multiword expression stored and reused as a unit. In service situations, chunks save processing time and sound more natural than assembled sentences. The core request is `Pardon, où se trouve le bureau d’accueil, s’il vous plaît ?`, and its variants use the same frame: `Où se trouvent les toilettes ?`, `Où est-ce que je peux payer ?`.

Floor indications differ from English. `Le rez-de-chaussée` is the ground floor, and `le premier étage` is the floor above it, so English first floor and French `premier étage` are not the same level. Directions reuse the spatial phrases: `au fond du couloir`, `au bout du corridor`, `en face de l’ascenseur`, `à droite`, `à gauche`. Finally, two shopping expressions must be kept apart: `faire les courses` is buying groceries and necessities, while `faire du shopping` or `faire les magasins` is browsing for pleasure.
points: Open a request with `Pardon` and close it with `s’il vous plaît`.
Use `Où se trouve` plus a singular noun and `Où se trouvent` plus a plural.
Read `le rez-de-chaussée` as the ground floor and `le premier étage` as the one above.
Reuse the direction chunks: `au fond de`, `en face de`, `à droite`, `à gauche`.
Use `faire les courses` for groceries and `faire du shopping` for leisure.
Use `retirer` for taking money out and `déposer` for paying it in.
Watch two nouns whose meaning changes with number: `le devoir` is duty, `les devoirs` are homework.

examples.french: Pardon, où se trouve le bureau d’accueil, s’il vous plaît ?
examples.english: Excuse me, where is the reception desk, please?
examples.note: The standard polite request frame.

examples.french: Le bureau d’accueil est au rez-de-chaussée de l’hôtel de ville.
examples.english: The reception desk is on the ground floor of city hall.
examples.note: « Rez-de-chaussée » is the ground floor, not the first floor.

examples.french: Le service des permis est au premier étage, au fond du couloir.
examples.english: The permits office is one floor up, at the end of the corridor.
examples.note: Two chunks combined in a direction.

examples.french: Nous devons réserver une voiture de location pour visiter la région.
examples.english: We need to book a rental car to visit the region.
examples.note: Fixed expression for renting a vehicle.

examples.french: Nous finissons notre dîner avant d’aller faire les courses.
examples.english: We finish lunch before going grocery shopping.
examples.note: In Canada « le dîner » is the midday meal; « faire les courses » is grocery shopping.

examples.french: Je dois retirer de l’argent à la banque avant de rentrer.
examples.english: I need to withdraw some money at the bank before going home.
examples.note: « Retirer de l’argent » is the standard expression; « déposer » is its opposite.

examples.french: Chaque citoyen a le devoir de voter, et mes enfants font leurs devoirs après l’école.
examples.english: Every citizen has a duty to vote, and my children do their homework after school.
examples.note: Singular for duty, plural for schoolwork.

mistakes.avoid: Pardon, où se trouvent le bureau d’accueil, s’il vous plaît ?
mistakes.prefer: Pardon, où se trouve le bureau d’accueil, s’il vous plaît ?
mistakes.why: `Se trouver` agrees with its subject; `le bureau d’accueil` is singular, so the verb stays singular.

mistakes.avoid: Je vais faire du shopping : il me faut du lait et du pain.
mistakes.prefer: Je vais faire les courses : il me faut du lait et du pain.
mistakes.why: Buying groceries is `faire les courses`; `faire du shopping` refers to leisure shopping.

mistakes.avoid: Mon fils termine son devoir de mathématiques et ses autres devoir ce soir.
mistakes.prefer: Mon fils termine son devoir de mathématiques et ses autres devoirs ce soir.
mistakes.why: A single assignment is `un devoir`, and the plural `des devoirs` covers the whole set of schoolwork.

vocabulary.example: Le bureau d’accueil fournit un plan aux nouveaux visiteurs.
vocabulary.note: Masculine compound; `l’accueil` alone also means reception.

vocabulary.example: Le rez-de-chaussée abrite la réception et la salle d’attente.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; invariable in the plural.

vocabulary.example: Une voiture de location nous permettra d’explorer la région.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun phrase; the gender comes from `voiture`.

vocabulary.example: Nous faisons les courses le samedi matin au marché du quartier.
vocabulary.note: Distinct from `faire du shopping`, which is leisure shopping.

vocabulary.example: Un arrêt d’autobus se trouve juste devant l’immeuble.
vocabulary.note: Masculine compound; `un arrêt de bus` is the usual form in France.

vocabulary.example: Elle a retiré cent dollars au guichet automatique.
vocabulary.note: Regular `-er` verb; `retirer une candidature` also means to withdraw an application.

vocabulary.example: Un ordinateur public est disponible à la bibliothèque du quartier.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; `un ordinateur portable` is a laptop.

vocabulary.example: La télévision de la salle d’attente diffuse les consignes en boucle.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; the clipped form `la télé` is informal.

vocabulary.example: Un canapé confortable occupe le fond du salon.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; `un sofa` is a common synonym.

vocabulary.example: Un verre d’eau est offert à chaque visiteur.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; also names the material glass.

vocabulary.example: Un outil en ligne permet de calculer les frais de dossier.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; the final `l` is silent.

vocabulary.example: Une caméra de surveillance filme l’entrée du bâtiment.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun for a video camera; a photo camera is `un appareil photo`.

vocabulary.example: Le devoir de réserve s’applique à tous les employés du service.
vocabulary.note: In the plural, `les devoirs (m. pl.)` normally means homework.

vocabulary.example: La caissière m’a rendu la monnaie sur vingt dollars.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; `l’argent` is money in general.

vocabulary.example: Un agenda partagé évite les rendez-vous en double.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun despite its final -a.

vocabulary.example: Une cafetière est à la disposition du personnel dans la cuisine.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; `une bouilloire` boils water for tea.

vocabulary.example: Une bouilloire électrique chauffe l’eau en deux minutes.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; `bouillir` is the related verb.

vocabulary.example: Une pelouse commune est entretenue par la coopérative.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; `le gazon` names the grass itself.

vocabulary.example: Elle fait les magasins avec sa sœur le samedi après-midi.
vocabulary.note: Leisure shopping; groceries and errands are `faire les courses`.

vocabulary.example: Nous avons assisté à la séance d’information de mardi.
vocabulary.note: Always takes `à`; it does not mean to assist.

vocabulary.example: La garderie demande de ne pas apporter de jouet personnel.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; `un jeu` is a game, `un jouet` the object played with.

practice.prompt: Ask politely where the permits office is, then say it is on the first floor above the ground floor.
practice.hint: Use the request frame and the French floor word.
practice.answer: Pardon, où se trouve le service des permis, s’il vous plaît ? Il est au premier étage.

takeaways: `Pardon, où se trouve…, s’il vous plaît ?` is the reusable request.
`Rez-de-chaussée` equals ground floor; `premier étage` is above it.
`Faire les courses` equals groceries, not leisure shopping.

lessons.title: Les échanges et les réactions idiomatiques
lessons.summary: Conversational chunks resist word-by-word translation and carry a register. `Ça va` covers both wellbeing and agreement; `ça y est` marks completion; `ça ne fait rien` dismisses a problem; `vas-y` and `allez-y` mean go ahead; `tenez` and `tiens` accompany handing something over; `le plaisir est partagé` returns a compliment. `Occupe-toi de tes oignons` is informal and belongs only to conversation between peers.
objectives: Use the frequent `ça` reactions accurately.
Choose a chunk that matches the formality of the situation.
Recognise informal expressions without reusing them in writing.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: Register is the level of formality suited to the audience. Several of these chunks are built on `ça`, which is itself informal but entirely normal in speech. `Ça va` asks or reports wellbeing (`Ça va ? — Ça va, merci`) and also signals that something is acceptable (`Ça va comme ça`). `Ça y est` announces that something is finally done. `Ça ne fait rien` and its slightly more formal variant `cela ne fait rien` dismiss an apology.

A second group accompanies actions. `Vas-y` and the polite `allez-y` mean go ahead, both as encouragement and as permission. `Tiens` and `tenez` accompany handing something over, close to English here you go. To return a compliment after `Enchanté` or `C’était un plaisir`, French says `Le plaisir est partagé` or `Tout le plaisir est pour moi`. Finally, `occupe-toi de tes oignons` means mind your own business: it is useful to recognise but too familiar for an exam text or any formal exchange.
points: Use `Ça va ?` to ask about someone and `Ça va` to answer.
Use `ça y est` only when the action is now complete.
Use `ça ne fait rien` to dismiss an apology or a small problem.
Use `tenez` with `vous` and `tiens` with `tu` when handing something over.
Keep `occupe-toi de tes oignons` for informal speech among peers.
Welcome a visitor with `Faites comme chez vous`, and agree emphatically with `tout à fait`.
Learn three frequent idioms with their register: `poser un lapin` and `avoir le cafard` are informal, while `faire le pont` is neutral.
Keep `ça ne sent pas la rose` for informal speech only; a written report would say `l’odeur est désagréable`.

examples.french: — Ça va ? — Ça va, merci. Tenez, voici votre reçu.
examples.english: “How are you?” “I’m fine, thanks. Here, this is your receipt.”
examples.note: Two everyday chunks in a service exchange.

examples.french: Ça y est, j’ai fini de remplir le dossier en ligne !
examples.english: That’s it, I have finished filling in the file online!
examples.note: « Ça y est » marks completion.

examples.french: Je suis désolé pour le retard. — Cela ne fait rien.
examples.english: I am sorry about the delay. — It does not matter.
examples.note: Slightly more formal variant of « ça ne fait rien ».

examples.french: Vous pouvez poser votre question. — Allez-y, je vous écoute.
examples.english: You can ask your question. — Go ahead, I am listening.
examples.note: Polite form of « vas-y ».

examples.french: Merci pour cette conversation. — Le plaisir est partagé.
examples.english: Thank you for this conversation. — The pleasure is mutual.
examples.note: Standard way of returning a compliment.

examples.french: Entrez, faites comme chez vous. — Merci, c’est tout à fait aimable.
examples.english: Come in, make yourself at home. — Thank you, that is very kind.
examples.note: A welcoming formula, then « tout à fait » reinforcing an adjective.

examples.french: Il m’a posé un lapin samedi, et depuis j’ai un peu le cafard.
examples.english: He stood me up on Saturday, and I have been feeling a bit down since then.
examples.note: Both idioms are informal and belong to conversation, not to written work.

examples.french: Le jeudi est férié, alors beaucoup de collègues font le pont vendredi.
examples.english: Thursday is a public holiday, so many colleagues take the Friday off as well.
examples.note: « Faire le pont » is neutral and usable in an email to a team.

mistakes.avoid: Merci beaucoup. — Plaisir partagé.
mistakes.prefer: Merci beaucoup. — Le plaisir est partagé.
mistakes.why: The expression requires the full clause; the bare noun phrase is not idiomatic.

mistakes.avoid: Ça fait rien, je vais attendre le prochain rendez-vous.
mistakes.prefer: Cela ne fait rien, je vais attendre le prochain rendez-vous.
mistakes.why: Dropping `ne` and using `ça` are normal in speech, but a written or formal exchange keeps `ne` and prefers `cela`.

mistakes.avoid: Je vous informe que le fournisseur nous a posé un lapin hier.
mistakes.prefer: Je vous informe que le fournisseur ne s’est pas présenté hier.
mistakes.why: `Poser un lapin` is informal spoken French and is out of place in a written professional message.

vocabulary.example: Ça y est, le formulaire est envoyé et confirmé.
vocabulary.note: Marks completion; informal but very frequent.

vocabulary.example: Vous êtes en retard de cinq minutes ? Ça ne fait rien.
vocabulary.note: `Cela ne fait rien` is the slightly more formal variant.

vocabulary.example: Merci de votre accueil. — Le plaisir est partagé.
vocabulary.note: Full clause; `plaisir partagé` alone is not idiomatic.

vocabulary.example: Un reçu officiel est remis après chaque paiement.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun, from the past participle of `recevoir`.

vocabulary.example: Installez-vous et faites comme chez vous.
vocabulary.note: Uses the `vous` imperative; the informal version is `fais comme chez toi`.

vocabulary.example: Vous avez tout à fait raison au sujet du délai.
vocabulary.note: Reinforces an adjective, an adverb, or a whole answer.

vocabulary.example: Les participants se sont très bien comportés pendant la visite.
vocabulary.note: Pronominal; `se comporter mal` means to behave badly.

vocabulary.example: Elle m’a posé un lapin sans même envoyer un message.
vocabulary.note: Informal, spoken only; the neutral equivalent is `ne pas se présenter`.

vocabulary.english: to take the bridging day off
vocabulary.example: Nous faisons le pont entre le jeudi férié et la fin de semaine.
vocabulary.note: Neutral register; describes taking the working day between a holiday and the weekend.

vocabulary.english: to feel down, to have the blues
vocabulary.example: Après trois semaines de pluie, tout le monde a un peu le cafard.
vocabulary.note: Informal; `être déprimé` is the neutral equivalent.

vocabulary.example: Nous avons rempli le formulaire ensemble à la séance d’accueil.
vocabulary.note: Invariable adverb placed after the verb; the noun `un ensemble` means a set or a whole.

vocabulary.english: to smell bad, to be unsavoury
vocabulary.example: Le local n’a pas été aéré depuis une semaine : ça ne sent pas la rose.
vocabulary.note: Informal and almost always negative; unusable in formal written production.

practice.prompt: Complete the exchange: « — ___ ? — ___, merci. ___, voici votre attestation. »
practice.hint: Greeting, reply, and handing something over politely.
practice.answer: — Ça va ? — Ça va, merci. Tenez, voici votre attestation.

takeaways: `Ça va`, `ça y est`, `ça ne fait rien` cover most everyday reactions.
`Tenez` with `vous`, `tiens` with `tu`.
Recognise very familiar idioms, but keep them out of formal writing.

lessons.title: Les pays et les nationalités
lessons.summary: Learn each country with its article and connect it to three related forms: the masculine adjective, the feminine adjective, and the capitalised noun for a person. Most feminine adjectives simply add `-e` (`allemand` gives `allemande`), several double the consonant (`canadien` gives `canadienne`), and some are identical in both genders (`belge`, `russe`, `suisse`).
objectives: Store a country, its adjective, and its person noun as one set.
Form the feminine adjective, including the doubled-consonant group.
Apply the capitalisation rule consistently.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: Each country gives a small family of words. `L’Allemagne` gives `allemand`, `allemande`, and `un Allemand` or `une Allemande`; `le Canada` gives `canadien`, `canadienne`, and `un Canadien` or `une Canadienne`. Building the set once is far more efficient than meeting each form separately, and it also fixes the gender of the country name.

Three feminine patterns cover most cases. Simple addition of `-e`: `allemand` gives `allemande`, `français` gives `française`. Doubling before `-e`: `canadien` gives `canadienne`, `italien` gives `italienne`. No change at all when the masculine already ends in `-e`: `belge`, `russe`, `suisse`, `roumain` being the exception that follows the first pattern. Capitalisation depends on function: lowercase for the adjective and for the language, capital for the noun naming a person.
points: Record the country with its article, then both adjective forms, then the person noun.
Add `-e` for most feminine adjectives.
Double the final consonant in the `-ien` and `-éen` groups.
Leave adjectives already ending in `-e` unchanged.
Capitalise only the noun that names a person.

examples.french: Elle est canadienne et travaille dans un organisme d’aide à l’intégration.
examples.english: She is Canadian and works for a settlement support organisation.
examples.note: Lowercase adjective after « être ».

examples.french: C’est un Britannique installé au Québec depuis dix ans.
examples.english: He is a British man who has lived in Quebec for ten years.
examples.note: Capitalised noun naming a person.

examples.french: L’Allemagne compte seize Länder et partage une frontière avec la France.
examples.english: Germany has sixteen states and shares a border with France.
examples.note: Feminine country with its article.

examples.french: Une étudiante roumaine et un collègue russe ont présenté le projet.
examples.english: A Romanian student and a Russian colleague presented the project.
examples.note: « Roumaine » adds -e; « russe » is identical in both genders.

examples.french: Le Royaume-Uni réunit quatre nations et reste un partenaire commercial important.
examples.english: The United Kingdom brings together four nations and remains an important trading partner.
examples.note: Masculine country name with a compound form.

mistakes.avoid: Elle est Canadienne et elle parle Anglais.
mistakes.prefer: Elle est canadienne et elle parle anglais.
mistakes.why: After `être` the word is an adjective, and a language name is always lowercase.

mistakes.avoid: J’ai rencontré une italien pendant la formation.
mistakes.prefer: J’ai rencontré une Italienne pendant la formation.
mistakes.why: The noun naming a person is capitalised and agrees in gender.

vocabulary.example: L’Allemagne accueille chaque année de nombreux travailleurs qualifiés.
vocabulary.note: Feminine country; adjective `allemand`, `allemande`.

vocabulary.example: Le Royaume-Uni réunit quatre nations.
vocabulary.note: Masculine country; the adjective is `britannique` for both genders.

vocabulary.example: La Roumanie possède de nombreuses régions montagneuses.
vocabulary.note: Feminine country; adjective `roumain`, `roumaine`.

vocabulary.example: Une entreprise canadienne a financé une partie du projet.
vocabulary.note: The feminine doubles the final consonant before -e.

vocabulary.example: Un organisme communautaire accompagne les familles nouvellement arrivées.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; the ending -isme is a masculine hint.

practice.prompt: Give the three forms for `le Portugal` and use the person noun in a sentence.
practice.hint: Masculine adjective, feminine adjective, capitalised noun.
practice.answer: portugais, portugaise, un Portugais / une Portugaise : Une Portugaise a présenté son parcours professionnel.

takeaways: One country equals four linked forms.
`-ien` doubles its consonant in the feminine; `-e` adjectives do not change.
Capital for the person, lowercase for the adjective and the language.

lessons.title: Les abréviations courantes et le registre
lessons.summary: Clipped nouns belong to informal spoken French and keep the gender of the full word: `un ado` for `un adolescent`, `le bac` for `le baccalauréat`, `une colo` for `une colonie de vacances`, `un dico` for `un dictionnaire`, `la fac` for `la faculté`, `un resto` for `un restaurant`. Recognise them in conversation, but use the full form in any written or formal context.
objectives: Link each clipped form to its full equivalent.
Keep the gender of the complete noun.
Select the form that matches the register of the situation.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: Clipping shortens a long word by keeping its first syllables: `adolescent` becomes `ado`, `dictionnaire` becomes `dico`, `restaurant` becomes `resto`. The gender never changes, because the word is the same one: `un adolescent` gives `un ado`, `une colonie de vacances` gives `une colo`, `la faculté` gives `la fac`.

The difference is purely one of register. Clipped forms are normal in conversation between peers and in informal messages, and they will appear in listening material. In an exam text, a formal letter, or an application, the full form is expected. A few clipped forms have become neutral in everyday writing, such as `le métro` for `le métropolitain` and `la photo` for `la photographie`, but the safe rule while learning is to write the full word.
points: Match each clipped form with its complete equivalent before using it.
Keep the article and the gender of the original noun.
Use clipped forms in speech and informal messages only.
Write the full form in a letter, a report, or an exam answer.
Note that `métro` and `photo` are now neutral in most writing.

examples.french: Un ado peut dire « un dico » entre amis, mais « un dictionnaire » convient mieux dans un écrit formel.
examples.english: A teenager may say “un dico” among friends, but “un dictionnaire” is better in formal writing.
examples.note: The same object, two registers.

examples.french: Après le bac, elle a travaillé dans une colo pendant l’été.
examples.english: After the baccalaureate exam, she worked at a summer camp during the summer.
examples.note: Two clipped forms in a spoken narrative.

examples.french: Il étudie à la fac de droit et prend le métro chaque matin.
examples.english: He studies at the law faculty and takes the subway every morning.
examples.note: « Fac » stays informal; « métro » has become neutral.

examples.french: Dans sa lettre de motivation, elle a écrit « baccalauréat » et non « bac ».
examples.english: In her cover letter, she wrote “baccalauréat” and not “bac”.
examples.note: Formal writing restores the full form.

mistakes.avoid: Je joins une copie de mon bac à ma candidature.
mistakes.prefer: Je joins une copie de mon baccalauréat à ma candidature.
mistakes.why: A formal application requires the complete noun rather than the clipped form.

mistakes.avoid: Elle a passé l’été dans un colo près du lac.
mistakes.prefer: Elle a passé l’été dans une colo près du lac.
mistakes.why: The clipped form keeps the feminine gender of `une colonie de vacances`.

vocabulary.example: Un ado ou une ado peut participer à cet échange scolaire.
vocabulary.note: Clipped form of `un adolescent`; both genders exist.

vocabulary.example: Le bac marque la fin des études secondaires en France.
vocabulary.note: Clipped form of `le baccalauréat`; write the full word in formal contexts.

vocabulary.example: Une colo accueille les enfants pendant les vacances d’été.
vocabulary.note: Clipped form of `une colonie de vacances`; a language stay is `un séjour linguistique`.

vocabulary.example: Un dico bilingue reste utile pour vérifier un sens rapidement.
vocabulary.note: Clipped form of `un dictionnaire`.

practice.prompt: Rewrite formally: « J’ai fait la fac, puis j’ai travaillé dans une colo. »
practice.hint: Restore both complete nouns.
practice.answer: J’ai étudié à la faculté, puis j’ai travaillé dans une colonie de vacances.

takeaways: A clipped noun keeps the gender of the full word.
Speech accepts them; formal writing restores the full form.
`Métro` and `photo` are the neutral exceptions.

lessons.title: Les jours, les dates, les saisons et les tarifs
lessons.summary: A definite article before a weekday makes it habitual: `Le vendredi, je travaille` means every Friday, while `Vendredi, je travaille` refers to one specific Friday. A full date takes `le` and a cardinal number, except the first of the month: `le 5 mars`, but `le 1er mars`. Seasons take `en hiver`, `en été`, `en automne`, but `au printemps`. A definite article also expresses a rate: `trois dollars le kilo`.
objectives: Distinguish a habitual day from a specific one.
Write a full date with the right number form.
Use the correct preposition for each season.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: The definite article turns a time word into a recurring reference. `Le vendredi` means every Friday, `le matin` means in the mornings, `le week-end` means at weekends. Without the article, the weekday points to one identified day, usually the nearest one: `Vendredi, je vais au centre de services`. Days and months are written in lowercase in French.

Dates use `le` plus a cardinal number plus the month: `le 5 mars`, `le 12 septembre`. Only the first day of the month uses an ordinal: `le 1er mars`. Seasons take `en` except spring, which takes `au`: `en hiver`, `en été`, `en automne`, but `au printemps`. The same definite article expresses a unit price, where English uses per: `trois dollars le kilo`, `deux dollars la pièce`, `quinze dollars l’heure`.
points: Add `le` to a weekday for a habit and leave it out for one specific day.
Write days and months in lowercase.
Use `le` plus a cardinal number in a date, except `le 1er`.
Use `en hiver`, `en été`, `en automne`, but `au printemps`.
Use `le`, `la`, or `l’` before the unit to express a rate.

examples.french: Le vendredi, je suis un atelier de conversation à la bibliothèque.
examples.english: On Fridays, I attend a conversation workshop at the library.
examples.note: The article marks a weekly habit.

examples.french: Mardi, je vais au centre de services pour renouveler mon permis.
examples.english: On Tuesday, I am going to the service centre to renew my permit.
examples.note: No article: one specific day.

examples.french: L’atelier reprendra le mardi 5 mars et se terminera le 1er juin.
examples.english: The workshop will resume on Tuesday, March 5 and will end on June 1.
examples.note: Cardinal numbers in dates, except « 1er ».

examples.french: En hiver, je fais du ski de fond ; au printemps, je marche dans le parc.
examples.english: In winter, I go cross-country skiing; in spring, I walk in the park.
examples.note: « En » for three seasons, « au » for spring.

examples.french: Les pommes coûtent trois dollars le kilo et le stationnement coûte deux dollars l’heure.
examples.english: Apples cost three dollars per kilo and parking costs two dollars per hour.
examples.note: The definite article expresses a rate.

mistakes.avoid: En printemps, la ville organise un grand nettoyage.
mistakes.prefer: Au printemps, la ville organise un grand nettoyage.
mistakes.why: Spring is the one season that takes `au` instead of `en`.

mistakes.avoid: La réunion aura lieu le premier mars, Lundi prochain.
mistakes.prefer: La réunion aura lieu le 1er mars, lundi prochain.
mistakes.why: Only the first of the month uses an ordinal, and weekdays are written in lowercase.

vocabulary.example: Le vendredi, notre groupe se retrouve à la médiathèque.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; with the article it expresses a weekly habit.

vocabulary.example: Le printemps arrive tard dans cette région.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; the only season introduced by `au`.

vocabulary.example: L’hiver apporte souvent de la neige dès novembre.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; used with `en hiver`.

vocabulary.example: Un atelier de conversation a lieu chaque vendredi soir.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; also means a craft workshop.

vocabulary.example: Le stationnement est gratuit après dix-huit heures.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun used in Canada; `le parking` is used in France.

practice.prompt: Say in French: I work on Saturdays, the course starts on 1 September, and it costs twenty dollars an hour.
practice.hint: Habit, date with an ordinal, and a rate.
practice.answer: Le samedi, je travaille ; le cours commence le 1er septembre et il coûte vingt dollars l’heure.

takeaways: `Le vendredi` recurs; `vendredi` is one day.
Dates use cardinals, except `le 1er`.
`En hiver`, `en été`, `en automne`, but `au printemps`.

lessons.title: La différence entre « la part » et « une partie »
lessons.summary: `La part` is someone’s share, allocation, or contribution, and appears in the fixed expressions `faire sa part`, `prendre part à`, and `de la part de`. `Une partie` is a section of a whole, a game or match, or one side in a dispute. English part covers both, so the choice must be made on meaning rather than on translation.
objectives: Choose `la part` when a share is distributed or contributed.
Choose `une partie` for a section of a whole.
Use the frequent fixed expressions built on `part`.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: `La part` refers to what is allotted to someone: a share of work, of food, of responsibility, or of a payment. It is the word used whenever something is divided among people: `Chacun doit faire sa part`, `la part du gâteau`, `la part des dépenses`. Three fixed expressions are worth memorising: `faire sa part` (to do one’s share), `prendre part à` (to take part in), and `de la part de` (on behalf of, from).

`Une partie` refers to a section of something, not to a distribution among people: `la deuxième partie du rapport`, `une partie du quartier`, `une partie des candidats`. It also names a game or a match (`une partie de cartes`) and, in legal or negotiation contexts, one side (`les parties en présence`). If you can replace the word with portion allotted to someone, use `part`; if you can replace it with section, use `partie`.
points: Use `la part` whenever something is divided among people.
Use `une partie` for a section, a chapter, or a proportion.
Learn `faire sa part`, `prendre part à`, and `de la part de` as blocks.
Use `une partie` for a game and for a side in a negotiation.
Test the word by substituting share or section in English.

examples.french: Chacun doit faire sa part du travail dans le projet collectif.
examples.english: Everyone must do their share of the work in the group project.
examples.note: A distribution among people.

examples.french: Dans la deuxième partie du rapport, l’autrice propose trois solutions.
examples.english: In the second part of the report, the author proposes three solutions.
examples.note: A section of a whole.

examples.french: Une partie des candidats a déjà reçu une réponse écrite.
examples.english: Some of the candidates have already received a written answer.
examples.note: A proportion of a group.

examples.french: Je vous appelle de la part de la conseillère en emploi.
examples.english: I am calling on behalf of the employment adviser.
examples.note: Fixed expression « de la part de ».

examples.french: Plus de deux cents personnes ont pris part à la consultation.
examples.english: More than two hundred people took part in the consultation.
examples.note: Fixed expression « prendre part à ».

mistakes.avoid: Chacun doit faire sa partie du travail.
mistakes.prefer: Chacun doit faire sa part du travail.
mistakes.why: A share allotted to a person is `la part`, not `la partie`.

mistakes.avoid: Dans la deuxième part du rapport, l’auteur conclut.
mistakes.prefer: Dans la deuxième partie du rapport, l’auteur conclut.
mistakes.why: A section of a text is `une partie`.

vocabulary.example: La part de chacun dépend de sa contribution au projet.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; used when something is divided among people.

vocabulary.example: Une partie du rapport doit encore être corrigée.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; used for a section, a proportion, or a match.

vocabulary.example: Je vous transmets ce document de la part du service des permis.
vocabulary.note: Fixed expression; the article contracts after `de`.

vocabulary.example: Une contribution équitable facilite le travail d’équipe.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; the ending -tion is a feminine hint.

practice.prompt: Choose the word: « Il a lu la première ___ du dossier, puis il a payé sa ___ des frais. »
practice.hint: Section first, then a share.
practice.answer: Il a lu la première partie du dossier, puis il a payé sa part des frais.

takeaways: Divided among people equals `la part`.
Section, proportion, or match equals `une partie`.
`Faire sa part`, `prendre part à`, `de la part de` are fixed.
keywords: distinguishing a share from a section

modules.title: Les compétences pour l’examen et pour l’écrit
modules.description: Organise formal requests, personal narratives, applications, and effective arguments.

lessons.title: La cohésion et le registre formel
lessons.summary: A formal French text keeps the full negation with `ne`, avoids clipped and conversational forms, and links its ideas with explicit connectors rather than repeated `et`. The standard courteous request is `Je vous prie de bien vouloir` plus an infinitive. A letter opens by stating its purpose, develops one idea per paragraph, and closes with a clear request and a set formula.
objectives: Open a formal message by naming its purpose and its context.
Link ideas with connectors of cause, consequence, and contrast.
Close with a conventional request and politeness formula.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: Cohesion is the set of links that make a text easy to follow; register is the level of formality chosen for the reader. In formal French, three things change at once: the negation keeps `ne` (`je ne peux pas` and never `je peux pas`), clipped nouns give way to full words, and connectors become explicit. Useful connectors are `en effet` and `car` for cause, `par conséquent` and `c’est pourquoi` for consequence, `cependant` and `toutefois` for contrast, `en outre` and `par ailleurs` for addition.

A formal request follows a predictable shape. The opening names the purpose and the reference: `Je vous écris au sujet de l’offre publiée le 3 mars`. The body gives one reason per paragraph, with evidence. The closing states exactly what you are asking for, using `Je vous prie de bien vouloir` plus an infinitive, and ends with a formula such as `Je vous prie d’agréer, Madame, Monsieur, mes salutations distinguées`. Note that `bien vouloir` is more courteous than `vouloir bien`, which sounds like an order.
points: State the purpose and the reference in the first sentence.
Keep `ne` in every negation and avoid clipped nouns.
Use one connector per logical link instead of repeating `et`.
Formulate the request with `Je vous prie de bien vouloir` plus an infinitive.
Proofread articles, agreements, accents, and verb complements before sending.
Prefer `effectuer` or `réaliser` to `faire` when the register is formal, and describe a text as `soigné` rather than `propre`.

examples.french: Je vous écris au sujet de l’offre publiée le 3 mars afin de vous soumettre ma candidature.
examples.english: I am writing regarding the position advertised on 3 March in order to submit my application.
examples.note: Opening that states purpose and reference.

examples.french: Je vous prie de bien vouloir examiner ma candidature.
examples.english: I would be grateful if you would consider my application.
examples.note: Standard courteous request formula.

examples.french: Mon dossier était incomplet ; par conséquent, je vous transmets aujourd’hui les pièces manquantes.
examples.english: My file was incomplete; consequently, I am sending you the missing documents today.
examples.note: Explicit consequence connector.

examples.french: Si cela était possible, j’aimerais également savoir quand les entretiens auraient lieu.
examples.english: If that were possible, I would also like to know when the interviews would take place.
examples.note: Conditional forms soften a second request.

examples.french: Je vous prie d’agréer, Madame, Monsieur, mes salutations distinguées.
examples.english: Yours faithfully.
examples.note: Conventional closing formula for a formal letter.

examples.french: Nous avons effectué les vérifications demandées et réalisé une nouvelle estimation.
examples.english: We carried out the requested checks and produced a new estimate.
examples.note: « Effectuer » and « réaliser » replace « faire » in formal writing.

mistakes.avoid: Je peux pas venir le 12, mais je vous prie de bien vouloir examiner mon dossier.
mistakes.prefer: Je ne peux pas venir le 12, mais je vous prie de bien vouloir examiner mon dossier.
mistakes.why: Formal writing keeps `ne`; dropping it belongs to informal speech.

mistakes.avoid: Je veux bien que vous examinez mon dossier avant vendredi.
mistakes.prefer: Je veux bien que vous examiniez mon dossier avant vendredi.
mistakes.why: `Vouloir que` is a subjunctive trigger, so the verb is `examiniez`, not the indicative `examinez`; in a formal request, `Je vous prie de bien vouloir examiner` is better still.

mistakes.avoid: J’ai envoyé le dossier et il était incomplet et j’ai envoyé les pièces.
mistakes.prefer: J’ai envoyé le dossier, mais il était incomplet ; c’est pourquoi je vous transmets les pièces manquantes.
mistakes.why: Repeated `et` hides the logical relations, which explicit connectors make visible.

vocabulary.example: Une candidature complète doit inclure une lettre de motivation.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; `poser sa candidature` means to apply.

vocabulary.example: Une lettre de motivation d’une page suffit pour ce poste.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun phrase; the gender comes from `lettre`.

vocabulary.french: je vous prie de bien vouloir
vocabulary.english: I would be grateful if you would
vocabulary.example: Je vous prie de bien vouloir me confirmer la date de l’entretien.
vocabulary.note: Always followed by an infinitive; more courteous than `vouloir bien`.

vocabulary.example: Le délai est dépassé ; par conséquent, une nouvelle demande est nécessaire.
vocabulary.note: Formal connector of consequence; `donc` is its neutral equivalent.

vocabulary.example: Un entretien bien préparé permet de présenter ses compétences avec assurance.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun used in France; `une entrevue` is the Canadian equivalent.

vocabulary.example: Le service effectue une vérification avant chaque versement.
vocabulary.note: Formal equivalent of `faire` with a process or an operation.

vocabulary.example: Une lettre soignée fait une meilleure impression qu’un texte rapide.
vocabulary.note: Describes care and finish; `propre` means clean and `net` means clear-cut.

practice.prompt: Write the opening sentence of a formal message asking for an appointment about a housing application.
practice.hint: Name the purpose and the reference before making the request.
practice.answer: Je vous écris au sujet de ma demande de logement déposée le 12 février, afin de solliciter un rendez-vous avec un conseiller.

takeaways: Purpose first, one reason per paragraph, explicit request last.
Formal register keeps `ne` and full nouns.
`Je vous prie de bien vouloir` plus infinitive is the safe request.

lessons.title: La présentation d’une candidature
lessons.summary: French uses `postuler à un poste` or `poser sa candidature à un poste`; the verb `appliquer` never carries the English meaning of applying for a job. Present relevant experience with the compound past for completed achievements and the present for current skills. Reserve the conditional for a genuine hypothesis or for a polite closing request.
objectives: Use the correct French verbs for applying.
Name the position and match it with relevant experience.
Reserve the conditional for hypotheses and polite requests.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: Three expressions cover the act of applying: `postuler à un poste`, `poser sa candidature à un poste`, and `soumettre sa candidature`. `Appliquer` in French means to apply a rule, a coat of paint, or a method, so `J’applique pour ce poste` is a direct translation error. The related nouns are `une candidature` for the application, `un candidat` or `une candidate` for the applicant, and `une lettre de motivation` for the cover letter.

Tense choice conveys the message. Completed achievements take the compound past: `J’ai coordonné une équipe de six personnes`. Current skills and situations take the present: `Je travaille actuellement dans un organisme communautaire`. The conditional is not a politeness decoration to be used throughout; it belongs in a genuine hypothesis (`Si j’obtenais ce poste, je pourrais…`) and in a closing request (`Je serais disponible dès le 1er mai`). Stating that you lack experience in a counterfactual is grammatically correct but rhetorically weak in an actual application.
points: Say `postuler à` or `poser sa candidature à`, never `appliquer`.
Name the exact position and where you saw it advertised.
Use the compound past for achievements and the present for current skills.
Keep the conditional for a real hypothesis or a closing request.
Match every claim with a concrete example rather than an adjective.

examples.french: J’ai posé ma candidature à ce poste de coordonnateur la semaine dernière.
examples.english: I applied for this coordinator position last week.
examples.note: Completed action in the compound past.

examples.french: Je travaille actuellement dans un organisme communautaire et je coordonne trois bénévoles.
examples.english: I currently work for a community organisation and I coordinate three volunteers.
examples.note: Present tense for a current situation.

examples.french: Mon expérience en milieu associatif correspond au profil recherché dans votre annonce.
examples.english: My experience in the non-profit sector matches the profile described in your advertisement.
examples.note: A claim linked directly to the advertisement.

examples.french: Si j’obtenais ce poste, je pourrais mettre en place un suivi bilingue des dossiers.
examples.english: If I obtained this position, I could set up bilingual case follow-up.
examples.note: The conditional used for a genuine hypothesis.

examples.french: Je serais disponible pour un entretien à partir du 1er mai.
examples.english: I would be available for an interview from 1 May.
examples.note: Conditional in a polite closing statement.

mistakes.avoid: J’applique pour ce poste depuis la semaine dernière.
mistakes.prefer: Je postule à ce poste depuis la semaine dernière.
mistakes.why: `Appliquer` does not mean to apply for a job; French uses `postuler à` or `poser sa candidature`.

mistakes.avoid: J’ai postulé ce poste la semaine dernière.
mistakes.prefer: J’ai postulé à ce poste la semaine dernière.
mistakes.why: `Postuler` is followed by `à` before the position; it never takes a direct object.

vocabulary.example: Je postule à ce poste de coordonnateur bilingue.
vocabulary.note: Takes `à`; `postuler pour` also occurs but `à` is the safest form.

vocabulary.example: Elle a posé sa candidature à trois offres publiées cette semaine.
vocabulary.note: Followed by `à` or `pour` plus the position.

vocabulary.example: Un poste à temps plein a été affiché sur le site de la ville.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; `une poste` means the postal service.

vocabulary.example: Une annonce détaillée précise les compétences attendues.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; `une offre d’emploi` is the fuller term.

vocabulary.example: Une compétence en gestion de projet est demandée pour ce poste.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; usually plural when listing skills.

practice.prompt: Write one sentence naming the position you are applying for and one relevant piece of experience.
practice.hint: Use `postuler à` or `poser sa candidature` and the compound past.
practice.answer: Je pose ma candidature au poste d’agent d’accueil, car j’ai travaillé deux ans dans un centre de services aux nouveaux arrivants.

takeaways: `Postuler à` and `poser sa candidature`, never `appliquer`.
Compound past for achievements, present for current skills.
The conditional is for hypotheses and closing requests only.

lessons.title: Construire une argumentation efficace
lessons.summary: An argued answer states a clear position, supports it with reasons and concrete evidence, acknowledges a limitation where that strengthens the case, and closes with a proportionate recommendation. Position markers include `Selon moi`, `À mon avis`, `Il me semble que`. Evidence markers include `par exemple`, `en effet`, `d’après`. Concession and conclusion use `certes… mais`, `en revanche`, `en conclusion`. Three cleft structures put the weight where you want it: `Ce que… c’est…` for an object, `Ce qui… c’est…` for a subject, and `C’est… qui/que…` for one isolated phrase.
objectives: State a defensible position that answers the exact question.
Support each reason with a concrete example or consequence.
Focus a sentence with the three cleft structures.
Close with a recommendation and its expected result.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: Structured argumentation has four moves: claim, support, concession, conclusion. The claim answers the exact question asked and takes a side: `Selon moi, la ville devrait investir davantage dans le transport en commun`. The support gives one reason per paragraph, each attached to something concrete: a figure, an example, a consequence. Vague praise is not support.

The concession acknowledges a genuine objection and then answers it, which makes the argument stronger rather than weaker: `Certes, ces travaux coûtent cher, mais ils réduisent les dépenses de santé à long terme`. The conclusion restates the position in different words and proposes a proportionate action: `Il faudrait donc étendre le réseau progressivement`. Several of these frames trigger the subjunctive, notably `il est important que`, `il faudrait que`, and `afin que`.

Three cleft structures let you focus a sentence. `Ce que… c’est…` uses `ce que` as the following verb’s object: `Ce que j’apprécie le plus dans ce quartier, c’est la proximité des commerces`. `Ce qui… c’est…` uses `ce qui` as its subject: `Ce qui me préoccupe, c’est le coût du logement`. `C’est… qui…` and `C’est… que…` isolate a phrase: `C’est la bibliothèque qui a transformé le quartier`. Choose the relative pronoun by its grammatical function. When listing several benefits, parallel noun phrases can make the sentence easier to follow; that is a clarity recommendation, not a ban on every combination of different structures.

Environmental and public-service topics recur often, and precise words help. Clean air is `l’air pur` (masculine); air quality is `la qualité de l’air` (feminine). `L’eau potable` means drinking water, whereas `l’eau claire` describes clear water without guaranteeing that it is safe to drink. Useful frames include `À mon avis, il est nécessaire de…`, `Si l’air est trop pollué, les gens peuvent tomber malades`, and `De nos jours, le transport en commun réduit la pollution`, each stating a position or a consequence.
points: Answer the exact question in the first sentence, taking a side.
Develop one reason per paragraph or speaking segment.
Attach every reason to an example, a figure, or a consequence.
Use `certes… mais` to concede and answer an objection.
Close with a recommendation proportionate to the argument.
Describe a trend with `grimper`, `augmenter`, `baisser`, or `diminuer` before drawing a conclusion from it.
Focus an object with `Ce que… c’est…` and a subject with `Ce qui… c’est…`.
Isolate one phrase with `C’est… qui…` for a subject and `C’est… que…` for anything else.
Prefer parallel phrases when listing benefits after c’est, for ease of reading.
Write `l’air pur` for clean air and `l’eau potable` for drinking water.

examples.french: Selon moi, la ville devrait investir davantage dans le transport en commun.
examples.english: In my view, the city should invest more in public transit.
examples.note: A clear position stated at the outset.

examples.french: En effet, un réseau plus fréquent réduirait la circulation et la pollution de l’air.
examples.english: Indeed, a more frequent network would reduce traffic and air pollution.
examples.note: A reason attached to a concrete consequence.

examples.french: Par exemple, le quartier voisin a vu sa fréquentation augmenter de trente pour cent.
examples.english: For example, the neighbouring district saw its ridership increase by thirty per cent.
examples.note: Concrete evidence supporting the reason.

examples.french: Certes, ces travaux coûtent cher, mais ils réduisent les dépenses de santé à long terme.
examples.english: Admittedly, this work is expensive, but it reduces health spending in the long run.
examples.note: Concession followed by an answer.

examples.french: Il est important que les nouveaux arrivants se sentent les bienvenus dans leur quartier.
examples.english: It is important that newcomers feel welcome in their neighbourhood.
examples.note: The impersonal frame triggers the subjunctive.

examples.french: En conclusion, il faudrait étendre le réseau progressivement afin que chaque quartier en bénéficie.
examples.english: In conclusion, the network should be extended gradually so that every neighbourhood benefits.
examples.note: Recommendation plus purpose clause in the subjunctive.

examples.french: Ce que j’apprécie le plus dans ce quartier, c’est la proximité des commerces et des services publics.
examples.english: What I appreciate most in this neighbourhood is how close the shops and public services are.
examples.note: « Ce que » because the focused element is the object of « apprécier ».

examples.french: Ce qui me préoccupe, c’est le coût du logement pour les jeunes familles.
examples.english: What worries me is the cost of housing for young families.
examples.note: « Ce qui » because the focused element is the subject of « préoccuper ».

examples.french: C’est la bibliothèque municipale qui a transformé la vie du quartier.
examples.english: It is the municipal library that transformed life in the neighbourhood.
examples.note: « C’est… qui » isolates and highlights the subject.

examples.french: À mon avis, il est nécessaire de protéger l’air pur et de garantir l’eau potable à tous les quartiers.
examples.english: In my view, it is necessary to protect clean air and to guarantee drinking water for every neighbourhood.
examples.note: « L’air pur » for clean air and « l’eau potable » for drinking water.

mistakes.avoid: Je pense que ce soit une bonne mesure pour le quartier.
mistakes.prefer: Je pense que c’est une bonne mesure pour le quartier.
mistakes.why: Affirmative `penser que` presents the idea as true and takes the indicative; only the negative or interrogative form takes the subjunctive.

mistakes.avoid: Il est important que la ville investit davantage dans les transports.
mistakes.prefer: Il est important que la ville investisse davantage dans les transports.
mistakes.why: `Il est important que` is a subjunctive trigger.

mistakes.avoid: Ce qui j’aime dans ce quartier, c’est le calme.
mistakes.prefer: Ce que j’aime dans ce quartier, c’est le calme.
mistakes.why: The focused element is the object of `aimer`, so the cleft opens with `ce que`; `ce qui` is reserved for a subject.

mistakes.avoid: C’est la bibliothèque que a transformé la vie du quartier.
mistakes.prefer: C’est la bibliothèque qui a transformé la vie du quartier.
mistakes.why: The relative pronoun is the subject of `a transformé`, so use `qui`, not `que`.

mistakes.avoid: La ville doit garantir un air pure et une eau potables à tous les résidents.
mistakes.prefer: La ville doit garantir un air pur et une eau potable à tous les résidents.
mistakes.why: `Air` is masculine singular, so use `pur`; `eau` is feminine singular, so use `potable` without a plural s.

vocabulary.example: Un enjeu environnemental majeur mérite une réponse collective.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; stronger than `un problème` in argued writing.

vocabulary.example: La santé mentale des salariés dépend aussi de bonnes conditions de travail.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun phrase; the gender comes from `santé`.

vocabulary.example: Certes, la mesure est coûteuse, mais elle bénéficie à tout le quartier.
vocabulary.note: Concession frame; the objection comes first, the answer second.

vocabulary.example: Le centre-ville est bien desservi ; en revanche, la périphérie reste isolée.
vocabulary.note: Formal contrast connector; `par contre` is more familiar.

vocabulary.example: Un immigrant récemment arrivé cherche souvent un logement près de son travail.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun used in Canada; feminine `une immigrante`.

vocabulary.example: Les loyers ont grimpé de douze pour cent en deux ans.
vocabulary.note: Used for a steep rise in figures; `augmenter` is the neutral verb.

vocabulary.example: Le nombre de demandes en attente a baissé depuis la réforme.
vocabulary.note: Intransitive for a fall; transitive in `baisser les prix`.

vocabulary.example: Un quartier solidaire organise des collectes pour les familles touchées.
vocabulary.note: Same form in both genders; `la solidarité` is the related noun.

vocabulary.example: Une émeute a été évitée grâce à la médiation des associations locales.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; frequent in news reports and argued texts.

vocabulary.example: Ce qui manque dans ce secteur, c’est une clinique sans rendez-vous.
vocabulary.note: Use `ce que… c’est` instead when the focused element is an object.

vocabulary.example: L’air pur reste un enjeu de santé publique dans les grandes villes.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; `l’air clair` would describe brightness, not cleanliness.

vocabulary.example: L’eau potable doit être accessible dans chaque logement locatif.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun phrase; `l’eau claire` only describes transparency.

vocabulary.example: Un commerce de quartier attire les résidents et crée des emplois locaux.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; `le commerce` can name trade in general, while `un commerce` can name a shop or business.

practice.prompt: Write a claim and one supported reason on whether French classes should be free for newcomers.
practice.hint: State the side first, then attach a concrete consequence.
practice.answer: Selon moi, les cours de français devraient rester gratuits pour les nouveaux arrivants. En effet, une meilleure maîtrise de la langue accélère l’accès à l’emploi et réduit l’isolement.

takeaways: Claim, support, concession, conclusion.
Every reason needs a concrete example or consequence.
`Il est important que` and `afin que` take the subjunctive.
`Ce qui` focuses a subject, `ce que` an object, `c’est… qui/que` one phrase.
Clean air is `pur`, drinkable water is `potable`.

lessons.title: Le récit d’un déménagement et la description d’un quartier
lessons.summary: A personal narrative can use the compound past for the move, the imperfect for background conditions, and the present for the current assessment. `S’habituer à` describes adaptation; `y` can replace a known thing in `je m’y suis habitué`, without making alternatives such as `je me suis habitué à ça` wrong. Evaluations use `ce que j’aime le plus`, `ce qui manque`, and `il y a`.
objectives: Introduce the move as a completed event.
Describe the initial situation with the imperfect.
Evaluate the neighbourhood in the present with a clear structure.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: This narrative has a fixed shape that can be reused for any change of situation. First, the event: `J’ai déménagé à Montréal il y a quelques semaines`, in the compound past. Second, the background: `Au début, c’était difficile, je ne connaissais personne`, in the imperfect. Third, the adaptation: `mais je me suis habitué au quartier`, again in the compound past because it is a completed change of state.

The evaluation moves to the present and benefits from ready-made frames. `Ce que j’aime le plus ici, c’est que…` highlights a strength; `ce qui manque encore, c’est…` names a gap; `il y a` and `on trouve` list amenities. `S’habituer à` takes `à`, and a known thing can be replaced by `y`: `Je m’y suis habitué`. Keeping the complement is also grammatical: `Je me suis habitué à ça`. For a person, use a stressed pronoun: `Je me suis habitué à elle`.
points: Open with the completed move in the compound past.
Set the initial difficulty or context in the imperfect.
Mark the adaptation with `s’habituer à` in the compound past.
Use `y` to avoid repeating a known thing after `à`; replacement is optional.
Evaluate in the present with `ce que j’aime le plus, c’est que…`.
Describe the outside of a building with `une façade` and any wall, inside or out, with `un mur`.
Describe a neighbourhood with `animé`, `calme`, `étroit`, and name what disrupts it, such as `la circulation` or `une panne d’électricité`.

examples.french: J’ai déménagé à Montréal il y a quelques semaines pour me rapprocher de mon travail.
examples.english: I moved to Montreal a few weeks ago to be closer to my job.
examples.note: Completed event in the compound past.

examples.french: Au début, c’était difficile : je ne connaissais personne et le loyer était élevé.
examples.english: At first it was difficult: I did not know anyone and the rent was high.
examples.note: Initial conditions in the imperfect.

examples.french: Je me suis habitué au quartier, et maintenant je m’y sens chez moi.
examples.english: I got used to the neighbourhood, and now I feel at home there.
examples.note: Completed change of state, then « y » for a known place.

examples.french: Ce que j’aime le plus ici, c’est qu’il y a beaucoup de services de proximité.
examples.english: What I like most here is that there are many local services.
examples.note: Ready-made frame for a positive evaluation.

examples.french: Ce qui manque encore, c’est une garderie accessible près de la station de métro.
examples.english: What is still missing is an affordable daycare near the subway station.
examples.note: Ready-made frame for naming a gap.

examples.french: La façade de l’immeuble a été rénovée, mais les murs intérieurs restent à peindre.
examples.english: The front of the building has been renovated, but the interior walls still have to be painted.
examples.note: « Une façade » is the outward face of a building; « un mur » is any wall.

examples.french: Le quartier est animé le jour, mais les rues étroites et la circulation compliquent le stationnement.
examples.english: The neighbourhood is lively during the day, but the narrow streets and the traffic make parking difficult.
examples.note: Evaluation adjectives plus the noun naming the difficulty.

examples.french: Je vous écris au sujet d’une panne d’électricité qui a touché l’immeuble ainsi que les commerces voisins.
examples.english: I am writing about a power outage that affected the building as well as the neighbouring shops.
examples.note: « Au sujet de » opens a formal request; « ainsi que » adds a second element.

mistakes.avoid: Au début, c’étais difficile et je ne connaissait personne.
mistakes.prefer: Au début, c’était difficile et je ne connaissais personne.
mistakes.why: Use third-person `était` in c’était and first-person `connaissais` with je. The imperfect presents background; a compound past can instead present a bounded episode.

mistakes.avoid: Je me suis habitué le quartier rapidement.
mistakes.prefer: Je me suis habitué au quartier rapidement.
mistakes.why: `S’habituer` requires the preposition `à`, contracted here to `au`.

mistakes.avoid: Nous avons repeint les mur de la cuisine le mois dernier.
mistakes.prefer: Nous avons repeint les murs de la cuisine le mois dernier.
mistakes.why: After plural `les`, write the regular noun plural `murs`.

vocabulary.example: Elle s’est habituée à l’hiver canadien après deux saisons.
vocabulary.note: Takes à; y can replace a known thing, but keeping the complement is also grammatical.

vocabulary.example: Un quartier animé offre de nombreux commerces de proximité.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; `de proximité` means local or nearby.

vocabulary.example: Un commerce de proximité vient d’ouvrir près de la station de métro.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun phrase; the gender comes from `commerce`.

vocabulary.example: Un loyer raisonnable reste difficile à trouver dans ce secteur.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; `louer` is the related verb.

vocabulary.example: Un logement lumineux facilite l’installation de toute la famille.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun and the standard administrative term; the feeling of home is `un chez-soi`.

vocabulary.example: Un mur mitoyen sépare les deux logements.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; used for interior and exterior walls alike.

vocabulary.example: Une façade bien entretenue améliore l’image de tout le quartier.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; only the outward face of a building.

vocabulary.example: La circulation est dense sur ce boulevard aux heures de pointe.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; it also means circulation in a medical sense.

vocabulary.example: Un quai couvert protège les voyageurs pendant l’hiver.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; used for both a station platform and a waterfront.

vocabulary.example: La campagne est plus calme, mais les services y sont plus éloignés.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; `une campagne` also means a campaign.

vocabulary.example: Une panne d’électricité a duré trois heures dans tout le secteur.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun phrase; the gender comes from `panne`.

vocabulary.example: Une rue animée rassure les résidents le soir.
vocabulary.note: Describes a place full of activity; the opposite here is `calme`.

vocabulary.example: Une rue étroite complique le passage des camions de livraison.
vocabulary.note: Regular feminine in `-e`; the opposite is `large`.

vocabulary.example: Je vous écris au sujet du bruit nocturne dans notre immeuble.
vocabulary.note: Formal alternative to `à propos de` in written requests.

vocabulary.example: Le quartier compte deux écoles ainsi qu’une bibliothèque municipale.
vocabulary.note: Here ainsi que joins objects; compte agrees with the singular subject le quartier. When ainsi que joins subjects in an additive sense, the verb normally takes the plural.

practice.prompt: Write three sentences: the move, the initial difficulty, and what you like most now.
practice.hint: Compound past, imperfect, then the present with a fixed frame.
practice.answer: J’ai déménagé à Laval en janvier. Au début, c’était difficile parce que je ne connaissais pas les transports. Ce que j’aime le plus ici, c’est qu’il y a une bibliothèque et une clinique tout près.

takeaways: Move in the compound past, background in the imperfect, assessment in the present.
`S’habituer à` plus `y` for a known place.
`Ce que j’aime le plus, c’est que…` is reusable in any evaluation.
keywords: describing a move and a neighbourhood

modules.title: La stratégie d’apprentissage
modules.description: Use focused study methods to organise learning, retain vocabulary, and correct recurring errors.

lessons.title: Organiser une progression d’apprentissage
lessons.summary: Work in three stages. First secure the noun phrase: article, gender, agreement, and basic sentence order. Then build communication and narration: present, compound past, imperfect, questions, negation, and frequent connectors. Only then take on complex pronouns, the subjunctive, the conditional, and independent written production. Each stage should end with a task you can complete without support.
objectives: Sequence grammar so that each new point rests on a secured one.
Close every stage with an independent production task.
Recognise when a point is secure enough to move on.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: A learning sequence orders material so that each new skill depends only on knowledge already practised. Stage one secures the noun phrase, because articles, gender, and agreement affect every later sentence you write. Stage two adds the tenses of narration and the tools of interaction: questions, negation, object pronouns, and the connectors that link two clauses. Stage three covers what depends on the earlier stages: the subjunctive needs a trigger clause, the conditional needs the future stem, and argued writing needs all of it.

A point is secure when you can produce it without consulting the rule, in a sentence you have not seen before. That is why each stage should end with a short independent task: describe a place, narrate a move, argue a position. If the task cannot be completed, the gap is usually in the previous stage rather than in the current one.
points: Begin with articles, gender, and adjective agreement.
Add the present, the compound past, and the imperfect before anything else.
Bring in questions, negation, and object pronouns for interaction.
Reserve the subjunctive and the conditional for stage three.
Test each stage with a short production task done without notes.

examples.french: Je maîtrise d’abord les articles, puis je les réemploie dans une argumentation complète.
examples.english: I first master the articles, then reuse them in a full argument.
examples.note: Each stage feeds the next.

examples.french: Après chaque notion, je réalise une activité guidée puis une tâche autonome.
examples.english: After each concept, I complete a guided activity and then an independent task.
examples.note: Support is gradually withdrawn.

examples.french: Cette semaine, je révise le passé composé ; la semaine prochaine, je raconterai mon installation.
examples.english: This week I revise the compound past; next week I will narrate my arrival.
examples.note: A rule is followed by a real production task.

examples.french: Si je ne peux pas écrire la tâche sans notes, je reviens à l’étape précédente.
examples.english: If I cannot write the task without notes, I go back to the previous stage.
examples.note: A concrete criterion for deciding when to move on.

mistakes.avoid: J’étudie le subjonctif avant de savoir former le présent des verbes irréguliers.
mistakes.prefer: Je sécurise le présent des verbes irréguliers, puis j’aborde le subjonctif.
mistakes.why: The present subjunctive is built on the present `ils` form, so that form must be secure first.

mistakes.avoid: Je lis la règle trois fois et je passe à la notion suivante.
mistakes.prefer: J’écris deux phrases nouvelles sans notes, puis je passe à la notion suivante.
mistakes.why: Reading again measures familiarity; independent production measures mastery.

vocabulary.example: Un apprentissage progressif relie chaque nouvelle notion aux acquis précédents.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; the ending -age is a masculine hint.

vocabulary.example: Une progression cohérente mène des bases grammaticales à la production autonome.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; the ending -ion is a feminine hint.

vocabulary.example: Une tâche autonome révèle immédiatement les points encore fragiles.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; distinct from `un travail`, which is broader.

vocabulary.example: Je maîtrise maintenant l’accord des adjectifs dans mes textes.
vocabulary.note: Regular `-er` verb; `la maîtrise` is the related noun.

practice.prompt: Name the three stages of your own sequence and the task that will close the second one.
practice.hint: Noun phrase, narration and interaction, then complex forms.
practice.answer: D’abord les articles et les accords, ensuite les temps du récit et les pronoms, enfin le subjonctif ; la deuxième étape se terminera par le récit écrit de mon installation.

takeaways: Noun phrase first, narration second, complex moods last.
Each stage closes with an unaided production task.
A failed task usually points to the previous stage.

lessons.title: Mémoriser les noms avec leur déterminant
lessons.summary: Store every French common noun as a complete group: determiner, noun, and an explicit gender or number marker. Use `un` or `une` for a countable noun, a definite article for a concept or a mass noun where that is the natural form, and record plural-only nouns as such. When the gender is uncertain, mark it as uncertain and check it rather than guessing.
objectives: Record a noun in the form you will actually use in a sentence.
Choose the article that matches the noun type.
Handle uncertain genders without guessing.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: A vocabulary card should store the noun as it appears in real sentences: determiner plus noun plus a gender marker such as `(m.)` or `(f.)`. Storing `stratégie` alone leaves two decisions unmade every time you use it, and both of them propagate: the article, and every adjective or participle that agrees with it. Storing `une stratégie (f.)` settles them once.

Choose the determiner by noun type. A countable noun takes `un` or `une`: `un dossier (m.)`, `une demande (f.)`. A concept or a mass noun is more naturally stored with a definite article: `le chômage (m.)`, `la santé (f.)`. A noun that exists only in the plural is stored that way: `les frais (m. pl.)`, `les céréales (f. pl.)`. When you genuinely do not know the gender, write the card with a question mark and verify it before reusing the word, because a guessed gender that is practised becomes a habit.
points: Write the determiner and the gender marker on the card itself.
Use `un` or `une` for a countable noun.
Use `le`, `la`, or `l’` for a concept or a mass noun.
Record plural-only nouns with `(m. pl.)` or `(f. pl.)`.
Flag an uncertain gender and verify it before reuse.

examples.french: J’ai adopté une stratégie de révision simple et régulière.
examples.english: I have adopted a simple, regular revision strategy.
examples.note: The card `une stratégie (f.)` produces the article and the agreement directly.

examples.french: Un argument illustré par un exemple convainc davantage le lecteur.
examples.english: An argument illustrated by an example is more convincing to the reader.
examples.note: Countable noun stored with « un ».

examples.french: Le chômage des jeunes diminue lentement dans cette région.
examples.english: Youth unemployment is slowly decreasing in this region.
examples.note: A concept stored with the definite article.

examples.french: Des frais de dossier s’appliquent après la date limite.
examples.english: File processing fees apply after the deadline.
examples.note: A plural-only noun, stored as « les frais (m. pl.) ».

mistakes.avoid: Je note « stratégie » dans mon carnet et je choisis l’article au moment d’écrire.
mistakes.prefer: Je note « une stratégie (f.) » et je réutilise le groupe complet.
mistakes.why: Deciding the article each time reproduces the same hesitation and the same agreement errors.

mistakes.avoid: Je devine le genre d’un mot nouveau et je l’emploie immédiatement.
mistakes.prefer: Je marque le genre comme incertain, je le vérifie, puis je l’emploie.
mistakes.why: A guessed gender that is practised becomes a habit that is hard to correct later.

vocabulary.example: Une stratégie de révision espacée améliore la mémorisation à long terme.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; stored with its article on the card.

vocabulary.example: Un exemple concret rend un argument beaucoup plus convaincant.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; `par exemple` is the fixed adverbial phrase.

vocabulary.example: Le chômage recule lentement dans les grandes villes.
vocabulary.note: Masculine mass noun; naturally stored with the definite article.

vocabulary.example: Une fiche complète comprend le déterminant, le nom et le genre.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; `une fiche de vocabulaire` is a vocabulary card.

practice.prompt: Write vocabulary cards for `travail`, `santé`, and `frais` in the required format.
practice.hint: Countable, mass noun, plural-only.
practice.answer: un travail (m.), la santé (f.), les frais (m. pl.)

takeaways: Determiner, noun, gender marker: one card, no decisions left open.
Countable takes `un`/`une`; a concept takes the definite article.
Never practise a guessed gender.

lessons.title: La récupération active et la révision espacée
lessons.summary: Active recall means retrieving an answer before seeing it; rereading is not recall. Spaced review schedules the next attempt after a delay that grows as the item becomes secure: the next day, then three days later, then a week, then a month. Difficult items come back sooner. Alternate the three modes: recognise, produce, and correct.
objectives: Retrieve before checking, on every item.
Space the intervals according to how secure the item is.
Alternate recognition, production, and correction.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: Active recall is the act of producing an answer from memory before any prompt is revealed. Rereading a card feels productive because the content becomes familiar, but familiarity is not retrieval: the test is whether you can restate the rule and build a new sentence with the card hidden.

Spaced review decides when the next attempt happens. A simple and effective schedule is the next day, then after three days, then a week, then a month, lengthening whenever the recall was easy and shortening whenever it failed. Combine this with three different modes so that the knowledge is usable in every direction: recognising the form in a text, producing it in a sentence of your own, and correcting a sentence that contains a deliberate error.
points: Hide the answer, restate the rule aloud, then check.
Write one new sentence rather than repeating the example on the card.
Lengthen the interval after an easy recall and shorten it after a failure.
Return difficult items the following day.
Alternate recognition, production, and correction across sessions.

examples.french: Je ferme la fiche, puis je reformule la règle avec mes propres mots.
examples.english: I close the card, then restate the rule in my own words.
